It improves controllability across two VLAs, analyzes transferability as tasks diverge, and reveals that behavioral features are decodable but not linearly steerable, motivating the distribution-centric approach.
AI.motivation: To achieve fine-grained, interpretable control of robotic manipulation policies that rely on flow-matching VLA models, addressing the limitation that linear steering methods fail to capture how internal representations govern behavior.
AI.method: Introduce Distribution-Matching Steering (DiMaS) that transports between distributions of representations associated with different behaviors, instead of applying a fixed directional shift. Apply DiMaS to two state-of-the-art flow-matching VLA models and evaluate across task pairs with increasing dissimilarity. Analyze the transferability of behavior control and investigate the representation structure to explain why linear steering falls short.
AI.result: DiMaS effectively controls behavior across two state-of-the-art flow-matching VLAs. The strategy generalizes to tasks with increasing dissimilarity, with identified regimes where control transfers well and where it weakens. The analysis of the action-expert representations shows features are linearly decodable but not linearly steerable, clarifying the need for distribution-based steering.
AI.conclusion: Distribution-matching steering is a viable and general approach for fine-grained behavioral control in VLA-based robotic policies, addressing limitations of linear steering and offering insights into representation geometry and transferability; code and supplementary results are publicly available.

title: How Much of a 10-K Matters? Aggregation-Dependent Value of Full-Text versus Risk-Factor Sentiment
summary: Financial sentiment extraction has largely relied on news text and supervised extraction against return labels alone, leaving 10-K filings -- and volatility, the target risk disclosure is arguably best suited to informing -- comparatively unexplored. We extend a supervised lexicon-learning approach to 10-K filings and their Item 1A risk-factor sections, training sentiment scores against both return and volatility labels at three levels of aggregation: sector, portfolio, and individual firm. Across 1,383 filings from 94 Nasdaq-100 technology constituents (2006--2023), we evaluate the resulting twelve sentiment metrics on classification accuracy, correlation with realised market outcomes, and qualitative lexical content. Full-filing text produces more accurate sentiment at the sector and portfolio level for both targets, but this reverses at the individual-firm level, where the narrower Item 1A section performs better -- an effect we attribute to the interaction between document volume and the amount of independent training signal available at each level of aggregation. A Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline is consistently, strongly negatively correlated with price at every level tested, underscoring the value of a supervised approach for regulatory disclosure text. These findings, and the design choices they motivate, establish the sentiment-generation methodology underlying a subsequent, larger-scale, multi-source system.

AI.tldr: A supervised lexicon-learning approach is extended to 10-K risk-factor sections, evaluating sentiment against return and volatility across sector, portfolio, and firm levels. Full filings excel at macro levels; Item 1A shines at the individual-firm level due to data-volume dynamics. The Loughran-McDonald baseline shows consistent negative price correlation. This supports building a larger multi-source sentiment system for regulatory disclosure text.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where sentiment in financial disclosures (10-Ks, especially Item 1A risk factors) has been underexplored compared to news text and return-focused supervision; assess whether supervised sentiment signals from regulatory text improve predictive alignment with returns and volatility.
AI.method: Train supervised sentiment scores using a lexicon-learning approach on 10-K filings and Item 1A risk-factor sections, with labels for both return and volatility. Evaluate twelve sentiment metrics across three aggregation levels (sector, portfolio, firm) using 1,383 filings from 94 Nasdaq-100 tech constituents (2006–2023). Compare against Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline on accuracy, price correlation, and qualitative lexical content.
AI.result: Full-text filings yield higher sentiment accuracy at sector/portfolio levels for both return and volatility targets; at the individual firm level, the narrower Item 1A section performs better due to more independent training signal relative to document volume. The Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline is strongly negatively correlated with price across all levels. These results support the utility of supervised sentiment generation for regulatory disclosure and motivate a larger-scale, multi-source system.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that document scope (full filings vs. targeted sections) interacts with aggregation level to influence sentiment performance, and that supervised lexicon learning can capture informative signals in regulatory disclosures, guiding future larger-scale sentiment systems.

title: Human AI Construction of Bayesian Networks for Operational Decision Support -- A Virtual Survey Approach
summary: Bayesian Belief Networks (BBNs) are powerful tools for decision-making under uncertainty. However, building their structures and estimating parameters are difficult. Currently, researchers must choose between relying on expert judgement or using large datasets to learn the structure and parameters of the network. We propose a new methodology using Large Language Models to bridge the gap between expert opinion and data-driven learning. This approach uses a panel of AI agents to estimate probabilities based on specific personas and context. We then apply a trimmed-mean rule to remove noise from these responses. We develop a six step BBN framework and illustrate it to model customer intention to consult a doctor in an alternative healthcare system. The model reveals that while self efficacy appears to be a major factor, its actual causal impact is small. In contrast, subjective norms have a much stronger effect in modelling customers' intention. The most effective strategy is to improve both confidence and community norms simultaneously.

AI.tldr: LLM-based panel of AI agents bridges expert judgement and data-driven learning for Bayesian Belief Networks; uses trimmed-mean to reduce noise; six-step framework applied to customer intention to consult a doctor; finds self-efficacy has weak causal effect, subjective norms are strong; best strategy is to improve both confidence and norms.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in constructing BBNs where expert opinion and large datasets are both needed but difficult to integrate; propose an AI-agent ensemble to elicit probabilities from domain personas.
AI.method: Panel of AI agents with specific personas and contexts estimates probabilities; responses trimmed via trimmed-mean to reduce noise; six-step BBN framework implemented; applied to model customer intention in an alternative healthcare system.
AI.result: Findings indicate subjective norms exert a stronger causal impact on intention than self-efficacy; self-efficacy's apparent importance may be non-causal; a combined improvement in confidence and community norms yields the most effective strategy.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven, agent-based elicitation can bridge expert judgement and data-driven learning for BBNs; applicable to policy and decision-making contexts; trimming noise enhances robustness; results emphasize social norms over self-efficacy in this setting.

title: DCVC-MB: Neural B-Frame Video Compression using State Space Models
summary: In this paper we propose DCVC-Mamba (DCVC-MB), a neural video codec framework for B-frame coding. Our approach incorporates an IBP frame strategy for low-delay B-frame coding, a spatio-temporal fusion model based on state-space models for bidirectional temporal prediction, and an entropy-aware skipping mechanism that selectively omits coding certain latents to reduce entropy coding times. In addition to our model contributions we also implement two inference-time strategies that enhance compression performance. Experimental evaluation shows that DCVC-MB compares favorably to existing NVCs and traditional codecs. The method demonstrates BD-rate reductions of up to $8.98\%$ on average compared to prior neural video codecs, and improvements of up to $30.45\%$ and $1.81\%$ over the VTM-19.0-LDP and VTM-19.0-RA(Inter-GoP=16) benchmarks, respectively, contributing to advances in neural video compression.

AI.tldr: DCVC-MB is a neural video codec for B-frame coding with an IBP frame strategy, a spatio-temporal fusion model using state-space bidirectional prediction, and entropy-aware latent skipping, plus two inference-time optimizations; it achieves BD-rate reductions vs prior neural codecs and gains on VTM benchmarks.
AI.motivation: to improve neural video compression efficiency for low-delay B-frame coding and reduce entropy coding time while boosting overall performance.
AI.method: introduces an IBP frame strategy; a spatio-temporal fusion model based on state-space models for bidirectional temporal prediction; entropy-aware skipping of latents; two inference-time strategies to enhance compression.
AI.result: BD-rate reductions up to 8.98% on average versus prior neural video codecs; improvements of up to 30.45% over VTM-19.0-LDP and 1.81% over VTM-19.0-RA(Inter-GoP=16).
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates advances in neural video compression with competitive performance relative to existing neural codecs and traditional codecs.

title: Beyond Visual Grasping: Benchmarking Complex Grasping from Detection to Execution
summary: Robust robotic grasping remains a fundamental challenge for complex real-world applications. Recent advances in large-scale models demonstrate promising capabilities for reasoning in robotic tasks. However, existing benchmarks for grasping primarily focus on isolated, visual-based grasp pose detection, failing to capture the complexity of grasping tasks that require multi-step reasoning and semantic understanding during execution. To address this gap, we propose GCA-Bench, a benchmark featuring challenging \textit{grasping with complex action} scenarios that involve both scene-level reasoning and semantic constraints. GCA-Bench enables the evaluation of recent large foundation models under the same settings. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our new benchmark, we implement a diverse set of baselines, ranging from traditional grasp detection pipelines to end-to-end learning methods. Empirical studies achieve success rates below 70\% on complex grasping scenarios, underscoring critical limitations. In addition, we propose new evaluation metrics, analyze critical failure models, and provide insights to guide the development of more robust and generalizable grasping strategies.

AI.tldr: Introduces GCA-Bench, a grasping benchmark with complex action requiring scene-level reasoning and semantic constraints; evaluates foundation models; reports sub-70% success; offers new metrics and failure analysis to guide robust grasping strategies.
AI.motivation: Current grasping benchmarks emphasize isolated, vision-based grasp pose detection and neglect multi-step reasoning and semantics in real tasks; a benchmark is needed to evaluate reasoning-enabled models and guide robust, generalizable grasping.
AI.method: Define GCA-Bench with tasks that combine scene-level reasoning and semantic constraints; implement a diverse set of baselines spanning traditional grasp detectors to end-to-end learning; evaluate under consistent settings; propose new evaluation metrics; perform failure analysis.
AI.result: Empirical studies show success rates below 70% on complex grasping scenarios; identify critical failure modes; provide metrics and insights to guide development of robust strategies.
AI.conclusion: GCA-Bench enables evaluation of large foundation models for grasping with reasoning; results reveal gaps and guide future work toward robust, generalizable grasping strategies.

title: Low-Latency Relay Selection in NR-V2X Vehicular Communications via Graph Isomorphism Networks with Edge Features
summary: Reliable, low-latency uplink connectivity is a key requirement for C-V2X networks in dense urban environments, where fast channel variations and blockages often degrade direct vehicle-to-infrastructure links. Multi-hop relaying can restore coverage, but relay-link activation under radio, capacity, and routing constraints results in an NP-hard optimisation problem, typically solved via Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), whose runtime scales poorly with graph size. This paper introduces an edge-aware Learning-to-Optimise framework for real-time relay selection. Each V2X snapshot is modelled as a directed graph: node features encode vehicle state and traffic demand, while edge features capture radio-link capacity. An offline MILP oracle generates optimal relay configurations that supervise a Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE), enabling edge-level relay activation through a single forward pass, with tightly bounded inference latency. To bridge learning and exact optimisation, we also propose a hybrid GINE-Pruned MILP (GP-MILP) strategy in which GINE predictions prune the MILP search space. Experiments on a large-scale dataset generated via an OSM-SUMO-GEMV$^2$ pipeline show that GINE closely matches MILP decisions at the link level (accuracy 0.9589), F1-score (0.9544) on validation) and yields consistent end-to-end connectivity gains over a 1-hop MILP baseline (up to 9.2% with four RSUs and 12% with two RSUs). Inference latency remains tightly bounded, with all evaluated instances completing within 5~ms. Moreover, GP-MILP preserves MILP-equivalent solutions (same objective value) while achieving solver runtimes below 30~ms for more than 98%) of the graph instances, making MILP-grade optimisation compatible with stringent NR-V2X latency budgets.

AI.tldr: Edge-aware learning-to-optimize for real-time relay selection in C-V2X. A GINE-based predictor, supervised by an offline MILP oracle, enables fast edge activation decisions; a GP-MILP hybrid further prunes MILP search. Results show near-MILP accuracy and substantial latency reduction, with MILP-equivalent solutions in most cases.
AI.motivation: Reliable, low-latency uplink connectivity in dense urban C-V2X is challenged by fast channel variation and blockages. Relay selection is NP-hard and current MILP approaches scale poorly in graph size, hindering real-time operation.
AI.method: Model each V2X snapshot as a directed graph with node features (vehicle state, demand) and edge features (radio-link capacity). Use an offline MILP oracle to generate optimal relay configurations to supervise a Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). Deploy a single forward pass for edge-level relay activation. Propose a hybrid GP-MILP by pruning MILP search space with GINE predictions. Evaluate on a large-scale OSM-SUMO-GEMV^2 dataset; compare to 1-hop MILP baseline.
AI.result: GINE achieves high fidelity to MILP: accuracy 0.9589; F1 0.9544. End-to-end connectivity gains over 1-hop MILP: up to 9.2% (four RSUs) and 12% (two RSUs). Inference latency bounded within 5 ms. GP-MILP preserves MILP-equivalent objective values and solves >98% of graphs in <30 ms, enabling MILP-grade optimization under NR-V2X latency budgets.
AI.conclusion: Edge-aware learning-to-optimize can provide near-MILP decisions with provable latency bounds, offering practical MILP-grade relay optimization for C-V2X. The GP-MILP hybrid combines learning speed with exact optimisation guarantees for most instances.

title: Capability from Access Structure, Not Scale: Lower Bounds and Pre-Registered Tests for Hybrid Sequence Models
comment: 41 pages, 16 figures. Pre-registered small-scale experiments (scorecard: 11 supported, 7 partial, 1 failed). Information-theoretic lower bounds plus controlled trained witnesses. Jianlin Chen and Ziyao Lin contributed equally. Corresponding author: Chi Man Vong (cmvong@um.edu.mo)
summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that as models scale, representations of heterogeneous networks converge toward a shared model of reality. We propose its sequel and boundary, the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH): under a fixed per-token inference budget, representational convergence does not entail capability convergence. Capability instead converges toward a class, the access-complete hybrid: any architecture holding both a compressive O(1)-state channel and a scalable verbatim-index channel. We anchor it on a witness task, the Newton's-apple problem in an infinite stream, and name three resource walls: a Shannon wall barring any o(Nb)-state architecture, a horizon wall barring any fixed window, and a circuit wall barring fixed-depth attention-only composition (conditional on TC0 != NC1). Under an explicit separability assumption a hybrid crosses all three by paying each wall's price, so capability is strictly super-additive under composition. We separate what we prove from what we conjecture: the access-completeness principle rests on information-theoretic lower bounds and pre-registered experiments, while the field-level convergence trend is an economics-motivated conjecture. We report the first pre-registered small-scale tests under criteria frozen before the data: the predicted scissors gap is measured (exact-retrieval error 0.994 vs. 0.000 once a 64-scalar state gains one global-attention layer), the state-tracking bifurcation lands at the registered boundary, and a conjunction witness shows an irreducibly two-channel solution; one prediction failed with its direction reversed and is reported as such. Representational convergence is given freely by scale; capability convergence must be purchased by access structure.

AI.tldr: Rep convergence with scale is predicted; capability convergence requires access structure. Introduces the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH) and an access-complete hybrid (compressive O(1)-state channel + scalable verbatim-index channel). Defines three resource walls (Shannon, horizon, circuit), a witness task (Newton's-apple in an infinite stream), and pre-registered tests. Some predictions hold, some fail; convergence is economics-like, capabilities must be purchased.
AI.motivation: Clarify the relationship between representation convergence and capability convergence in scaled heterogeneous networks; separate proven results from conjectures; ground claims in information theory and test with pre-registered experiments.
AI.method: Theoretical framing with information-theoretic lower bounds; explicit separability assumption; construct an access-complete hybrid crossing three resource walls at their costs; anchor with a witness task; report first pre-registered small-scale tests measuring exact-retrieval error, state-tracking bifurcation, and a conjunction witness.
AI.result: Representations converge with scale; capabilities converge toward an access-complete hybrid class but require paying access-structure costs; the three resource walls bound possible architectures; the hybrid is strictly super-additive under composition; some predictions (direction of one result) failed in tests.
AI.conclusion: Scale drives representation convergence freely; capability convergence is not automatic and must be purchased via access structure; empirical support exists for the main predictions, with at least one reversal in a pre-registered test; clear separation between proven aspects and conjectures; invites economic framing of field-level convergence.

title: SD-MAR: Multi-image Analytical Reasoning via Synthetic Data and Reinforcement Learning
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate strong perceptual abilities but remain limited in tasks requiring analytical reasoning across multiple visual states, such as multi-image comparison, change detection, and multi-step visual inference. These capabilities are critical for real-world multimodal applications where reasoning must be grounded in systematic differences between visual contexts. However, existing benchmarks rarely require both explicit visual comparison and analytical reasoning, leaving this capability underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce SD-MAR (Synthetic Data for Multi-image Analytical Reasoning), a framework for training and evaluating VLMs on multi-image analytical reasoning. SD-MAR constructs paired visual scenarios through controlled perturbations and generates reasoning tasks spanning semantic change attribution and quantitative comparison. We further train VLMs using GRPO-lite with Backward Discounted Allocation (BDA), a reinforcement learning approach that removes KL regularization to encourage stronger policy optimization while allocating greater credit to the later reasoning steps where analytical conclusions are formed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B show that GRPO-lite fine-tuning on SD-MAR improves in-domain accuracy by up to 36.95%, with Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforming GPT-4.1 on the SD-MAR benchmark. Importantly, out-of-domain generalization is preserved or improved: performance remains within 1% on MME, MMMU-Pro, and MathVista, while improving by up to 4% on MMBench. LLM-as-judge evaluation further demonstrates consistent improvements in logical coherence and explanation quality across both models.

AI.tldr: SD-MAR: Synthetic data for Multi-image Analytical Reasoning; introduces paired visual scenarios via perturbations; trains VLMs with GRPO-lite + Backward Discounted Allocation; improves in-domain accuracy and generalization; LLM-as-judge shows better coherence.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where VLMs struggle with cross-image analytical reasoning requiring explicit visual comparison across multiple states. Existing benchmarks lack joint emphasis on explicit comparison and analytical reasoning, hindering development of grounded multimodal reasoning.
AI.method: SD-MAR constructs paired visual scenarios through controlled perturbations to support tasks like semantic change attribution and quantitative comparison. Training uses GRPO-lite with Backward Discounted Allocation (BDA) reinforcement learning that removes KL regularization to encourage stronger policy optimization and allocates greater credit to later reasoning steps where conclusions form.
AI.result: In-domain accuracy improves by up to 36.95% on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B. Qwen2.5-VL-7B even outperforms GPT-4.1 on SD-MAR. Out-of-domain generalization maintained or improved: within 1% on MME, MMMU-Pro, MathVista; up to 4% on MMBench. LLM-as-judge evaluation shows consistent gains in logical coherence and explanation quality across both models.
AI.conclusion: SD-MAR coupled with GRPO-lite (BDA) is effective for training and evaluating VLMs on multi-image analytical reasoning, yielding strong in-domain gains while preserving or improving cross-domain generalization and explanation quality.

title: An offline approach to fNIRS-guided reinforcement learning for robot behavior
summary: Human-in-the-loop Reinforcement Learning has become a popular approach to training, finetuning, and aligning robot behavior with user preferences. Our paper explores the feasibility of using brain signals via functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to modulate robot learning in simulation. We compare agents trained on passive (observational) versus active (demonstrative) interaction tasks, and test multiple methods for enhancing the RL algorithm with the neural signal, focusing on parameter augmentation rather than replacement. We further examine how model granularity and noise affect agent learning. Our results show that this framework is effective: the neural signal improves learning when augmenting trajectory priorities and state-action q-values. Additionally, the framework learns successfully from offline data, offering a practical alternative for settings where real-time BCI setups are impractical or only limited data is available.

AI.tldr: fNIRS signals can augment reinforcement learning via parameter augmentation, improving learning in simulation; effective for both passive and active tasks, and viable with offline data when real-time BCI is impractical.
AI.motivation: To align robot behavior with user preferences by leveraging non-invasive brain signals (fNIRS) within human-in-the-loop RL; to assess practicality via offline data and analyze effects of signal quality.
AI.method: Compare agents trained with passive (observational) and active (demonstrative) interaction tasks; implement multiple neural-signal augmentation methods focused on parameter augmentation (not replacement); study effects of model granularity and noise; evaluate augmentation on trajectory priorities and state-action Q-values; test learning with offline data.
AI.result: Neural signals improved learning when used to augment trajectory priorities and Q-values; the framework supports offline learning, offering a practical alternative when real-time BCI setups are impractical; results hold across varying granularity and noise conditions.
AI.conclusion: fNIRS-based parameter augmentation is an effective and practical approach for human-in-the-loop RL, enabling improved learning in simulation and potential real-world applications where real-time neural interfacing is constrained.

title: RENEW: Towards Learning World Models and Repairing Model Exploitation from Preferences
summary: World models are widely used in offline reinforcement learning (RL) to improve sample efficiency and generate experience beyond a fixed dataset. However, they are vulnerable to model exploitation where data coverage is thin. Prior work addresses this either by collecting more expert demonstrations, which is often expensive, unsafe, or unavailable, or by conservative algorithms that avoid uncertain regions, which limits generalization. We propose instead to repair exploitation directly using human preferences over imagined rollouts, leveraging the strong intuitive physics that allows humans to easily spot egregious dynamics hallucinations. We formalize this as Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF), a Bradley-Terry preference loss over trajectory log-likelihoods under a learned dynamics model. Unfortunately, naive DLHF is sample inefficient, so we introduce RENEW, which uses epistemic uncertainty to focus finetuning where the model is most exploitable. We evaluate on several Jumanji and classic control environments and find that while naive DLHF requires an outsize preference budget, RENEW makes the framework practical by improving sample efficiency, limiting catastrophic forgetting, and reducing exploitation in pretrained world models. Taken together, our results provide initial evidence that preferences can supervise world model dynamics directly, offering a new approach to addressing exploitation in offline model-based RL.

AI.tldr: DLHF with RENEW uses human preferences over imagined rollouts to repair exploitation in offline world models; RENEW increases sample efficiency by focusing fine-tuning on epistemic-uncertainty regions, improving stability and reducing forgetting.
AI.motivation: Offline model-based RL suffers exploitation when data coverage is thin; existing remedies (more expert data or conservatism) have drawbacks. Human preferences offer a direct supervision signal for dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF) with Bradley-Terry loss over trajectory log-likelihoods from a learned dynamics model. To address sample inefficiency, propose RENEW that uses epistemic uncertainty to prioritize updates in exploitable regions.
AI.result: Naive DLHF is sample-inefficient; RENEW makes it practical, improving sample efficiency, limiting catastrophic forgetting, and reducing exploitation in pretrained world models; tested on several Jumanji and classic control tasks.
AI.conclusion: Preferences can supervise world model dynamics directly, offering a new approach to mitigating exploitation in offline model-based RL.

title: ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability
summary: Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical. We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia: the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: ToolAnchor mitigates behavioral inertia in tool-augmented LLM agents by injecting counterfactual anchor contexts to utilize new tools without full retraining, via teacher-guided hypotheses, verified by student rollouts and agentic post-training; it achieves competitive performance across expanded toolsets.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tool-augmented LLM agents underperform when new tools appear because they default to familiar toolsets and reasoning patterns. Retraining from scratch is costly, creating a need for scalable adaptation that integrates new tools without extensive retraining.
AI.method: ToolAnchor employs teacher models to hypothesize counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points. These contexts are verified through student rollouts, and successful interventions are internalized through agentic post-training, enabling dynamic adaptation to expanded toolsets.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on GAIA (general AI assistant), BrowseComp (textual search), and VDR-Bench (visual search) show ToolAnchor delivering competitive performance under expanded toolsets, bridging static post-training and dynamic adaptation.
AI.conclusion: ToolAnchor presents a scalable pathway for agentic reinforcement learning by combining counterfactual reasoning with post-training, enabling robust adaptation to new tools without full retraining.

title: MixCompress: Mixture of Experts for Variable Rate Learned Image Compression
summary: Learned image compression (LIC) is bottlenecked by the need to store independent models for each rate-distortion operating point. Existing variable bit-rate (VBR) methods aim to reduce this overhead via dense parameter modulation, but forcing a shared backbone to approximate divergent mappings causes severe feature entanglement. Specifically, low-rate smoothing gradients inherently conflict with the preservation of high-frequency textural details, leading to sub-optimal performance. To resolve this, we propose MixCompress, a unified VBR framework based on sparse structural specialization. While sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing successfully mitigates gradient conflict, it operates on a fixed computational budget. To address the increased representational demands of higher bit-rates we introduce a Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) extension to dynamically scale model capacity. Combined with Conditional Auxiliary Transforms (CAT) for dynamic sub-band energy modulation, our hierarchical framework effectively dynamically scales capacity. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MixCompress not only matches individually optimized single-rate baselines but can even surpass them, establishing a new Pareto frontier for computationally efficient image coding.

AI.tldr: MixCompress integrates sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing with a Mixture-of-Depths capacity scaling and Conditional Auxiliary Transforms to enable unified variable-rate image compression, achieving Pareto-efficient performance by matching or exceeding single-rate baselines with dynamic capacity control.
AI.motivation: To eliminate the overhead and gradient-conflict issues of maintaining separate models for every rate–distortion point in learned image compression (LIC), enabling dynamic capacity as bitrate increases.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework combining sparse MoE gating (to mitigate gradient conflict with a fixed budget), Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) to dynamically scale model capacity for higher bit-rates, and Conditional Auxiliary Transforms (CAT) for dynamic sub-band energy modulation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show MixCompress matches or surpasses individually optimized single-rate baselines, establishing a new Pareto frontier for computation-efficient image coding.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, sparse, depth-aware capacity scaling with auxiliary transforms yields an effective unified VBR LIC framework that reduces overhead while maintaining or improving performance.

title: ConFlow: Constraints-Guided Learning with Flow Matching for Motion Generation
comment: RSS 2026 Workshop on Diffusion for Robot Learning
summary: In recent years Flow Matching has become a prominent method for generative modeling robot motion generation. In its generic form Flow Matching is an ODE-based neural sampler that is trained by regressing empirical flow fields associated with motion samples as data. However, in robot motion generation we often have additional constraints that might not be present in the collected data. The majority of current approaches train the flow on the available data and use inference-time guidance to enforce task-specific constraints. To address this mismatch, we propose \textbf{ConFlow}, a constraint-guided flow matching framework that incorporates constraint information directly into the training objective via differentiable barrier or cost functions. To address design specifications such as smoothness and boundary conditions, we propose replacing the standard Gaussian source distribution used in flow matching training with a conditional Gaussian Process. Our approach also uses infeasible demonstrations as negative supervision, improving constraint satisfaction without requiring additional expert data. Experiments on a two-robot navigation task demonstrate that ConFlow achieves lower collision rates and higher trajectory quality than standard flow matching baselines, with or without inference-time guidance. These results validate training-time constraint integration as an effective approach to closing the training--inference gap in generative motion models.

AI.tldr: ConFlow embeds constraints into the flow-matching training objective via differentiable barriers/costs and uses a conditional GP as the source distribution, improving constraint satisfaction and trajectory quality in robotic motion generation.
AI.motivation: Address the training–inference mismatch: constraints present during deployment are often absent in training data, causing suboptimal constraint satisfaction when inferring samples.
AI.method: Integrate constraint information directly into the training objective using differentiable barrier or cost functions. Replace the standard Gaussian source with a conditional Gaussian Process to encode smoothness and boundary conditions. Use infeasible demonstrations as negative supervision to further enforce constraints without extra expert data. Evaluate on a two-robot navigation task.
AI.result: ConFlow achieves lower collision rates and higher trajectory quality than standard flow matching baselines, with or without inference-time guidance.
AI.conclusion: Training-time constraint integration is effective for closing the training–inference gap in generative motion models and improves constraint satisfaction without requiring additional expert data.

title: Closed-Loop Knowledge Dynamics: An Operational Framework for Saturation and Escape
summary: Feedback-driven loops support iterative improvement in large language models, reinforcement learning, and autonomous discovery, yet their gains often diminish under repeated internal feedback. We study why closed-loop knowledge systems saturate and what external information can move them beyond their current attractors. We introduce a three-level operational framework in which knowledge states $x_t$ evolve through transition kernels $K_θ$ indexed by a structural parameter $θ$. The governing structure is defined as the observational equivalence class of $θ$ induced by these kernels, while attractors and basins are properties of the fixed-$θ$ dynamics. A structural intervention changes $θ$ and produces a detectable kernel discrepancy on pre-specified probe states, making structural change falsifiable. Using a Lyapunov drift condition, we show that stable internal dynamics approach bounded stability regions with exponentially attenuated transients and a noise-controlled residual floor. We characterize escape through a metric condition on intervention-induced attractor displacement and a baseline-relative KL lower bound for increasing escape probability. This analysis also explains why conditional mutual information alone cannot certify escape: it measures variation among intervention-conditioned updates rather than departure from the no-intervention law. Case studies in LLM code repair, sparse-reward reinforcement learning, and Bayesian optimization use matched continuation controls to illustrate how feedback strength and alignment affect quality-improving escape. Our contribution is an operational connection among stability tools, measurable intervention effects, and cross-domain diagnostics.

AI.tldr: Stability–intervention framework for knowledge-state dynamics in feedback-driven AI, with Lyapunov analysis and KL-based escape criteria; demonstrated across LLM code repair, sparse-reward RL, and Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Explain saturation of gains in closed-loop AI knowledge systems due to internal feedback and identify principled, falsifiable external interventions to move dynamics beyond current attractors; connect stability tools with measurable intervention effects across domains.
AI.method: Three-level model: knowledge states x_t evolving via transition kernels K_θ; θ as a structural parameter; the structure defined as the observational equivalence class of θ induced by the kernels; attractors and basins arise from fixed-θ dynamics; structural interventions alter θ causing detectable kernel discrepancies on probe states; Lyapunov drift condition yields bounded stability regions with exponentially attenuated transients and a noise-controlled residual floor; an escape metric based on intervention-induced attractor displacement plus a baseline-relative KL lower bound; argument that conditional mutual information alone cannot certify escape; case studies with matched continuation controls in LLM code repair, sparse-reward RL, and Bayesian optimization to illustrate effects of feedback strength and alignment.
AI.result: Derives conditions for stable dynamics to remain within bounded regions with decaying transients and a residual floor; provides quantitative criteria (attractor displacement metric and KL lower bound) to signal increasing escape probability under interventions; clarifies limitations of MI as a sole escape certifier; demonstrates applicability across domains through concrete case studies.
AI.conclusion: Establishes an operational link between stability-theoretic tools, measurable intervention effects, and cross-domain diagnostics for improving knowledge-state evolution in feedback-driven systems.

title: Enhancing Small Language Models Reasoning through Knowledge Graph Grounding
comment: Presented at the 2nd Causal Neuro-symbolic Artificial Intelligence (Causal NeSy): Toward Agentic LLMs with Neuro-Symbolic and Graph Based Reasoning Workshop @ ESWC2026
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have set benchmarks for zero-shot reasoning, their deployment remains cost-prohibitive and environmentally taxing. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a sustainable alternative, but prone to errors, on tasks requiring complex, multi-hop logical grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to enhance the reasoning capabilities of SLMs, specifically Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B), using the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. Our approach transforms the SLM into a minimalist agent utilizing two specialized tool calls: extract_facts for symbolic triplet extraction and get_hint for expert reasoning via a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). We evaluate these models across two configurations, both in an Oracle scenario with ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge. Our results reveal that while RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5 - 2x performance gain over story-only baselines, the system is constrained by the extraction bottleneck and sequential deductive fragility, where early extraction errors compound over multi-hop chains. Furthermore, we identify a "distraction effect" in specific architectures where noisy, self-generated facts degrade performance despite the presence of expert hints. This work characterizes the challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems and provides a roadmap for iterative verification in neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic augmentation of small LMs on CLUTRR using two tools (extract_facts and get_hint) with RGCN reasoning; yields 1.5–2x gains over story-only baselines but is hampered by extraction bottlenecks and distraction effects, highlighting symbolic grounding challenges in low-resource agents and a path for iterative verification.
AI.motivation: Address the cost and environmental impact of LLMs while maintaining multi-hop reasoning; exploit symbolic grounding and relational graph reasoning to bolster SLMs without full-scale LLMs.
AI.method: Implement minimalist agent for Gemma 3 and Llama 3.2; two tool calls: extract_facts to extract symbolic triplets; get_hint to obtain expert reasoning via an RGCN; evaluate in Oracle (ground-truth triplets) and Realistic (self-extracted) settings on CLUTRR kinship benchmark.
AI.result: RGCN-provided hints improve performance by ~1.5–2x over story-only baselines; however extraction bottlenecks and sequential error propagation limit gains; noisy self-generated facts can cause a distraction effect reducing performance even with hints.
AI.conclusion: Highlights the challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems; offers an actionable roadmap for iterative verification and improvement in neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

title: Beyond scalar losses: calibrating segmentation models via gradient vector field surgery
summary: Region-based loss functions, such as the Dice loss, have established themselves as the de facto standard for highly class- and region-imbalanced segmentation tasks. However, models trained using region-based loss functions are notoriously miscalibrated and typically yield over-confident predictions. In medical imaging applications, such as defining tumor resection margins, this miscalibration is hindering clinical adoption. In this work, we outline a novel gradient perspective on this overconfidence and show how it affects region-based loss functions. We propose a "surgery" on the gradient vector field as a simple, yet effective intervention to mitigate calibration issues. This surgery adds a factor to the loss's partial derivative, scaling the gradient's magnitude linearly with the prediction error. In empirical evaluations across 2D and 3D medical segmentation tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this intervention while maintaining high prediction accuracy when used in conjunction with any region-based loss function.

AI.tldr: Gradient-based intervention (gradient surgery) on region-based losses (e.g., Dice) to mitigate miscalibration/overconfidence in 2D/3D medical segmentation, preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Region-based losses excel at imbalanced segmentation but yield over-confident predictions, hindering clinical adoption; improved calibration is essential for safe medical decision-making.
AI.method: Introduce a simple gradient-vector-field modification: add a factor to the loss's partial derivatives that scales the gradient magnitude linearly with the prediction error, effectively 'surgery' on the gradient. This can be applied on top of any region-based loss (e.g., Dice).
AI.result: Empirical results on 2D and 3D medical segmentation tasks show improved calibration (reduced overconfidence) while maintaining high segmentation accuracy when used with region-based losses.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight, gradient-based calibration mechanism can be integrated with existing region-based losses, improving model calibration without sacrificing accuracy, aiding clinical deployment.

title: Motion Planning with Model-Based Diffusion via Constraint Optimization and Adaptive Scheduling
summary: Single-Robot Motion Planning (SRMP) in highly non-convex constrained environments, where robots must satisfy collision-free guarantees, dynamic feasibility, and task-related constraints, is challenging under complex constraints and computational limits. Recent Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) approaches recast the SRMP as trajectory optimization that samples from a posterior over trajectories, using known dynamics, and analytically estimates the score function from rollout samples to guide diffusion denoising toward a low-cost, clean trajectory without demonstration learning. While existing works further adapt MBD to constrained environments and showcase promising performance, they are still limited by (1) enforcing safety either via soft feasibility diffusion priors or hard projection operators, but lack a unified framework to integrate both, and (2) fixing safety enforcement to neglect the changing of diffusion scheduling. Therefore, we introduce Model-Based Diffusion via Constraint Optimization and Adaptive Scheduling (MD-COAS) for SRMP that unifies the inexact Augmented Lagrangian Method (iALM) soft diffusion prior with a Convex Feasible Set (CFS)-based hard projection operator, and adaptively schedules and co-optimizes safety enforcement, along with diffusion scheduling. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves higher safety \& success rates, faster convergence, and lower final costs than baseline planners on randomly generated highly non-convex 2D benchmarks and a 7-DoF robot arm avoidance task.

AI.tldr: MD-COAS unifies inexact Augmented Lagrangian method (iALM) soft priors with a Convex Feasible Set (CFS) hard projection and adaptive scheduling for Model-Based Diffusion in single-robot motion planning, improving safety, success rate, and convergence speed in highly non-convex constraints.
AI.motivation: Current MBD-based SRMP methods struggle to jointly enforce safety via soft priors and hard projections while keeping diffusion scheduling fixed. A unified framework that co-optimizes constraint enforcement and diffusion scheduling can yield more robust, data-efficient planning in non-convex environments.
AI.method: Introduce MD-COAS: a unified framework that combines an inexact Augmented Lagrangian (iALM) soft diffusion prior with a Convex Feasible Set (CFS) hard projection operator for constraint handling, and an adaptive scheduler that co-optimizes safety enforcement and diffusion steps during trajectory optimization.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on randomly generated highly non-convex 2D benchmarks and a 7-DoF robotic arm avoidance task shows higher safety and success rates, faster convergence, and lower final costs compared with baseline planners.
AI.conclusion: MD-COAS provides a unified, adaptive framework that integrates soft and hard constraint enforcement with diffusion scheduling in model-based diffusion for SRMP, delivering improved performance in challenging constrained environments.

title: A Temporal Machine Learning-Based Time-to-Event Model for Predicting ALS Progression and Healthcare Utilization
summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease in which predicting clinically meaningful milestones, such as assistive device use, remains challenging. We developed a time-to-event, digital-twin-inspired framework that integrates longitudinal ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) trajectories with survival modeling to support individualized prediction of functional decline and assistive device utilization. We constructed a harmonized longitudinal dataset by integrating diagnosis records, ALSFRS-R assessments, activities of daily living, and demographic information, followed by preprocessing to ensure data quality, temporal alignment, and cohort consistency. Correlation-based clustering identified coherent functional domains spanning bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, and respiratory systems. Generalized additive mixed models characterized nonlinear, domain-specific functional decline across all domains. In addition, a temporal machine learning model was developed to predict longitudinal functional decline and capture stage-dependent disease progression. Cox proportional hazards modeling further identified lower limb function, particularly walking and stair climbing, as the strongest predictors of earlier wheelchair access. Building on these results, we implemented a digital twin-inspired temporal machine learning-based time-to-event (TTE) model that generates individualized survival curves and dynamically predicts wheelchair-free survival. This framework provides a scalable, interpretable, and clinically actionable approach for linking ALS progression with personalized decision support, with applications in proactive care planning, clinical trial stratification, and precision medicine.

AI.tldr: Time-to-event, digital-twin-inspired framework linking longitudinal ALSFRS-R trajectories with survival modeling to predict wheelchair-free survival and assistive device use in ALS, using harmonized multi-source data, domain clustering, GAMs, temporal ML, and Cox PH.
AI.motivation: Address heterogeneity and progression in ALS to predict meaningful milestones and support individualized care planning and trial stratification.
AI.method: Data harmonization of diagnosis, ALSFRS-R, ADLs, demographics; correlation-based clustering to define functional domains (bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, respiratory); generalized additive mixed models for nonlinear domain decline; temporal machine learning model for longitudinal predictions; Cox proportional hazards to identify predictors; a digital twin-inspired time-to-event model to produce individualized survival curves and wheelchair-free survival.
AI.result: Identified coherent functional domains; nonlinear, domain-specific decline patterns; lower limb function, especially walking and stair climbing, as strongest predictor of earlier wheelchair access; digital-twin TTE model provides individualized survival curves and dynamic wheelchair-free predictions; scalable, interpretable framework with potential for proactive care planning, trial stratification, precision medicine.
AI.conclusion: Provides a scalable, interpretable, clinically actionable approach linking disease progression with personalized decision support; applicable to proactive care planning, clinical trial stratification, and precision medicine in ALS.

title: Orchestrating Power Grid Studies with Multi-Agent AI and MCP Servers
summary: This position paper explores how Agentic AI and Model Context Protocol (MCP) can support power-grid studies in a Transmission System Operator (TSO) context. We focus on integrating Large Language Models with numerical simulation tools, structured workflows, and human supervision. We identify key industrial requirements for agent assisted grid studies and introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface exposing selected capabilities of our simulation tool, pypowsybl to AI agents. This first step provides a testbed to study how agents can setup simulations, execute analyses, retrieve results, and interact with power-system simulators through standardized tool calls. We also discuss principles for human-in-the-loop, multi-agent workflows and outline an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback. The paper positions MCP-based tool integration as a step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes agentic AI and an MCP-based interface to connect pypowsybl with AI agents for TSO grid studies; introduces pypowsybl-mcp as a testbed to automate simulations, analyses, and results retrieval via standardized tool calls.
AI.motivation: Address the need for automated, auditable, and scalable grid-studies in TSOs by integrating AI agents with numerical simulation tools through a standardized, auditable workflow protocol.
AI.method: Conceptual framework plus a first prototype (pypowsybl-mcp) exposing selected pypowsybl capabilities via MCP; outlines agent-enabled workflows, human-in-the-loop supervision, and multi-agent coordination; defines an evaluation plan combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback.
AI.result: Proposes a working interface and testbed to study agent-augmented grid studies; no empirical results reported, but lays out design choices and evaluation strategy.
AI.conclusion: MCP-based tool integration is presented as a viable step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments, with future work focusing on implementation, validation, and broader evaluation.

title: Dynamic Manipulation Hypergraphs for HAR: Beyond Pairwise Relations: Dynamic Manipulation Hypergraphs for Vision-Based Human Activity Recognition
summary: Fine-grained manipulation recognition requires modeling evolving relations among hands, objects, tools, and supporting surfaces. Conventional graph-based methods use pairwise edges that can fragment a coordinated event into disconnected binary relations. We propose a dynamic manipulation hypergraph framework that represents multi-entity configurations as higher-order relational units. At each temporal step, relevant entities are encoded using appearance, spatial, motion, and semantic-role features. Hyperedge candidates are instantiated and ranked using proximity, contact, and motion-coupling predicates. A hypergraph reasoning network performs node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node message passing, followed by temporal attention over the evolving interaction structure. The framework provides class-agnostic hyperedge-importance scores that identify entity configurations and temporal intervals emphasized by the model without treating them as causal explanations. Quantitative evaluation is conducted on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and Assembly101 under an annotation-assisted entity-localization protocol. Video-only and entity-based methods provide contextual comparisons, while a matched pairwise graph and a static hypergraph serve as the principal controlled baselines because they use identical entity inputs and comparable relational settings. The proposed method improves HO-F1 over the matched pairwise graph by 6.9 percentage points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and 9.5 points on Assembly101, and exceeds the static hypergraph by 4.4 and 5.8 points, respectively. Qualitative analysis on ARCTIC further shows correspondence between highly ranked hyperedges and contact-rich manipulation intervals. These results demonstrate the value of time-varying higher-order relational modeling for fine-grained manipulation activity recognition.

AI.tldr: Proposes a dynamic manipulation hypergraph to model higher-order, time-varying relations among hands, tools, objects, and surfaces for fine-grained action recognition; yields substantial improvements over pairwise graphs and static hypergraphs on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and Assembly101.
AI.motivation: Pairwise relational graphs fragment coordinated manipulation events; higher-order and temporal modeling is needed to capture evolving multi-entity interactions and accurately localize relevant configurations.
AI.method: Construct a dynamic hypergraph per time step with entities encoded via appearance, spatial, motion, and semantic-role features; instantiate hyperedge candidates based on proximity, contact, and motion-coupling; perform node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node message passing, followed by temporal attention; produce class-agnostic hyperedge-importance scores; evaluation under annotation-assisted entity localization; compare to video-only/entity-based baselines, matched pairwise graph, and static hypergraph.
AI.result: HO-F1 gains of 6.9 pp (EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR) and 9.5 pp (Assembly101) over a matched pairwise graph; 4.4 pp and 5.8 pp over a static hypergraph; qualitative ARCTIC analysis confirms alignment between high-ranked hyperedges and contact-rich intervals.
AI.conclusion: Time-varying higher-order relational modeling effectively improves fine-grained manipulation activity recognition, by capturing evolving multi-entity configurations without assuming causal explanations.

title: Mixed-Agent Museum Tour Guide Design Improves Gendered Learning Outcomes and Visitor Preferences
summary: Robots are increasingly integrated into everyday contexts, including museums, where they can both entertain and educate visitors. To enhance visitor experience and engagement, we present a novel mixed-agent tour guide system that combines a physical robot with a projected virtual agent that actively participates in the tour through conversation and interaction, achieving the interaction richness of two mobile agents from a single platform. We validate the system through a within-subjects study with 30 participants to assess engagement, quality of experience, and learning performance. Participants experienced different conversational styles and agent configurations, and data were collected via surveys, behavioral sensors, and interviews. Results showed that engagement and quality of experience remained consistent across conditions. Learning performance revealed a significant gender-moderated difference: the mixed-agent conditions improved learning performance for female participants. This suggests that the proposed dyadic conversational style in this paper influenced learning performance differently by gender. Nonetheless, in interviews, participants reported a greater preference for mixed-agent teams regardless of gender, citing interaction as a key factor in their experience.

AI.tldr: A dyadic mixed-agent tour guide (robot + projected virtual agent) maintains engagement and QoE across styles; learning gains are gender-moderated (women benefit more); participants prefer mixed-agent collaboration.
AI.motivation: Enhance visitor experience and learning in museum settings by increasing interaction richness with a single platform.
AI.method: Within-subjects design with 30 participants; varied conversational styles and agent configurations; data collected via surveys, behavioral sensors, and interviews.
AI.result: Engagement and quality of experience stable across conditions; learning performance improves for female participants in mixed-agent conditions; interviews show a preference for mixed-agent teams regardless of gender.
AI.conclusion: A dyadic conversational style on a single platform can achieve interaction richness akin to two agents; gender modulates learning benefits; user preference favors mixed-agent configurations, informing museum guide design.

title: TEDDY: A Pediatric Foundation Model for Risk Forewarning from ICD-Coded Diagnostic Histories
summary: Pediatric electronic health records capture developmentally structured clinical trajectories, yet their potential for generative healthcare foundation models remains largely unexplored. Here we present TEDDY (Temporal Event Decoder for Disease in Youth), a 1.84-million-parameter decoder transformer trained on approximately 73 million ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6 million children at a single pediatric institution. TEDDY models longitudinal diagnosis trajectories and visit timing. Predictions were made before visit codes were revealed, limited to first occurrences, and evaluated against sex- and age-matched controls. Across 797 disease-onset prediction tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters, TEDDY achieved a median AUC of 72.0%, outperforming same-data DenseNet (50.0%), CNN (57.2%), RNN (60.1%), and LSTM (62.7%) baselines on 96-99% of tasks. Performance held across sex and age and was strongest among lower-prevalence diagnoses; 202 of the 225 rarest conditions (90%) had 95% confidence intervals above chance. Predictive signal remained detectable more than two years before first recorded diagnosis, with median AUCs of 59.7% in the unrestricted analysis and 64.4% in a fixed-cohort sensitivity analysis. In asthma and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder benchmarks, AUCs were 79.3% and 84.7%, compared with 62.7% and 71.7% for the strongest comparators, including a general-purpose language model three orders of magnitude larger. Visit-timing predictions had a 3.0-day mean absolute restricted mean survival-time error over 365 days, although median and long-tail return intervals remained miscalibrated. Together, these results establish pediatric diagnostic histories as a substrate for compact generative models supporting broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without population-scale data or billion-parameter models.

AI.tldr: TEDDY is a compact 1.84M-parameter decoder transformer trained on ~73M ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6M children to predict pediatric disease trajectories, outperforming several baselines and enabling long-horizon risk forecasting without population-scale data or billion-parameter models.
AI.motivation: Pediatric EHRs contain rich, developmentally structured trajectories that are underutilized by generative foundation models; there is a need for accurate, scalable, long-horizon disease onset prediction using pediatric data without requiring massive, population-wide datasets.
AI.method: Train a 1.84M-parameter decoder transformer (TEDDY) on longitudinal ICD-10 diagnoses (~73M events from 1.6M children) to model diagnosis trajectories and visit timing. Predictions are made before unveiling visit codes, restricted to first occurrences, and evaluated against sex- and age-matched controls across 797 disease-onset tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters. Benchmarked against DenseNet, CNN, RNN, and LSTM baselines; included asthma/ADHD benchmarks and a long-horizon component.
AI.result: Median AUC of 72.0% across tasks, outperforming baselines on 96-99% of tasks (DenseNet 50.0%, CNN 57.2%, RNN 60.1%, LSTM 62.7%). Robust across sex/age; strongest for rare diagnoses (202 of 225 rarest conditions with 95% CI above chance). Predictive signal detectable >2 years before first diagnosis (AUC 59.7% unrestricted; 64.4% fixed-cohort). Asthma AUC 79.3%; ADHD AUC 84.7% (vs 62.7% and 71.7% for strongest comparators). Visit-timing predicted with ~3.0-day MAE RMSE over 365 days; long-tail calibration limited.
AI.conclusion: Pediatric diagnostic histories can serve as a substrate for compact generative models that provide broad, rare-disease, long-horizon risk forecasting without population-scale data or billion-parameter models.

title: MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience
summary: An agent harness is the external control layer that turns a base LLM into an executable agent by managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling. While harness design strongly affects agent behavior, most automatic improvement methods optimize narrower artifacts such as prompts, pipelines, or workflows, and deployed agents usually reuse a single global harness for all cases. We introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions. MemoHarness decomposes the harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the learned harness to each test case using retrieved experience without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. In our evaluation across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness improves over the fixed harnesses we compare against and shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models. Its additional context can also remain cost-competitive when much of the retrieved experience is cacheable. These results provide evidence that execution experience is a practical substrate for building agent harnesses that are more adaptive than a single static configuration, while leaving broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

AI.tldr: MemoHarness is an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from execution to customize an external control layer for LLM agents, using a dual-layer experience bank to retrieve per-case and global patterns, improving performance across multiple benchmarks and enabling selective transfer with competitive cost.
AI.motivation: To overcome reliance on fixed, global harnesses and narrow optimization targets by enabling per-case adaptation through accumulated experience, without test-time labels or additional search.
AI.method: Decompose the harness into six editable control dimensions; maintain per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank; retrieve and apply learned harness to new test cases without test-time labels, feedback, or extra search; evaluate on shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical reasoning benchmarks.
AI.result: Outperforms fixed harnesses; shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models; context expansion remains cost-competitive due to cacheable retrieved experience.
AI.conclusion: Execution experience can serve as a practical substrate for building adaptive, more flexible harnesses; broader claims about robustness and component attribution are left to future work.

title: $K$-NeAS: Scalable Multi-Material CT Reconstruction Using Neural SDFs
summary: Computed Tomography (CT) carries significant ionizing radiation risks, driving the need for sparse-view reconstruction. Implicit scene representations (ISRs) address this by recovering continuous volumetric attenuation fields directly from sparse projections, and recent geometry-aware extensions jointly model surface geometry alongside attenuation to improve fidelity and enable clean tissue segmentation without manual thresholding. However, these methods remain limited by manually tuned attenuation bounds and rigid two-material constraints. This paper proposes $K$-NeAS, a unified and scalable architecture for automated, multi-material surface reconstruction. We replace independent material networks with a shared latent backbone and introduce a fully differentiable $K$-material sequential soft selector to model an arbitrary number of overlapping tissues. To eliminate manual tuning, we automate attenuation bounding using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and implement a scheduled auxiliary floater loss to mitigate geometric hallucinations common under extreme sparsity. Evaluated across four clinical Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) datasets, $K$-NeAS successfully scales to arbitrary material counts, achieving superior 3D volumetric fidelity at $K=3$ materials on complex multi-tissue regions such as the Abdomen ($33.28\text{ dB}$ 3D PSNR vs. $31.40\text{ dB}$ single-material NeAS baseline, a $+1.88\text{ dB}$ improvement). Furthermore, our model exhibits enhanced robustness under sparse-sampling conditions, outperforming baseline 3D PSNR by up to $1.17\text{ dB}$ under 5- and 10-view constraints.

AI.tldr: Introduces K-NeAS, a scalable, fully differentiable multi-material ISR for sparse-view CT that automates attenuation bounds with a Gaussian Mixture Model and uses a shared backbone plus a differentiable K-material sequential soft selector to model overlapping tissues; demonstrates improved fidelity and robustness on CBCT data.
AI.motivation: Reduce ionizing radiation exposure in CT by enabling accurate multi-material surface reconstruction from sparsely-sampled projections without manual tuning or fixed two-material constraints.
AI.method: A unified architecture with a shared latent backbone, a fully differentiable K-material sequential soft selector for overlapping tissues, automated attenuation bounding via a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), and a scheduled auxiliary floater loss to mitigate geometric hallucinations under extreme sparsity.
AI.result: On four clinical CBCT datasets, K-NeAS with K=3 materials achieves superior 3D volumetric fidelity compared to a single-material baseline (abdomen region: 33.28 dB 3D PSNR vs 31.40 dB; +1.88 dB). It also shows enhanced robustness under sparse sampling, with improvements up to 1.17 dB in 3D PSNR under 5- and 10-view constraints.
AI.conclusion: K-NeAS scales to arbitrary material counts, eliminates manual attenuation tuning, and improves fidelity and robustness in sparse-view CT reconstructions while enabling multi-tissue surface reconstruction without manual thresholding.

title: MIDAS Hand: Modular low-Impedance Direct-drive Anthropomorphic Sensing Hand
summary: Dexterous manipulation is limited not only by algorithms but by a shortage of accessible hand hardware that combines human-scale morphology, ease of manufacturing or maintenance, tactile sensing, and practical cost. Existing dexterous hands tend to optimize some of these properties at the expense of others. We present MIDAS Hand, a low-cost, open-source, human-scale dexterous hand with integrated tactile sensing for manipulation research. MIDAS Hand provides 16 total degrees of freedom (DoF) with 13 active DoF, directly driven actuation with measurably low backdrive torque, and 283 three-axis tactile taxels in a compact 700 g package with a bill of materials under 3,000 USD. Built from 3D-printed components, it assembles in under three hours while providing the strength, repeatability, and maintainability needed for repeated real-world experiments. Alongside the hardware, we release a full stack: design files, build documentation, control and tactile Python APIs, simulation models, and retargeting and teleoperation pipelines. We characterize MIDAS Hand through workspace and grasp-taxonomy analysis, payload and reliability tests, backdrivability measurements, and teleoperation demonstrations with tactile sensing, showing that it offers a balanced, reproducible platform for tactile dexterous manipulation and human-to-robot data collection. Project page: https://midas-hand.com

AI.tldr: MIDAS Hand is a low-cost, open-source, human-scale dexterous hand with integrated tactile sensing: 16 DoF (13 active), direct drive with low backdrive torque, 283 three-axis tactile taxels, 700 g, < $3k BOM; 3D-printed, <3 h assembly; full software stack and simulations provided; validated via workspace/grasp taxonomy, payload/reliability, backdrivability, and tactile teleoperation demonstrations.
AI.motivation: To address the trade-off among morphology, manufacturability, tactile sensing, and cost in dexterous hands by providing an affordable, open-source, human-scale platform with integrated tactile sensing for manipulation research and data collection.
AI.method: Design and fabricate MIDAS Hand using 3D-printed components to achieve 16 DoF (13 active) with direct actuation and low backdrivability; integrate 283 three-axis tactile taxels; keep mass ~700 g and BOM under $3,000; release full-stack: design files, build docs, control and tactile Python APIs, simulation models, and teleoperation/retargeting pipelines.
AI.result: Characterization includes workspace and grasp-taxonomy analysis, payload and reliability tests, backdrivability measurements, and teleoperation demonstrations with tactile sensing, demonstrating a balanced, reproducible platform for tactile dexterous manipulation and human-to-robot data collection.
AI.conclusion: MIDAS Hand delivers a cost-effective, open-source, human-scale dexterous hand with tactile sensing that is manufacturable and maintainable, enabling reproducible experiments and data collection in tactile manipulation research while lowering barriers to entry.

title: Long-term User Engagement Optimization through Model-agnostic Downstream Rewards Learning
summary: As recommender systems mature in the past few years, their optimization objectives have evolved from a primary focusing on short-term behavioral signals to a broader emphasis on long-term user engagement and retention. However, directly optimizing retention is difficult because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to earlier recommendations. Prior work has addressed this challenge with sequential modeling and reinforcement learning, but these approaches typically require task specific reward engineering, substantial computational overhead, and surface specific implementations that are difficult to generalize. In this paper, we present a unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommendation systems. First, we formulate the downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session level behaviors that are both observable early and predictive of future retention. We then propose several model-agnostic downstream rewards signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources. We further discuss the engineering effort to productionize the proposed rewards derivations and challenges we faced when adding them to our ranking models. Online A/B experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics, and the framework has been deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.

AI.tldr: Model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommendation systems; uses offline screening to identify early predictive signals and derives multiple observable reward signals; demonstrates online gains and is deployed across Pinterest surfaces.
AI.motivation: Retention signals are sparse, delayed, and not easily attributable to early recommendations, making direct optimization difficult; existing sequential/RL approaches require task-specific rewards and heavy engineering, limiting generalization.
AI.method: 1) offline screening to identify session-level behaviors that are observable early and predictive of retention; 2) derive several model-agnostic downstream reward signals from observed user actions across multiple sources; 3) productionization considerations and integration with ranking models.
AI.result: Online A/B experiments show consistent improvements in engagement and retention metrics; framework deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces (Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, Notifications).
AI.conclusion: A unified, generalizable approach to optimize long-term value without task-specific reward engineering; scalable to large systems and production-friendly.

title: When a Verified World Model Still Loses: Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy in LLM-Synthesized Code World Models
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. Code and reproduction log: https://github.com/JaviMaligno/code-world-models
summary:
Large language models can synthesize a game's rules as executable code - a Code World Model (CWM) - which a classical planner then searches over. Such models are typically accepted when they reach high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. We argue this is the wrong notion of adequacy for planning.
  We show four things. (1) An LLM-synthesized CWM can pass a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and be $\geq 98\%$ state-accurate on the planner's own search distribution, yet lose systematically at play, because the $<1\%$ it gets wrong is exactly the pivotal dynamics; the play cost of the omitted rule is $0.091$ (seed-clustered 95% CI $[0.065,0.117]$, $n=4800$). We call this the verified-vs-correct gap, and confirm it end-to-end through the synthesis pipeline. (2) The harm follows a quantitative law, $\mathrm{danger}=\mathrm{play\_cost}\times(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$, whose $(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$ gate-miss factor is proven exact and whose play cost is empirically bounded. (3) The failure is not repaired by more data: LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not rule inference, and did not infer the omitted rule across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples). (4) The same mechanism recurs on the belief-inference function of imperfect-information CWMs: we prove a coverage bound (a size-$N$ gate is identifying when $N\gtrsim b^{d_{\max}}$), explaining why shallow games such as Kuhn poker show no gap, and hand-construct Beacon, a verified-but-wrong inference function that passes the gate yet loses every game.
  These results suggest adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by play directly, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

AI.tldr: LLM-synthesized Code World Models can appear perfect under transition/state-accuracy tests yet fail in actual play; adequacy for planning must be judged by search outcomes or play, not sampled transitions.
AI.motivation: Current planning with LLM-synthesized world models relies on predicting sampled transitions with high accuracy. The paper argues this is an inadequate adequacy criterion for planning and seeks to understand and quantify the gap between predicted transitions and play performance.
AI.method: 1) Empirical analysis of CWM pipelines showing a verified-vs-correct gap. 2) Derivation of a quantitative danger law: danger = play_cost * (1 - rarity)^N with a proven gate-miss factor. 3) Experiments across models/data regimes showing data cannot repair the gap; CWMs behave as rule-translation. 4) Extension to belief-inference in imperfect-information CWMs with a coverage bound; construction of Beacon as a verified-but-wrong inference function.
AI.result: Four findings: (1) 100% transition accuracy and ≥98% state accuracy on the search distribution do not guarantee good play; pivotal missed rules drive losses. (2) The harm follows danger = play_cost × (1 − rarity)^N with a proven gate-miss factor. (3) More data does not fix the gap; synthesis remains as translation, not inference. (4) Coverage bounds explain why simple games may show no gap and demonstrate Beacon as a verified-but-wrong function; implying evaluation should focus on search distribution or play outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Planning-oriented world-model adequacy should be measured by performance on the planner's search distribution or actual play, not by sampled-transition prediction accuracy; this has broad implications for evaluating LLM-based planning systems.

title: Emergent Region-Level Facial Correspondence in Frozen Vision Foundation Models
