LDMR monitors per-class detection quality at periodic training checkpoints and uses these learning-dynamics signals to drive two innovative mechanisms, namely (i) human-like intra-stage review that divides each incremental stage into multiple sub-stages' training and concentrates on remembering the most-forgotten objects, and (ii) scene-aware cross-stage memory evolution that evolves a memory bank to transfer knowledge between two consecutive stages by jointly considering scene learnability and diversity. Extensive experiments across multiple long-incremental protocols on indoor benchmarks SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 show that LDMR substantially mitigates the model forgetting and outperforms all baselines by a clear margin. Code is available at https://github.com/qianpeisheng/LDMR.

AI.tldr: A learning-dynamics-driven framework (LDMR) for long-incremental 3D object detection that uses per-class learning signals to drive intra-stage reviews and cross-stage memory evolution, achieving substantial forgetting mitigation on SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2.
AI.motivation: Address severe forgetting in long-incremental 3D detection caused by a self-reinforcing cycle: novel-class data distribution shifts induce old-class forgetting, which increases pseudo-label errors and further degrades the model.
AI.method: Propose LDMR that (1) monitors per-class detection quality at checkpoints and (2) introduces two mechanisms: intra-stage review (divide each incremental stage into sub-stages focusing on most-forgotten objects) and scene-aware cross-stage memory evolution (memory bank evolves to transfer knowledge between consecutive stages by considering scene learnability and diversity).
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 across long-incremental protocols shows LDMR substantially mitigates forgetting and outperforms baselines by a clear margin; code available.
AI.conclusion: LDMR provides a practical, dynamics-driven approach to mitigating forgetting in long-incremental 3D detection, validating the importance of learning-dynamics signals and memory-review strategies for continual learning in complex scenes.

title: Reinforcement Learning for the Full Strawberry Harvesting Process: Obstacle Separation, Detachment, and Placement
summary: Severe occlusions and deformable plant structures introduce complex contact dynamics that challenge robotic strawberry harvesting. A policy-driven reinforcement learning (RL) framework with heuristic phase coordination was developed, in which obstacle separation, fruit detachment, and placement were formulated as a sequential decision-making task. A shared interaction-aware policy generated Cartesian motions across all task phases, while lightweight heuristic logic coordinated task progression and gripper events. A shared structured observation space was used to represent target, obstacle, end-effector, and task-context information. A hierarchical architecture combined the high-level policy with low-level Cartesian impedance control for compliant interaction. To support zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, feasibility-first observation alignment and domain randomization were adopted. The policy achieved success rates of 89.7% in simulation and 82.0% in real-world experiments. As the occlusion level increased from 1 to 5, the average execution time increased from 12.99 s to 21.73 s, reflecting greater interaction complexity. These results demonstrated effective transfer of interaction-aware harvesting behaviors to a structurally different robotic platform.

AI.tldr: A policy-driven RL framework with a shared interaction-aware policy and heuristic phase coordination enables robust strawberry harvesting under occlusion and deformable plant dynamics, achieving high sim-to-real transfer and improved performance as occlusion increases.
AI.motivation: Robotic strawberry harvesting is hindered by severe occlusions and deformable plant structures that create complex contact dynamics; robust, transferable control policies are needed to ensure reliable picking and placement across varied scenarios and platforms.
AI.method: A hierarchical approach: a shared, interaction-aware policy generates Cartesian motions across obstacle separation, detachment, and placement, with lightweight heuristic logic coordinating task phases. A shared observation space encodes target, obstacle, end-effector, and task-context. High-level policy is paired with low-level Cartesian impedance control. Feasibility-first observation alignment and domain randomization support zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: The policy achieved 89.7% success in simulation and 82.0% in real-world experiments. With occlusion level rising from 1 to 5, average execution time increased from 12.99 s to 21.73 s, indicating greater interaction complexity.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates effective transfer of interaction-aware harvesting behaviors to a structurally different robotic platform and shows robustness to occlusion via hierarchical policy design, structured observations, and domain randomization.

title: A Noise-Robust Elicit-to-Optimize Framework for Distortion Riskmetrics via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: We propose a noise-robust elicit-to-optimize framework that integrates inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and reinforcement learning (RL) for eliciting agents' risk preferences and optimizing policies under a broad class of risk objectives characterized by distortion riskmetrics. On the elicitation side, we propose an adaptive Bayesian IRL method that infers agents' latent risk objectives from their noisy observed decisions, explicitly allowing agents to take stochastic and suboptimal actions. We establish the existence of a finite set of distinguishing questions that identifies the preferred distortion riskmetric within the candidate class and prove that the convergence rate of the algorithm is of order $O(\exp(-cm+O(\sqrt{m\log m})))$ under general settings, where $c>0$ is a constant and $m$ denotes the number of algorithm iterations. On the optimization side, we develop a model-free RL algorithm for optimizing policies under conditional distortion riskmetrics. By representing the objective as an integral of the conditional cost quantile function with respect to the distortion function, the method unifies distortion-riskmetric objectives. We optimize diverse risk objectives by extending the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm with policy, value, and quantile neural networks, where the quantile network estimates the full conditional cost quantile function and enables numerical evaluation of general risk objectives. A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates the framework's elicitation accuracy and effectiveness in complex financial environments.

AI.tldr: A noise-robust elicit-to-optimize framework integrating IRL and RL to elicit agents' risk preferences and optimize policies under distortion riskmetrics; includes Bayesian IRL with finite distinguishing questions and exponential convergence, and a model-free RL framework (PPO-based) with quantile networks to handle conditional distortion riskmetrics; demonstrated via empirical study in financial settings.
AI.motivation: To infer latent risk objectives from noisy, suboptimal decisions and to optimize policies under a broad class of risk objectives (distortion riskmetrics) in finance; address stochasticity in human/agent behavior and unify risk measures.
AI.method: Elicitation: adaptive Bayesian IRL infers latent risk objectives from noisy decisions, allows stochastic/suboptimal actions, proves finite set of distinguishing questions exists and convergence rate O(exp(-cm + O(sqrt(m log m)))). Optimization: model-free RL with objective as integral of conditional cost quantile function w.r.t. distortion, using PPO extended with policy, value, and quantile networks; quantile net estimates full conditional cost quantile to evaluate general risk objectives.
AI.result: Theoretical results: finite distinguishing questions; convergence rate bound. Empirical results: framework achieves elicitation accuracy and effective policy optimization under distortions in complex financial environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed elicitation-optimization framework effectively recovers agents' risk preferences and optimizes under distortion riskmetrics, with a unified approach to diverse risk objectives and strong empirical validation in finance.

title: CatalogAgent: A Supervisor-mediated Self-Learning System Enabling Context Engineering for GenAI Models
summary: Product catalogs are the backbone of e-commerce sites, yet a large number of structured attributes (SAs) -- such as material, color, and shape -- often have missing values. Typically, SA values are extracted from product information, including titles and descriptions. While LLM-based generator-evaluator frameworks have demonstrated effectiveness for SA prediction -- where an LLM generates SA values and another evaluates them -- they face challenges when the Generator and Evaluator produce conflicting outputs, as either component can make mistakes. We introduce \texttt{CatalogAgent}, a novel agentic system that continuously improves Generator and Evaluator models for e-commerce catalog enrichment. When disagreements arise from (1) internal conflicts between the LLM-based Generator and Evaluator, or (2) external feedback from sellers on LLM outputs, a Supervisor Agent intervenes to mediate these conflicts and make final decisions. The system also incorporates a Memory Base and a Memory Summarizer that stores Supervisor Agent activities from individual cases and aggregates patterns into learnings. These learnings are fed back to the worker Generator and Evaluator LLMs, enabling self-improvement without human intervention. Through context engineering -- injecting learnings and insights into worker LLMs' contexts -- the system successfully transfers the Supervisor's capabilities to the Generator and Evaluator, improving their performance by 15.24\% and 13.98\%, respectively. Our experiments demonstrate a new paradigm of Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning systems for improving generative AI model accuracy.

AI.tldr: A supervisor-mediated agentic system, CatalogAgent, improves SA prediction in e-commerce catalogs by mediating generator/evaluator conflicts and leveraging a memory base and summarizer for self-learning; yields ~15.24% improvement for the Generator and ~13.98% for the Evaluator.
AI.motivation: Structured attributes (SAs) often have missing values in product catalogs. LLM-based Generator-Evaluator frameworks can misfire when Generator and Evaluator conflict or err; a Supervisor Agent mediates conflicts and aggregates learnings via memory to enable self-improvement without human input.
AI.method: Architectural design with Generator, Evaluator, and Supervisor agents, plus a Memory Base and Memory Summarizer. Disagreements (internal or external feedback) trigger Supervisor mediation; learnings are summarized and injected as context to workers to drive self-improvement. The system uses context engineering to transfer Supervisor capabilities to Generator and Evaluator and evaluates on SA prediction tasks.
AI.result: Demonstrates that supervision-mediated self-learning improves Generator and Evaluator performance by 15.24% and 13.98%, respectively, on catalog enrichment tasks.
AI.conclusion: Shows a viable paradigm for continuous, automated improvement of generative AI in e-commerce catalogs via Supervisor-mediated feedback loops and memory-informed context propagation; suggests broader applicability to other generator–evaluator workflows.

title: Advanced Image Generation: Negative Prompt Optimization and Latent Classifier Guidance
summary: We present a novel system that integrates negative prompt optimization via a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence LLM and latent-space classifier guidance to improve the quality of images generated by Stable Diffusion. Our approach automatically generates optimized negative prompts, and employs a CNN-RNN hybrid classifier to evaluate and guide diffusion steps, rolling back low-quality latent updates. Experimental results demonstrate that our dual-guidance framework reduces artifacts and improves semantic fidelity compared to baseline diffusion.

AI.tldr: A dual-guidance diffusion enhancement: automatic negative-prompt optimization via a fine-tuned seq-to-seq LLM plus latent-space classifier guidance to roll back low-quality latent updates, improving image quality and semantic fidelity in Stable Diffusion.
AI.motivation: Reduce artifacts and semantic misalignment in diffusion models and minimize manual negative-prompt crafting by automating negative-prompt generation; leverage latent-space guidance to steer diffusion towards higher-quality, semantically faithful outputs.
AI.method: Two components: (1) a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence LLM generates/optimizes negative prompts; (2) a CNN-RNN hybrid latent-space classifier evaluates latent updates during diffusion and signals rollbacks of low-quality steps; integrate these into a dual-guidance pipeline that jointly modulates diffusion steps.
AI.result: Experimental results indicate reduced artifacts and improved semantic fidelity compared with baseline diffusion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-guidance framework effectively enhances diffusion quality via automatic negative-prompt optimization and latent-space guidance; future work could include ablations, cross-dataset validation, and analysis of computational overhead.

title: BridgeFlow: Fast and Robust SE(2)-Equivariant Motion Planning with Flow Matching
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). 8 pages, 7 figures
summary: In robotic motion planning, equivariance to rigid body transformations is crucial for robust spatial generalization. However, current learning-based planners face a critical dilemma: they either lack inherent equivariance, treating transformed tasks as novel scenarios, or enforce it via computationally expensive specialized architectures that bottleneck real-time inference. To break this trade-off, we propose BridgeFlow, a fast and strictly SE(2)-equivariant generative motion planning framework. Rather than relying on heavy equivariant networks, BridgeFlow achieves exact spatial equivariance via a lightweight task-centric canonicalization module, enabling generalization using standard architectures. To further accelerate inference, we pair a Brownian bridge informative prior with context-aware mini-batch optimal transport. This constructs a straightened vector field that minimizes transport costs and stabilizes training. Furthermore, environmental awareness is explicitly embedded via Classifier-Free Guidance. Evaluations in dense 2D environments and on a 7-DoF Franka manipulator demonstrate that BridgeFlow achieves up to a 15x inference speedup and a 2x higher valid trajectory rate over state-of-the-art diffusion baselines, alongside robust generalization to entirely unseen environments and arbitrary spatial transformations.

AI.tldr: BridgeFlow is a fast, strictly SE(2)-equivariant generative motion planning framework that uses a lightweight canonicalization module to achieve exact equivariance without heavy equivariant networks, and combines a Brownian bridge prior with context-aware mini-batch optimal transport and Classifier-Free Guidance to accelerate inference and embed environmental awareness. It reports up to 15x speedup and 2x higher valid trajectory rate over diffusion baselines, with strong generalization to unseen environments and arbitrary spatial transformations.
AI.motivation: Robotic motion planning requires robust spatial generalization under rigid-body transformations. Current approaches face a trade-off: lack of inherent equivariance or reliance on computationally expensive equivariant architectures that hinder real-time inference. A fast, generalizable, and equivariant planner is needed.
AI.method: BridgeFlow achieves exact SE(2) equivariance via a lightweight, task-centric canonicalization module rather than heavy, specialized equivariant networks. It uses a Brownian bridge informative prior combined with context-aware mini-batch optimal transport to create a straightened vector field that reduces transport costs and stabilizes training. Environmental awareness is incorporated via Classifier-Free Guidance. Evaluations are conducted in dense 2D environments and on a 7-DoF Franka manipulator.
AI.result: The approach yields up to 15x faster inference and up to 2x higher valid trajectory rate compared to state-of-the-art diffusion baselines, with robust generalization to unseen environments and arbitrary spatial transformations.
AI.conclusion: BridgeFlow provides a practical balance between speed and equivariance by avoiding heavy equivariant networks, enabling fast, robust, and spatially generalizable motion planning.

title: Integration Matters: Rollout-Based Training for Constrained Diffusion Models
summary: Constrained generative models aim to produce samples that satisfy complex feasibility constraints while remaining faithful to the data distribution. Existing constrained generation methods typically enforce constraints either through training-time optimization or sampling-time correction. Training-time optimization approaches optimize on states induced by the training distribution, which can differ substantially from those encountered during sampling. Sampling-time correction methods instead modify the sampling process at inference, introducing distribution shift and requiring expensive tuning, particularly for few-step sampling. We propose a fine-tuning framework that incorporates constraint guidance obtained through online rollout into the training process, which aligns training with sampling by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule used to numerically integrate the denoising process. This exposes the model to violations that arise along the denoising trajectory and aligns diffusion learning with the sampling process. Experiments across multiple tasks show that our method improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior methods.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based constrained generation method fine-tunes with online constraint guidance by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule to align training with sampling, improving constraint satisfaction while preserving sampling quality.
AI.motivation: Existing constrained generation approaches suffer from a training-time distribution mismatch (optimize on training states) or a sampling-time distribution shift requiring tuning; improving alignment between training and inference can enhance constraint satisfaction.
AI.method: A fine-tuning framework that incorporates constraint guidance from online rollout into training by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule used in denoising diffusion, exposing the model to constraint-violating trajectories and aligning diffusion learning with sampling.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple tasks show improved constraint satisfaction with competitive sampling quality compared to previous constrained-generation methods.
AI.conclusion: Aligning diffusion training with the sampling process via differentiating through the denoising trajectory reduces constraint violations while maintaining sampling quality.

title: Instrument Effects in Language-Model Honesty Evaluation: An Auditable Single-System Demonstration
summary: Evaluations of language-model honesty read the model's verdicts as evidence about the model. We test the instrument instead. We built a text-adventure world where the game engine, not any model, knows whether the quest can be completed. A language model plays under a budget and must eventually declare its quest complete, unreachable, or not yet decidable; the engine scores every verdict. Decision rules were recorded before results were read, and run artifacts bind the revisions they executed; the strength of preregistration varies by series and is disclosed. With the player held fixed, instrument choices substantially changed measured behavior. On four byte-identical anchors, expanding a two-verdict grammar to three verdicts moved strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40, while the new incomplete verdict took 28/40 outcomes; across series 2, 93/158 valid games ended incomplete. One sentence disclosing the success criterion took matched-instance false verdicts from 18/59 to 0/58, through fewer decision points and cleaner decisions. Repeated runs of one fixed configuration produced non-stable verdict distributions on 3 of 4 instances: single runs report samples as dispositions. A formally preregistered narrative-register gradient was falsified; two post-hoc, hypothesis-generating patterns remain: register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering moved verdicts more than register content (.383 meter vs .150 lantern). The narrator compressed abundant budgets toward scarcity landmarks, yet the registered mediation test returned a null. We propose a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments.

AI.tldr: Instrumental effects in evaluating LLM honesty; a text-adventure setup shows verdict rules and budgets shape outcomes; preregistration fails to constrain results; authors propose a four-check integrity protocol.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether evaluations of model honesty reflect true model behavior or artifacts of the evaluation instrument, revealing sensitivity to verdict grammar, budget constraints, and preregistration.
AI.method: Create a text-adventure engine that determines quest completion; the LLM must declare complete/unreachable/not yet decidable under a budget. Decision rules are preregistered; instruments (grammar, budgets, register presence) are varied; multiple series with repeated runs. The engine scores the model's verdicts; results are analyzed for stability and false verdicts.
AI.result: Instrument choices substantially altered measured behavior. Expanding a two-verdict grammar to three verdicts shifted strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40; incomplete verdicts yielded 28/40. Across series, 93/158 valid games ended incomplete. One-sentence success criterion reduced matched-instance false verdicts from 18/59 to 0/58. Repeated runs showed non-stable verdict distributions in 3 of 4 instances. A preregistered narrative-gradient was falsified; two post-hoc patterns remained: register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget effects moved verdicts more than register content. The narration suggested budgets biased toward scarcity; mediation test remained null. Authors propose a four-check integrity protocol for evaluation instruments.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation integrity is compromised by instrument design; preregistration alone does not guarantee valid conclusions. A structured four-check protocol is recommended to ensure reliable evaluation of model honesty.

title: MagicPrompt: Ultra-Lightweight Prompt Tuning for Video Generation
summary: Large-scale video diffusion models (VDMs) deliver strong generation performance, but full fine-tuning for downstream tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have two critical flaws on billion-scale models: they still require substantial trainable parameters, and reward-based training suffers from noise-induced optimization instability in condition-guided tasks. We propose MagicPrompt, a lightweight framework that achieves extreme parameter efficiency and stable reward optimization. It first adopts Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning, which steers generation via lightweight soft prompts with orders of magnitude fewer parameters while preserving pre-trained knowledge. It further introduces Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization, which uses self-supervised latent objectives to improve condition-guided reward training. Experiments show MagicPrompt reaches competitive performance with less than 1\% trainable parameters and notably reduces training costs.

AI.tldr: MagicPrompt enables extreme parameter efficiency for large-scale video diffusion models by combining Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning with Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization, achieving competitive performance with <1% trainable parameters and lower training costs.
AI.motivation: Full fine-tuning of billion-scale video diffusion models is computationally prohibitive. Existing PEFT methods still rely on substantial trainable parameters and reward-based training can be unstable due to noise in condition-guided tasks.
AI.method: Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning: lightweight soft prompts guided by attention embeddings to preserve pre-trained knowledge with orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization: self-supervised latent objectives to stabilize and improve reward-based training for condition-guided generation.
AI.result: Experimental results show MagicPrompt achieves competitive performance while using less than 1% of trainable parameters and substantially reduces training costs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework delivers high parameter efficiency and more stable reward optimization for condition-guided video diffusion, making large-scale VDMs more practical for downstream tasks.

title: Hybrid Rigid-Soft Robotic Gripper with Shape Adaptation, Uniform Force Distribution, and Self-Locking Capabilities
summary: Conventional robotic grippers face a significant challenge in agricultural automation: the trade-off between compliant, adaptive grasping, pressure balancing among all joints, and high load capacity, often at the cost of high energy consumption. This paper presents a novel hybrid rigid-soft gripper that integrated low-cost, membrane-based pneumatic actuators with 3D-printed dual ratchet-pawl mechanisms to simultaneously achieve shape adaptation, uniform force distribution, and energy-free self-locking. The dual-ratchet structure assembled in an offset configuration significantly increased the angular resolution of the joint locking mechanism. Key experimental results demonstrated the gripper's superior performance: a remarkable maximum load capacity of 4200 g, far exceeding that of conventional soft grippers (45-210 g); more uniform force distribution across object sizes (1.75-35.29% difference ratio) compared to a rigid gripper (56.77-66.44%), with peak contact forces remaining below surface damage thresholds; and a 50.05% reduction in total energy consumption to 42.6 J per grasp cycle, achieved by eliminating the need for continuous pneumatic pressure through the self-locking mechanism, compared to 85.28 J for a conventional soft gripper. The combination of additive manufacturing for ratchets and commercially available materials for pneumatic chambers ensured a low-cost and easily fabricated design. These findings validated that the proposed gripper successfully bridged the gap between soft compliance and rigid reliability, offering a robust and efficient solution for scalable agricultural harvesting and manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: A hybrid rigid-soft gripper using membrane-based pneumatics and 3D-printed dual ratchet-pawl mechanisms achieves adaptive grasping, uniform force distribution, and energy-free self-locking, delivering high load capacity with reduced energy per grasp.
AI.motivation: Address the persistent trade-off in agricultural grippers between soft compliance, force distribution, load capacity, and energy consumption; enable robust, scalable harvesting with low-cost fabrication.
AI.method: Integrates low-cost membrane pneumatic actuators with 3D-printed dual ratchet-pawl structures in an offset arrangement to provide shape adaptation, uniform force distribution, and energy-free self-locking. Experimental evaluation includes load capacity tests, force distribution across object sizes, surface damage checks, and energy per grasp.
AI.result: Max load 4200 g (significantly higher than conventional soft grippers 45–210 g); more uniform force distribution (1.75–35.29% difference vs 56.77–66.44% for rigid); peak contact forces below surface damage thresholds; 50.05% energy reduction per grasp cycle (42.6 J vs 85.28 J) due to eliminating continuous pressure through self-locking.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that the proposed gripper combines soft compliance with rigid self-locking to deliver robust, energy-efficient manipulation suitable for scalable agricultural harvesting, with low-cost, easily fab fabrication via additive manufacturing.

title: LATTICE: Graph Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Spatial Omics Integration
summary: Spatially resolved omics studies increasingly combine transcriptomic and epigenomic assays, yet downstream analysis is often still performed using single-modality pipelines. We present LATTICE (Latent Alignment of Tissue-level and Transcriptomic Information for Cross-modal Embedding), a graph-based self-supervised framework that learns spot-level representations from harmonized multimodal features. LATTICE integrates five aligned modality blocks per Visium spot: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT\&Tag. These modalities capture spatial transcriptomic measurements, single-cell inferred regulatory activity, and in situ chromatin and histone states within a unified lattice representation. LATTICE constructs a spatial neighborhood graph and trains a TransformerConv encoder using masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness objectives. On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort from an anonymized clinical collaborator comprising 54{,}912 total spots, LATTICE demonstrated stable optimization behavior, reproducible embeddings across analysis seeds, and complete multimodal integration across all samples. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA alone substantially improved concordance with Space Ranger clusters across 11 runs (adjusted Rand index [ARI] +0.157, normalized mutual information [NMI] +0.143, and spatial contiguity +0.174). Additional modalities further improved spatial contiguity and multimodal utility score (MUS), although they sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived reference labels, likely because the learned embeddings captured chromatin and regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity alone. These results position LATTICE as a practical and empirically grounded framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, while also highlighting the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking.

AI.tldr: Graph-based self-supervised multimodal integration (LATTICE) for Visium-like spatial omics, fusing five modalities into unified spot representations via a TransformerConv encoder over a spatial graph; shows improved clustering concordance and spatial contiguity in a melanoma dataset, with trade-offs and a call for stronger supervision and external benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Address the reliance on single-modality pipelines in spatial omics by enabling robust multimodal integration to better capture regulatory and chromatin context alongside transcriptomics.
AI.method: Build a graph-based TransformerConv encoder over a spatial neighborhood graph. Learn five modality blocks (Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, spatial CUT&Tag) in a unified lattice. Train with masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness objectives to produce spot-level embeddings.
AI.result: On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort (54,912 spots), LATTICE showed stable optimization, reproducible embeddings across seeds, and complete multimodal integration. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA substantially improved Space Ranger cluster concordance (ARI +0.157, NMI +0.143, spatial contiguity +0.174). Additional modalities further improved spatial contiguity and multimodal utility score (MUS), though sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived reference labels, suggesting embeddings captured chromatin/regulatory structures beyond transcriptional similarity.
AI.conclusion: LATTICE is a practical framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, but the results underscore the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking to validate multimodal benefits across datasets.

title: Reward-Free Evolving Agents via Pairwise Validator
summary: A self-evolving agentic loop repeatedly proposes a tweaked version of an agent (its prompt template or program) and accepts or rejects the change based on a per-iteration quality signal. Designing that signal is often the costly part of the project: a reliable scalar reward requires domain expertise and labeled examples that are themselves as expensive to assemble as the agent's underlying task. We propose replacing the scalar at the accept/reject gate with a pairwise validator: a frozen LLM that, given the parent and child candidate, returns a binary verdict on which is better. Pairwise judgment is generally easier and more stable than absolute scoring, due to its contrastive nature, which mitigates the need for strict scale calibration. The validator also requires no training of its own. We integrate the validator into three published self-evolving engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) and report two flavors: Adaptive Focus, which retains the engine's existing val-set parent selection, and Soft Elo, which lets the validator's verdicts drive parent selection so that val-set rewards drop as well. Across multiple agents and two artifact substrates (prompt and code), our method matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline on the majority of settings we evaluate, and the pattern survives a cross-family validator swap. The pairwise gate is thus a drop-in replacement for per-step reward design at competitive task accuracy without the labeling cost.

AI.tldr: Pairwise validator replaces per-step scalar reward in self-evolving agents, matching or exceeding full-reward baselines while reducing labeling cost; acts as a drop-in replacement across engines and substrates.
AI.motivation: Designing a reliable scalar reward per iteration is costly due to domain expertise and labeled data requirements. A pairwise, contrastive judgment is easier to calibrate and can be supplied by a frozen LLM without training.
AI.method: Replace the accept/reject scalar gate with a frozen LLM that compares parent and child candidates and returns which is better. Implement two flavors: Adaptive Focus (keep existing val-set parent selection) and Soft Elo (validator verdicts influence parent selection). Integrate into three engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) and test on two substrates (prompt, code).
AI.result: Across multiple agents and substrates, the pairwise gate matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline in the majority of settings. The results hold under cross-family validator swap, indicating robustness. It serves as a competitive, cost-reducing drop-in replacement for per-step reward design.
AI.conclusion: A pairwise validator offers a practical, label-efficient alternative to scalar rewards for self-evolving agents, achieving competitive accuracy with broad applicability across engines and task modalities.

title: Hough-SIFT: Robust Image Registration for Linear Structures via Hough Space
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Supplementary video is available as an ancillary file. Accepted for oral presentation at the 29th Meeting on Image Recognition and Understanding (MIRU2026)
summary: Image registration is essential in applications such as electronic image stabilization. Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), a widely used local keypoint detector and descriptor, typically provides accurate registration; however, it often fails in scenes with strong linear structures (e.g., shutters), where local features become ambiguous. We propose Hough-SIFT, a robust registration method that performs SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space. In this domain, linear structures form distinctive peaks that restore descriptor discriminability. Experiments demonstrate that Hough-SIFT is robust in linear scenes where SIFT frequently fails, while maintaining accuracy comparable to SIFT in normal scenes.

AI.tldr: Hough-SIFT performs SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space to improve registration in scenes with strong linear structures, while preserving SIFT-like accuracy in normal scenes.
AI.motivation: SIFT often fails in scenes with strong linear structures due to descriptor ambiguity; robust registration is needed for such scenarios.
AI.method: Apply SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space; linear structures produce distinctive peaks in Hough space which restore descriptor discriminability.
AI.result: Experimental results show that Hough-SIFT is robust in linear scenes where SIFT fails, while maintaining accuracy comparable to SIFT in normal scenes.
AI.conclusion: Hough-SIFT provides improved robustness for image registration in challenging scenes without sacrificing performance in typical scenes.

title: Curvature-Constrained and Constant-Speed Distributed Simultaneous Arrival Control for Multi-Robot Systems
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: The simultaneous arrival of multiple mobile robots at a target point is crucial for cooperation tasks such as cooperative encirclement, disaster relief, and environmental monitoring. Although the simultaneous arrival problem itself is already complex, the problem becomes more challenging when there are constraints on the robot trajectory curvatures and the speeds are required to be constant (possibly different for different robots), and the control law for robots needs to be distributed. These constraints are typical for a multi-robot system consisting of, e.g., fixed-wing UAVs. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a distributed switching control method based on the maximum consensus protocol. By exploiting the geometric properties of Dubins paths along with optimization principles, a virtual time variable is introduced, and a hybrid control law that combines optimal control with saturated proportional control is designed. Under the proposed control law, each robot is driven to approach the maximum virtual time among its neighbors, thereby achieving simultaneous arrival under some mild conditions. Furthermore, we prove that in certain cases the proposed method attains a theoretically optimal arrival time. The approach is scalable and real-time, with low communication overhead. Its effectiveness and robustness are validated through extensive simulations and experiments.

AI.tldr: Distributed switching control using maximum consensus with Dubins-path geometry to achieve simultaneous arrival for multiple fixed-wing robots under curvature and constant-speed constraints; introduces a virtual time and a hybrid optimal/saturated control law; scalable and real-time with experimental validation.
AI.motivation: Achieve simultaneous arrival for multi-robot systems with curvature-constrained trajectories and constant speeds, typical of fixed-wing UAVs, while using a distributed control scheme.
AI.method: Proposes a distributed switching control based on maximum consensus. Uses Dubins-path geometry to define constraints, introduces a virtual time variable, and designs a hybrid control law combining optimal control with saturated proportional control. Each robot drives to the maximum virtual time among its neighbors.
AI.result: The control law drives robots to achieve simultaneous arrival under mild conditions; in some cases it attains a theoretically optimal arrival time. The approach is scalable, real-time, with low communication overhead, and validated by extensive simulations and experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method is effective and robust for coordinating curvature-constrained, constant-speed robots in distributed settings, achieving simultaneous arrival with low communication costs and potential optimality under certain conditions; demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments.

title: Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment
summary: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm -- exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee for the e-LAAL architecture. In a platform-level production deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue--conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Ad-load expansion boosts revenue but may harm user outcomes; strong heterogeneity; novel adaptive e-LAAL algorithm with guarantees improves revenue-conversion trade-off in production.
AI.motivation: Understand how sponsored-slot quantity affects revenue and user outcomes; design adaptive policy to optimize the trade-off across heterogeneous queries and advertiser mixes.
AI.method: Large-scale randomized field experiment (5M users; 1–6 sponsored slots) in an Android app store; development of e-LAAL (LAAL + fixed exploration arms); finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee; production deployment (22.3M users; 77.6M searches).
AI.result: Revenue up to 43% with more ad load; average declines in conversions up to 5% and engagement up to 2.2%; heterogeneity; e-LAAL improves revenue-conversion trade-off vs static benchmarks; outperforms baselines in production.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, query-aware ad-load policies can unlock revenue without excessive user harm; e-LAAL offers practical gains plus theoretical guarantees; evidence supports deploying adaptive load strategies in sponsored-search platforms.

title: CausalGraphX: A Counterfactual Graph Neural Network Framework for Explainable Systemic Risk Assessment
comment: Accepted in AAAI'26 Workshop, Agentic AI in Financial Services
summary: The interconnected nature of global financial systems makes them vulnerable to systemic risks, where the failure of a few institutions can trigger catastrophic cascading defaults. Traditional risk models often fail to capture the complex, non-linear dynamics of these networks. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promise in modeling relational data, they primarily learn correlative patterns and function as black boxes, offering little insight into the causal mechanisms of shock propagation. This limitation is critical for regulators who require explainable models to perform stress tests and devise effective interventions. We introduce CausalGraphX, a novel framework that integrates GNNs with counterfactual reasoning to provide explainable assessments of systemic risk. CausalGraphX employs a Graph Attention mechanism to learn representations of institutional vulnerability and uses an adversarial regularization technique to ensure these representations capture causal drivers rather than spurious correlations. Furthermore, we propose an optimization-based approach to generate counterfactual explanations, answering questions such as, "What minimum capital injection would have prevented Bank A's default under a specific stress scenario?" We validate CausalGraphX on large-scale synthetic financial networks. Our results demonstrate that CausalGraphX significantly outperforms traditional and deep learning baselines in predicting cascading defaults while providing sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.

AI.tldr: CausalGraphX blends graph neural networks with counterfactual reasoning to yield explainable systemic-risk predictions and counterfactual explanations, outperforming baselines on synthetic financial networks.
AI.motivation: Regulators require explainable, causal insights into shock propagation in financial networks; existing GNNs capture correlations but not causal mechanisms necessary for stress testing and intervention planning.
AI.method: A Graph Attention–based GNN learns representations of institutional vulnerability; adversarial regularization encourages causal rather than spurious patterns; an optimization-based framework generates counterfactual explanations (e.g., minimal capital injections to prevent a default under a given stress).
AI.result: On large-scale synthetic financial networks, CausalGraphX significantly outperforms traditional and deep-learning baselines in predicting cascading defaults and provides sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that integrating GNNs with counterfactual reasoning yields both strong predictive performance and explainability for systemic-risk assessment, with validations on synthetic data; future work should address real-world validation, scalability, and robustness to network structure changes.

title: Knowing You at First Glance: Inferring Apparent Personality from Faces
comment: Accepted by The 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision, PRCV2026
summary: Inferring apparent personality from facial images is important in social scenarios for embodied agents in human-robot interaction. Unlike inferring intrinsic personality traits via conversation, this task models first-impression personality perception based solely on facial appearance before interaction begins. Existing studies mainly focus on the Big Five personality model and often rely on language or multimodal inputs. As a result, it remains unclear whether facial cues alone can support meaningful associations with perceived personality traits. This question is particularly relevant for MBTI types, which are widely used in practice and more readily interpretable by large language models. To this end, we propose \textbf{GlanceFace}, an end-to-end framework for apparent personality inference leveraging vision-language models to introduce semantic priors and a semantic-enhanced facial representation module to capture subtle personality-related cues, together with an uncertainty-aware learning strategy to handle noisy and subjective annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks and reveal relationships between facial characteristics and perceived personality traits, highlighting its potential to support adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/MrHuan3/GlanceFace.

AI.tldr: GlanceFace proposes an end-to-end MBTI-based apparent personality inference from facial images, using vision-language priors, a semantic-enhanced facial representation module, and uncertainty-aware learning; shows strong results on MBTI benchmarks; code and dataset released.
AI.motivation: There is a gap in the literature: while prior work often targets Big Five or multimodal approaches, MBTI-based apparent personality from facial cues alone is underexplored. MBTI provides interpretable categories, and aligning facial cues with these traits can facilitate initial interactions for embodied agents.
AI.method: An end-to-end framework 'GlanceFace' that uses vision-language models to inject semantic priors, a semantic-enhanced facial representation module to capture nuanced personality cues, and an uncertainty-aware learning strategy to handle noisy, subjective annotations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks; analyze relationships between facial traits and perceived personality; supports adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents; code and dataset are released.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates feasibility of MBTI-based apparent personality inference from facial appearance, with interpretable cues and practical implications for social robotics; resources are publicly available for replication.

title: Interventional Causal Circuits for Safe Robot Action Testing and Failure Recovery
comment: 1st IJCAI Workshop on Safe Physical AI IJCAI 2026 workshop on Safe Physical AI
summary: Safe physical AI for robot actions are required not only likely to succeed but tested to be safe before execution. In practice, however, formal testing of motion parameters is computationally expensive, and the cost scales poorly with the dimensionality of the action space. When a proposed action is rejected by a tester, the naive response is to resample blindly until a passing candidate is found. This is wasteful, uninformative, and offers no convergence. We argue that rejection should instead trigger causal diagnosis: a principled identification of which action parameter caused the failure and what corrective value maximises the probability of passing testing under the interventional probability distribution. We propose a closed-loop framework that couples a Joint Probability Tree (JPT) with a Causal Circuit derived from a Marginal-Deterministic Variable Tree, enabling exact polytime computation without retraining, or additional data collection. The framework validates tractability of all interventional queries before the robot begins operating, and out-of-support candidates are detected and excluded from correction automatically. We perform experiments in a ROS2 simulation environment, and the framework demonstrates complementary roles across quality of distribution: under a high-quality JPT, the Causal Circuit reduces failed attempts by 10.3% and under a degraded JPT, it reduces total failed attempts by 37%. Every rejected plan produces a structured, interpretable causal report naming the primary cause variable, its observed value, and the recommended corrective region, supporting operator oversight and autonomous recovery without a separately trained failure model.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop causal diagnosis framework using Joint Probability Tree (JPT) and a Causal Circuit derived from a Marginal-Deterministic Variable Tree for safe robot action testing. It enables exact polytime interventional queries, automatic rejection correction, and interpretable failure reports without retraining. It achieves significant reductions in failed attempts in ROS2 simulations (10.3% with high-quality JPT, 37% with degraded JPT).
AI.motivation: Formal testing of motion parameters in high-dimensional action spaces is computationally expensive; naive blind resampling after a rejection is wasteful and lacks convergence.
AI.method: Couple a Joint Probability Tree (JPT) with a Causal Circuit derived from a Marginal-Deterministic Variable Tree to enable exact polytime interventional queries, validate tractability, and automatically exclude out-of-support corrections. The approach requires no retraining or additional data collection and yields interpretable causal reports per rejected plan.
AI.result: In ROS2 simulations, the framework reduces failed attempts: 10.3% reduction under a high-quality JPT and 37% reduction under a degraded JPT. Each rejected plan yields a structured causal report with the primary cause variable, observed value, and recommended corrective region.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides tractable, interpretable causal diagnostics for robot action safety, enabling operator oversight and autonomous recovery without a separate failure model and without retraining.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Code, configs, experiment log, and checkpoint at https://github.com/jlognn/depth-recurrent-convergence
summary: A depth-recurrent transformer applies a weight-tied core a variable number of times, and prior work has shown that training with a randomized recursion count yields one checkpoint usable across a range of inference depths. We ask what such a model actually computes per token, and measure it directly. On a 135M-class model trained on FineWeb-Edu, the recurrent state converges to a per-token fixed point: mean successive-output KL divergence falls from 3.9e-1 at the second loop to 8.5e-6 by the sixteenth, and per-token state change decays in step. Crucially, this convergence is not uniform across tokens. The median token converges by loop six, while approximately 10 percent of tokens continue to update at the training-mean depth of eight, and mean convergence depth is ordered by token type (whitespace shallowest, content words deepest). This per-token variation is the central object of the paper. We show it is directly readable and that reading it outperforms learning to predict it: a training-free rule that halts each token once its output stabilizes attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (a 38 percent reduction in average depth) and matches uniform depth across the average-depth range, whereas a linear router trained on convergence labels harvested from the same model requires nearly full depth and yields no reduction. The elasticity that makes this possible reproduces here as background (validation loss decreases monotonically from 3.80 at one loop to 3.20 at eight and remains stable to 32 loops). We report average depth as a FLOP proxy with a three-point wall-clock bracket rather than a realized speedup, make no FLOP-matched parity claim, and note that the allocation results are established at a single scale and seed. The complete study runs on a single RTX 4090 in approximately 100 GPU-hours.

AI.tldr: Per-token convergence depth in a depth-recurrent transformer is heterogeneous and directly readable; a simple, training-free halting rule achieves uniform depth and substantial depth reduction, outperforming a learned router; elasticity of recurrence persists but results are scale/seed-specific.
AI.motivation: To understand what a weight-tied, depth-recurrent transformer computes per token, by measuring per-token convergence to a fixed point and evaluating practical implications for adaptive computation.
AI.method: Train a 135M-class depth-recurrent transformer on FineWeb-Edu; analyze per-token state convergence across loops via successive-output KL divergence; quantify convergence depth by token type; compare a training-free halting rule to a learned router; report FLOP proxy depth and runtime characteristics on a single RTX 4090 (~100 GPU-hours).
AI.result: The recurrent state converges to per-token fixed points; KL divergence decays from 0.39 at loop 2 to 8.5e-6 by loop 16; median token converges by loop 6; ~10% continue updating at training-mean depth (8); convergence depth is token-type dependent (whitespace shallower than content words). A training-free halting rule that stops tokens when stabilized achieves uniform depth-8 quality with 4.94 average loops (38% depth reduction) and matches uniform depth across the depth range; a linear router trained on convergence labels requires nearly full depth and yields no reduction. The study also notes monotonic validation loss decrease during training (3.80 to 3.20, stable to 32 loops) and presents average depth as a FLOP proxy with rough wall-clock brackets rather than real speedup. All results are scale- and seed-specific.
AI.conclusion: Per-token convergence depth is the central observable and is directly readable; exploiting convergence via a simple halting rule can materially reduce average depth while preserving quality, whereas learned routing offers little advantage. The depth-recurrent model exhibits elasticity that persists under training, but generalizability remains to be established beyond the reported scale/seed; practical takeaways point toward adaptive-computation strategies in weight-tied recurrent transformers.

title: Autoregressive Modeling of Film with Applications in Video Montage
summary: This work introduces FilmGPT, an autoregressive transformer designed to address the challenge of video montage--turning a collection of raw, "unwatchable" footage into coherent cinematic sequences. Inspired by language learning in modern LLMs, we train a long-context autoregressive transformer on a large corpus of movies. The aim is to implicitly capture the "grammar" of film directly from data rather than from hand-coded rules. Unlike other generative models, FilmGPT does not generate any new video frames. Instead, at inference time, we introduce a footage-constrained decoding algorithm to select the best next shot from the input raw footage according to the statistical patterns learned from films. We first evaluate these learned statistics directly by using the FilmGPT autoregressive model for next shot prediction on a standard benchmark of shot sequence ordering, outperforming the previous state of the art. We then evaluate our footage-constrained decoding algorithm on the full film editing task via a user study, and find that our FilmGPT-based editing significantly outperforms previous approaches. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of FilmGPT to a wide range of applications in video montage, from automatic video segment trimming to human-in-the-loop film editing.

AI.tldr: FilmGPT learns the film grammar via a long-context autoregressive model trained on movies and applies a footage-constrained decoding to select the best next shot from raw footage, enabling effective montage without new frames.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of a learnable, generalizable grammar of film; rely on data-driven patterns learned from a large film corpus, inspired by LLM training; solve the montage problem by selecting shots rather than generating frames.
AI.method: Train a long-context autoregressive transformer on a large corpus of films; at inference, perform footage-constrained decoding to choose the next shot from raw footage based on learned statistics; evaluate on shot-sequence ordering benchmark; conduct user-study editing evaluation; showcase applications (automatic trimming, human-in-the-loop editing).
AI.result: Outperforms prior SOTA on next-shot prediction for shot ordering; user study shows FilmGPT-based editing significantly outperforms previous approaches; demonstrates versatility for automatic trimming and human-in-the-loop workflows.
AI.conclusion: FilmGPT provides a data-driven grammar of cinematic editing that operates on existing footage, enabling effective montage without new frame generation and broad video-editing applications.

title: KineFuse: Kinematic-Aware Haptic Fusion for In-Hand Occluded-Object Pose Tracking
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Dexterous in-hand manipulation requires continuous 6D pose tracking, yet the manipulating fingers inevitably occlude the object from the camera. We study how to structure the sparse haptic signals already available on multi-fingered hands, including proprioception, proximal force/torque, and binary contact, to complement a pretrained visual pose tracker under occlusion. We propose a kinematic-aware finger-level encoder and systematically compare it against four alternative designs through three levels of evaluation: per-frame refinement, sequential open-loop tracking, and closed-loop manipulation. Our experiments reveal that (i) per-frame evaluation cannot distinguish encoder quality, while sequential tracking amplifies architectural differences by up to 15 times; (ii) the structured encoder learns task-specific cross-modal gating, using vision exclusively for translation and dedicating one attention head to haptics for rotation, without explicit supervision; and (iii) compact finger-level tokenization with 4 tokens outperforms both flat fusion and joint-level representations, which suppress vision through norm dominance. We validate that improved tracking yields higher success in a downstream reorientation task and provide qualitative real-world demonstrations. Our project page is available at https://cold-young.github.io/kine-fuse/.

AI.tldr: A finger-level, kinematic-aware encoder improves multi-modal in-hand pose tracking under occlusion, enabling better sequential tracking and manipulation with a compact tokenization.
AI.motivation: Dexterous in-hand manipulation suffers from occlusion of the object by manipulating fingers; the work investigates how to structure sparse haptic signals (proprioception, proximal forces/torques, binary contact) to complement a pretrained visual pose tracker.
AI.method: Introduce a kinematic-aware finger-level encoder and compare it against four alternatives across three evaluation levels: per-frame refinement, sequential open-loop tracking, and closed-loop manipulation. Use a compact finger-level tokenization (~4 tokens) and assess cross-modal gating patterns without explicit supervision.
AI.result: The structured encoder enables task-specific cross-modal gating (vision for translation; one haptic-attention head for rotation). Sequential tracking magnifies architectural differences (up to 15x). Compact 4-token finger-level representation outperforms flat fusion and joint-level methods that suffer from vision suppression by norm dominance. Improved tracking leads to higher success in a downstream reorientation task; real-world demonstrations provided; a project page is available.
AI.conclusion: A kinematic-aware, compact finger-level encoding effectively fuses vision and haptics for occluded in-hand manipulation, improving tracking accuracy and downstream task success; results validated both in simulation and real-world experiments.

title: Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Generalist robot manipulation policies trained on large, diverse datasets have shown remarkable promise across a wide range of tasks. However, rigorously evaluating these policies remains a fundamental challenge. Real-world performance depends on a large combinatorial space of task factors including object poses and camera viewpoints, making full, exhaustive evaluation intractable. Additionally, real hardware evaluation is slow and resource-intensive, so current practice is to use narrow test suites that can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent true deployment readiness. We propose an active evaluation framework that addresses this challenge by treating policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. Our approach fits a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and adaptively selects evaluation configurations to maximize information gain over the policy's performance distribution, allowing for sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and a systematic identification of failure-prone regions. We conduct 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations and find that our approach typically saves the evaluator at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing.

AI.tldr: An active evaluation framework for generalist robot manipulation policies that treats evaluation as a sequential experimental design, using a probabilistic surrogate over a structured task-factor space to adaptively select informative evaluation configurations; demonstrated with 2331 real-world trials across 3 tasks and 3 factor variations, achieving 20–40% reduction in trials compared with random testing.
AI.motivation: Exhaustive evaluation over all combinations of task factors (e.g., object poses, viewpoints) is intractable and real hardware experiments are slow and costly. Narrow test suites can miss critical failure modes and misestimate deployment readiness. There is a need for sample-efficient, systematic evaluation across unseen conditions.
AI.method: Construct a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and their configurations. Use adaptive, information-theoretic selection of evaluation settings to maximize information gain about the policy’s performance distribution. Treat evaluation as a sequential design problem to efficiently map performance and locate failure-prone regions, validated on real hardware.
AI.result: Real-world experiments: 2331 evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations. The active evaluation approach typically saves 20–40% of trials compared to random testing, indicating improved efficiency and broader behavioral characterization.
AI.conclusion: Active, information-guided evaluation yields more efficient and thorough assessment of generalist manipulation policies across diverse conditions, reducing hardware evaluation burden and enabling better identification of failure-prone regions; the approach is applicable to a range of policies and deployment scenarios.

title: Tactile: Giving Computer-Using Agents Hands and Feet
summary: Computer-use agents are becoming capable software operators, but their interface to desktop applications is still often a brittle motor layer: they look at screenshots, predict coordinates, click, and hope that the visible state changed as intended. This collapses target grounding, action execution, and outcome verification into a single ambiguous operation. We present Tactile, an open-source tool layer that gives agents a more reliable "hands and feet" for desktop use. Tactile converts heterogeneous UI evidence--operating-system accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, and visual fallback regions--into action-grounded interface states: compact target candidates with source labels, roles or text, state, geometry, executable affordances, and verification cues. Agents operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop that prefers native semantic actions when available, falls back to OCR-grounded coordinates when visible text is the best evidence, and keeps full provenance for replay and failure attribution. On macOSWorld-style tasks, adding Tactile improves Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks; a 96-task cross-agent subset shows consistent gains across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose. These results suggest that reliable computer use requires not only stronger models, but also a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than anonymous screen coordinates.

AI.tldr: Tactile provides a semantic, auditable execution substrate for desktop agents, improving action grounding and verification by combining OS accessibility, OCR, and visual cues to operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop; results show meaningful gains in Codex and other agents on macOS tasks.
AI.motivation: Current automation for desktop apps relies on brittle, coordinate-based actions with little ground truth for state or verification, leading to fragile performance. A reusable, semantic execution substrate could enable more reliable agent-driven software use.
AI.method: Integrate heterogeneous UI evidence (OS accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, and visual regions) into action-grounded interface states; prefer native semantic actions when available, fall back to OCR-based coordinates when necessary; operate in an observe-ground-act-verify loop with provenance for replay and failure attribution.
AI.result: On macOS desktop tasks, Codex Success@100 improves from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks. A 96-task cross-agent subset shows gains across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose.
AI.conclusion: Reliability in computer-use agents requires a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than opaque screen coordinates; Tactile demonstrates tangible performance gains and sets a foundation for robust desktop automation.

title: VIABench: A Comprehensive Video Benchmark Collected from Blind Individuals for Visual Impairment Assistance
summary: Visually impaired individuals (VIIs) encounter significant daily challenges due to limited access to visual information. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive results on general vision and language tasks, their practical utility in real-world blind assistance still remains largely underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce VIABench, a comprehensive video benchmark specifically designed to evaluate MLLMs in Visually Impaired Assistance scenarios using first-person videos recorded or shared by VIIs themselves. VIABench defines three core tasks, each targeting a distinct requirement in visual assistance. Proactive Reminder: Assesses the model's ability to interpret ongoing video content while proactively anticipating and verbally describing upcoming navigation-critical events; Visual Question Answering (VQA): Evaluates the model's capacity to answer user-posed questions about the environment or objects within the video; Vision-Guided Interaction: Tests context-aware reasoning to accomplish intentional interactions between user and environment. To ensure a robust and fair evaluation, we propose a rigorous benchmarking pipeline that supports both online (real-time) and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle to deliver comprehensive support for VIIs, especially in the Proactive Reminder task, which demands accurate anticipation and real-time responsiveness. We hope VIABench will drive future research toward developing customized MLLMs for real-world assistance, ultimately improving navigation and interaction experiences for visually impaired individuals. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/VIABench.

AI.tldr: VIABench is a first-person video benchmark to evaluate Multimodal LLMs for visually impaired assistance, with Proactive Reminder, VQA, and Vision-Guided Interaction; supports online/offline benchmarking; current MLLMs struggle, especially in proactive tasks; code/data to be released.
AI.motivation: There is a gap between MLLMs' general multimodal capabilities and practical, real-world aid for visually impaired individuals; existing benchmarks lack first-person, proactive, and interaction-centric evaluation; a dedicated benchmark is needed to guide model development.
AI.method: Design and implement VIABench with three tasks aligned to real assistance needs; dataset comprises first-person videos shared or recorded by VIIs; define evaluation pipeline for online and offline settings; perform experiments with current MLLMs to benchmark performance.
AI.result: Current MLLMs show limited capability to provide comprehensive VI assistance; especially Proactive Reminder task requires anticipation and real-time responsiveness; results motivate development of customized MLLMs for VIIs.
AI.conclusion: VIABench can steer research toward tailored models for blind assistance, improving navigation and interaction; code and data will be released to facilitate community adoption.

title: Towards Human-like Physical Intelligence: LifelongVision-Language-Action Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Similar to the natural capabilities of humans to sequentially learn new tasks, robots with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models should possess lifelong learning ability to learn a new task when deployed in open-world environments. However, most recently proposed lifelong learning models aim to effectively learn the current task (plasticity) or maintain high accuracy on previous tasks (stability), while the plasticity-stability trade-off remains largely unsolved in robotic manipulation models. To address this fundamental challenge, we propose a cache-efficient lifelong Vision-Language-Action learning framework for robotic manipulation (i.e., LifelongVLA), which alleviates the plasticity-stability trade-off with a dual-timescale adaptation mechanism while achieving low-cost robotic deployment with a cache-efficient replay strategy. More concretely, we propose a dual-timescale LoRA gating module to decompose VLA adaptation into two lightweight pathways: a short-term adapter for plasticity and a long-term adapter for stable consolidation. These pathways are integrated via a task-aware gate, enabling explicit control of the plasticity-stability trade-off. In the skill replay phase, a cache-efficient stochastic replay strategy is proposed to preserve more balanced retention signals without full-trajectory storage. Finally, experiments show that LifelongVLA outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating efficient skill expansion, robust retention of learned manipulation behaviors, and reduced reliance on retraining for real-world deployment on an xArm robot.

AI.tldr: A dual-timescale, cache-efficient lifelong Vision-Language-Action learning framework (LifelongVLA) using short-term and long-term LoRA adapters gated by a task-aware mechanism, plus cache-efficient replay, to balance plasticity and stability in robotic manipulation and enable efficient real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Address the plasticity–stability trade-off in lifelong robotic manipulation and enable continual, data-efficient learning in open-world environments without heavy retraining or full trajectory storage.
AI.method: Introduce a dual-timescale LoRA gating module with a short-term adapter for plasticity and a long-term adapter for stability, integrated via a task-aware gate to control the trade-off. Add a cache-efficient stochastic replay strategy to preserve retention signals without storing full trajectories. Validate on a robotic platform (xArm) against baselines.
AI.result: Outperforms existing baselines in skill expansion, robust retention of learned manipulation behaviors, and reduced retraining requirements, demonstrating practical and efficient lifelong VLA learning for real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: Dual-timescale adaptation with cache-efficient replay effectively mitigates the plasticity–stability trade-off in lifelong VLA learning, enabling scalable, efficient manipulation in open-world environments.

title: Depth-Dependent Hidden-State Collapse in Dynamical System Autoencoders for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the 2026 IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference (HPEC 2026)
summary: We study Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification using spatial coordinates and Product Coefficient feature augmentations. The experiments compare separately trained DSAE architectures at encoder depths $K=1,\ldots,5$ and evaluate the resulting hidden representations with Random Forest, kNN, and a majority-class Dummy baseline. The main finding is a hidden-state collapse at $K=5$. For both xyz and xyz plus Product Coefficient inputs, the hidden-state standard deviation falls to the order of $10^{-5}$, while all three classifiers attain the same macro F1 score of $0.224688$. We prove that between-class hidden scatter is bounded by total hidden scatter, which in turn is controlled by the reported hidden-state variance. Thus a nearly constant hidden representation cannot retain substantial class-separating structure. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse macro F1 nor prevent the $K=5$ collapse in the present DSAE setting. These results identify large-depth representation collapse as a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification.

AI.tldr: Encoder depth in Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAEs) for LiDAR classification leads to hidden-state collapse at depth 5, yielding no class separation; Product Coefficients do not mitigate the collapse; all classifiers show the same poor macro F1 (~0.225).
AI.motivation: Investigate whether deeper DSAEs retain discriminative information for LiDAR point clouds and assess the effectiveness of Product Coefficient feature augmentations in preserving separability.
AI.method: Evaluate DSAE encoders with depths K=1..5 on LiDAR xyz and xyz+Product Coefficient inputs. Assess hidden representations with Random Forest, kNN, and a dummy baseline. Analyze hidden-state variance and between-class scatter, and derive/bespeak a bound: between-class scatter is bounded by total scatter, which is governed by hidden-state variance.
AI.result: At K=5, hidden-state standard deviation falls to the order of 1e-5 for both input types; all three classifiers achieve macro F1 = 0.224688. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse macro F1 nor prevent the K=5 collapse.
AI.conclusion: Large-depth representation collapse is a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification; Product Coefficients do not salvage performance in the present setting.

title: Step-Level Preference Learning for Generative Agents in Social Simulations
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based generative agents simulate human behavior through long-horizon decision-making processes that comprise intermediate steps such as planning, memory retrieval, reflection, and action selection. However, fine-grained human annotations of these intermediate steps remain scarce, and existing agents are not grounded in human preferences over such intermediate decisions. To address this gap, we introduce \method, an interactive simulation interface that enables us to collect step-level human preference supervision over agent decision trajectories, leading to a dataset of 57K fine-grained annotations. We conduct step-level preference learning on open-weight language models using supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on this data, consistently improving simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality, and inducing more socially effective agent behavior. Our results show that step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.

AI.tldr: Introduces method, an interactive interface to collect step-level human preferences over agent decision trajectories, yielding 57K annotations and enabling step-level preference learning that improves long-horizon LLM agent behavior and social effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Addresses scarcity of fine-grained annotations for intermediate decision steps (planning, memory retrieval, reflection) and lack of grounding in human preferences over these steps to improve fidelity and sociality of LLM-based agents.
AI.method: Develops an interactive simulation interface (method) to collect step-level preferences; builds a dataset of 57K annotations; trains open-weight language models using supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization on this data.
AI.result: Step-level supervision consistently improves simulation fidelity, coordination, interaction quality, and socially effective behavior; demonstrates that aligning models to human preferences over intermediate decisions enhances both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.
