AI.conclusion: Step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving micro-decisions and macro-behavior in LLM-based agents, suggesting broader utility for alignment and behavior shaping through intermediate-step preferences.

title: ReBind: Multi-Reference Video Editing via Structured Instructions with Explicit Reference Relationships
summary: Recent diffusion-based video generation models have made significant progress in multi-reference image-conditioned video editing. However, existing methods still struggle to coordinate information from multiple visual sources accurately. We identify a critical deficiency in existing approaches. Existing editing instructions lack explicit reference relationships, and most multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot generate them reliably. To address this problem, we propose ReBind, a systematic framework that introduces semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens as the intermediate representation for multi-reference image-conditioned video editing. Our key insight is embedding reference tokens at semantic positions to eliminate ambiguity and establish precise bindings between visual attributes and their sources. We develop ReBind-Instruct, a specialized MLLM that learns to establish explicit bindings between visual attributes and their reference sources through a two-stage progressive scheme for precise reference relationships. We further develop ReBind-Edit, which enables lightweight adaptation of text-to-video models to coordinate multiple references by binding visual attributes to their designated sources. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReBind substantially outperforms general-purpose MLLMs in instruction quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods on reference image conditioned video editing. Our project webpage: https://rebind-mrv2v.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Introduces ReBind framework to embed reference tokens in semantic instructions for precise multi-reference image-conditioned video editing; includes ReBind-Instruct (MLLM with two-stage binding) and ReBind-Edit (lightweight T2V adaptation); demonstrates superior instruction quality and state-of-the-art open-source performance.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based video editing methods struggle to coordinate information from multiple visual references due to lack of explicit reference relationships; most multimodal LLMs cannot reliably generate such bindings, leading to ambiguity in outputs.
AI.method: Proposes semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens as an intermediate representation. ReBind-Instruct learns explicit bindings between visual attributes and their reference sources via a two-stage progressive scheme. ReBind-Edit enables lightweight adaptation of text-to-video models to coordinate multiple references by binding attributes to designated sources.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ReBind outperforms general-purpose MLLMs in instruction quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods on reference image-conditioned video editing; project page provided.
AI.conclusion: Embedding reference tokens at semantic positions yields unambiguous, explicit bindings between attributes and their sources, enabling accurate multi-reference video editing and enabling effective adaptation of text-to-video models.

title: Modeling and Validation of Quality of Control for Edge-Offloaded Collaborative Navigation
summary: Collaborative control in complex environments is severely challenged by stochastic wireless delay and reliability variations, which can degrade navigation, tracking, and collision avoidance. These network-induced uncertainties complicate the maintenance of energy efficiency during collaborative tasks, and can potentially lead to over-provisioning of resources. In this paper, for a navigation setup with dynamic collision avoidance, we address this challenge by expanding the quality of control (QoC) framework from prior works to practical robotic models. Our approach (i) models end-to-end network effects on closed-loop performance, (ii) systematically explores the impact of various control parameters dictating robotic motion on network latency-reliability (iii) validates these models through experiments on a private 5G testbed across varying delay, reliability and control configurations. Our analysis indicates the optimal control-communication co-design operating regimes for practical robots and also compares the QoC performance of standard ROS~2 quality of service (QoS) policies under real-world conditions and showing how RELIABLE QoS offers 51.5% better QoC than BEST-EFFORT under certain experimental settings.

AI.tldr: QoC-aware co-design for robotic navigation with dynamic collision avoidance over stochastic wireless networks; end-to-end network effects modeled, control-parameter impacts on latency-reliability analyzed, validated on a private 5G testbed, showing RELIABLE QoS can beat BEST-EFFORT by ~51.5% in QoC under certain conditions.
AI.motivation: Mitigate network-induced uncertainties (delay, reliability variations) that degrade navigation, tracking, and collision avoidance, and prevent over-provisioning while maintaining energy efficiency in collaborative tasks.
AI.method: Model end-to-end network effects on closed-loop performance; systematically study how control parameters affect network latency-reliability; validate with experiments on a private 5G testbed across varying delays, reliabilities, and control configurations.
AI.result: Characterized optimal control-communication co-design operating regimes for practical robots; demonstrated QoC gains and compared ROS2 QoS policies, with RELIABLE QoS achieving ~51.5% better QoC than BEST-EFFORT under certain conditions.
AI.conclusion: Extends QoC to practical robotic models, enabling improved navigation, tracking, and collision avoidance in uncertain networks and guiding ROS2 QoS policy selection.

title: Interleaved Noise Injection Improves Clean, Corrupted, and OOD Performance
summary: Noise injection is a well-known technique in stochastic optimization. We report its surprising effectiveness with an interleaved (on-off-on-off...) rather than the usual monotonic decay schedule. We present a theoretical analysis of noise injection, which confirms that corruption by impulse noise approximates a Jacobian regularization, whereas Gaussian noise acts as a curvature penalty. This regularization behavior has been invoked to explain why noise injection increases model robustness. But the interleaved nature of our proposed schedule produces superior results even for the optimization objective: mixing phases of noisy data permits the optimizer to escape local minima and increase exploration without the risk of catastrophically forgetting the important features from the clean data. To stabilize this training scheme against the rapid changes of the loss when switching between clean and noisy data, we introduce a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates based on clean gradient magnitudes. We compare this method with other common augmentation methods and find substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for ResNet and ViT architectures, with the best results being achieved by stacking our method on top of other augmentations. Through saliency and attention maps we show that the effect of interleaved noise injection stems from penalizing the failure modes encouraged by the inductive bias of the models: impulse noise works against the locality bias of convolutional (ResNet) architectures, and Gaussian noise reduces the tendency of attention-based models to pick up large-scale spurious features. Interleaved noise injection is therefore an effective tool to improve the test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data at essentially zero computational cost.

AI.tldr: Interleaved noise injection (on-off-on-off) with gradient-norm stabilization improves robustness and optimization performance, outperforming monotonic noise decay; impulse noise regularizes Jacobian, Gaussian noise regularizes curvature; effective across CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C/R for ResNet/ViT with minimal cost.
AI.motivation: Enhance model robustness and generalization under corrupted/noisy inputs and distribution shifts by improving optimization dynamics and regularization effects.
AI.method: Propose interleaved noise schedule (on-off-on-off). Theoretically analyze impulse vs Gaussian noise: impulse acts as Jacobian regularization, Gaussian as curvature penalty. Introduce gradient-norm stabilization to scale noisy updates by clean-gradient magnitudes. Empirically compare with standard augmentations on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R using ResNet and ViT; reveal saliency/attention analyses.
AI.result: Interleaved schedule yields better exploration, escapes local minima, and prevents catastrophic forgetting of clean features. Significant improvements in corruption tolerance and distribution shift robustness, especially when stacked with other augmentations. Impulse noise counters locality bias in CNNs; Gaussian noise mitigates reliance on large-scale spurious features in attention models. Zero additional computational cost at test-time.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved noise injection is an effective, low-cost augmentation strategy to improve performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data by counteracting inductive biases; it complements existing augmentations and can be integrated into standard training pipelines.

title: SAGA: Schema-Aware Grounding for Agentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation
summary: Complex knowledge base question answering (KBQA) is commonly approached through either information retrieval over a question-specific subgraph or semantic parsing into an executable logical form. We study the latter paradigm. Recent large language model agents make semantic parsing interactive: they alternate between reasoning, querying the knowledge base, and extending a partial SPARQL query. This interleaving reduces reliance on one-shot generation, but makes the quality of \emph{KB grounding} depend on what the interaction tools expose. Existing agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains and ranges, or the expected answer type. We call this failure mode \emph{type-blind grounding}. It enlarges the grounding search space and often produces plausible-looking but semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results. We propose SAGA (\underline{S}chema-\underline{A}ware \underline{G}rounding for \underline{A}gentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation), a training-free framework that turns property exploration into a schema-constrained grounding operation. SAGA maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents the remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence. Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

AI.tldr: SAGA is a training-free, schema-aware grounding framework for interactive text-to-SPARQL generation in complex KBQA. It counteracts type-blind grounding by maintaining a bidirectional type state, filtering incompatible properties at construction, and presenting schema-annotated patterns, handling missing schema with empirical evidence. It yields strong results across Wikidata/Freebase benchmarks, achieving top F1 on all nine settings and near-maximum exact-match on eight, while reducing empty results.
AI.motivation: Address the type-blind grounding problem in interactive semantic parsing for KBQA, where current agents rely on lexical cues and local evidence and often generate semantically incompatible patterns leading to empty results.
AI.method: SAGA is a training-free framework that maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction, presents remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively via empirical and trace-local evidence.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase shows SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while consistently reducing empty-result queries in Wikidata.
AI.conclusion: Schema-aware grounding improves property exploration in interactive SPARQL generation and SAGA is effective without training, enabling more semantically aligned KBQA.

title: GlobalForge: Towards Robust AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: AI-generated image (AIGI) detectors achieve strong accuracy on clean benchmarks, but their performance drops sharply after images are propagated through real-world channels. We trace this fragility to what these detectors actually learn: they overfit to local artifacts left by generators in small spatial neighborhoods, which are easily destroyed by common propagation degradations such as JPEG compression and blur. Instead, we shift the discriminative cue from fragile local artifacts to more robust global structure. Building on this, we propose GlobalForge, a framework with two complementary modules. The Local Information Bottleneck (LIB) suppresses local components to block shortcut learning, while the Global Structural Reasoning (GSR) module forces every token to gather evidence from distant regions. Both modules are trained jointly under a contrastive structural loss based on degradation that keeps the resulting features stable under degradation. To support fine-grained robustness evaluation, we further introduce RealDeg-Bench, covering 7 common degradation operators and multi-step compound chains. GlobalForge improves average BAcc on 8 in-the-wild benchmark groups by $\mathbf{5.89\%}$ over the previous state-of-the-art, and is clearly ahead of representative baselines on RealDeg-Bench under both single and compound degradations. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GlobalForge-BE0F/.

AI.tldr: GlobalForge introduces two complementary modules, Local Information Bottleneck (LIB) and Global Structural Reasoning (GSR), to shift AI-generated image detectors from fragile local artifacts to robust global structure. Trained with a degradation-aware contrastive loss, it improves robustness to real-world degradations. It also introduces RealDeg-Bench for fine-grained evaluation, reporting a 5.89% absolute gain in average balanced accuracy (BAcc) across 8 in-the-wild groups and outperforming baselines on RealDeg-Bench. Code is released.
AI.motivation: AIGI detectors trained on clean benchmarks overfit to local, generator-specific artifacts. Real-world channels introduce degradations (JPEG, blur) that destroy these cues, leading to sharp performance drops. There is a need for detectors that rely on robust, global cues and for a granular benchmark that captures degradation diversity.
AI.method: LIB suppresses local components to block shortcut learning. GSR enforces long-range evidence gathering by making every token attend to distant regions. Both modules are trained jointly with a degradation-based contrastive loss to keep features stable under degradation. RealDeg-Bench assesses robustness across 7 degradation operators and multi-step chains.
AI.result: GlobalForge achieves an average BAcc improvement of 5.89 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art across 8 in-the-wild groups and outperforms representative baselines on RealDeg-Bench under both single and compound degradations.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from fragile local artifacts to robust global structure improves AIGI detector robustness in real-world conditions. RealDeg-Bench provides a rigorous platform for evaluating degradation robustness. The framework and benchmark together advance practical detection of AI-generated imagery, with code availability to enable replication.

title: OASIS-Map: Object-Level Change Detection in Multi-Session Mapping using Semantic Correspondence Matching
summary: Map representations which are consistent across repeated visits to a real-world semi-static environment are very useful for long-term robotic inspection. In such settings, the scene may evolve while the robot is absent, with objects appearing, disappearing, moving, or being replaced, quickly making a static map outdated. Existing change-detection methods reason through geometry, category-level semantics, or object persistence. However, achieving reliable object association across revisits remains a key challenge, especially under partial views, occlusion, and imperfect segmentation. In this work, we propose OASIS-Map, a multi-session mapping system that maintains a spatio-temporally consistent object-level map by establishing dense patch-level semantic correspondences between temporal observations. These correspondences detect where the scene has changed and incrementally associate objects across revisits as the robot re-observes the environment. We demonstrate OASIS-Map on three challenging real-world scenarios: object rearrangements in 3RScan, visually similar car replacements in a car park, and large-scale scene changes in an outdoor market. We achieve 0.783 F1 on change detection in a car replacement scenario in a car park and 0.667 F1 on moved object association in 3RScan. https://dynamic.robots.ox.ac.uk/projects/oasis-map/

AI.tldr: OASIS-Map introduces dense patch-level semantic correspondences to build a spatio-temporally consistent object-level map across multiple sessions, enabling reliable change detection and object association during revisits in semi-static real-world environments.
AI.motivation: Long-term robotic inspection in semi-static environments requires maps that remain accurate despite scene changes between visits; existing methods struggle with reliable object association under partial views, occlusion, and imperfect segmentation; a robust multi-session, object-level mapping approach is needed.
AI.method: Proposes OASIS-Map, a multi-session mapping system that establishes dense patch-level semantic correspondences across temporal observations to maintain a spatio-temporally consistent object-level map and incrementally associate objects across revisits, enabling detection of scene changes.
AI.result: Demonstrated on three real-world scenarios (3RScan, car park, outdoor market); achieves 0.783 F1 on change detection for car replacements in a car park and 0.667 F1 on moved object association in 3RScan, illustrating improved robustness to partial views and occlusions.
AI.conclusion: OASIS-Map advances long-term, object-level mapping by leveraging dense semantic correspondences to achieve consistent representations across revisits, with strong quantitative performance on challenging change-detection and object-association tasks; suitable for real-world robotic inspection in evolving environments.

title: Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), the generalizability of the resulting models remains poorly understood. In this work, we establish the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale. Our approach adapts PAC-Bayes compression bounds to this setting, and addresses the inherent stochasticity of token generation by applying the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick. To operationalize these bounds, we propose the Progressive RLVR framework, which integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization. Progressive RLVR empirically retains 84-97% performance of standard LoRA fine-tuning while producing models that are 14,796x more compressible. We show that this framework yields non-vacuous generalization bounds in four domains: mathematical problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, and Text-to-SQL. Our bounds exceed the accuracy of the base model by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of the accuracy of the fine-tuned models.

AI.tldr: Non-vacuous PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning on billion-parameter LLMs, via Gumbel-max reparameterization; introduces Progressive RLVR, combining RLVR, on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and quantization to achieve high compressibility with near-finetuned performance across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: The generalization of RLVR-tuned LLMs remains poorly understood at scale. There is a need for non-vacuous generalization bounds that account for stochastic token generation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning in large models.
AI.method: Adapt PAC-Bayes compression bounds to RLVR with stochastic token generation using the Gumbel-max reparameterization. Propose Progressive RLVR, a framework that integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization.
AI.result: Progressive RLVR retains 84-97% of standard LoRA fine-tuning performance while achieving ~14,796x greater compressibility. Non-vacuous generalization bounds observed in four domains (math problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, Text-to-SQL); bounds exceed base model accuracy by 9-51% and are within 6-11% of the fine-tuned model accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Progressive RLVR demonstrates that non-vacuous generalization bounds are attainable for large-scale, parameter-efficient RLVR-tuned LLMs, with substantial compression and robust performance across diverse tasks.

title: Contextualized Evaluation of Vision Language Models through Dynamic, Multi-turn Interactions
summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial advances on benchmarks, yet their real-world effectiveness remains uncertain. This gap stems from the fundamental misalignment between benchmarks in controlled, static settings and the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we propose CEDI (Contextualized Evaluations of MLLMs through Dynamic, multi-round Interactions), a framework that recasts evaluation as a three-party interaction between an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversation guided by a graph-based representation of the task. By navigating state-space transitions, CEDI deploys diverse strategies, from clarification requests to adversarial probes, to elicit performance evidence. We apply CEDI to visual hallucinations. Empirical results across multiple models, diverse settings, datasets, and domains show that contextualized, interactive evaluations reveal not only significantly more hallucinations than conventional static evaluation but also ones that more closely resemble those arising in practical use cases. We further show that hallucinations often accumulate over long contexts, through self-reinforcing dialogue history, and models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. Together, these findings highlight CEDI as a step toward realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessments of MLLMs' capabilities. Code is available at github.com/williamium3000/cedi.

AI.tldr: CEDI is a novel, three-party, interactive evaluation framework for multi-modal LLMs that uses a graph-guided, multi-turn examiner to elicit evidence of performance, revealing more hallucinations and more ecologically valid behavior than static benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To address the mismatch between static benchmarks and real-world, interactive use of MLLMs by providing ecologically valid, context-aware evaluations.
AI.method: A three-party setup (evaluatee model, automated examiner, and a grader) where the examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversations guided by a graph-based task representation. The method navigates state-space transitions and employs strategies such as clarification requests and adversarial probes to elicit evidence of performance, particularly focusing on visual hallucinations.
AI.result: Contextualized evaluations uncover significantly more hallucinations than static benchmarks and produce results that better resemble real-world use. Hallucinations tend to accumulate over long contexts via dialogue history, and models are especially vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. The approach is demonstrated across multiple models, settings, datasets, and domains.
AI.conclusion: CEDI advances realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessment of MLLMs by capturing dynamic, interactive behavior; it is applicable across domains with code available for replication.

title: Team RAS in 11th ABAW Competition: Multimodal Ambivalence Recognition Approach
summary: Automatic recognition of ambivalence and hesitancy is challenging because these states may be expressed through inconsistent linguistic, acoustic, facial, and contextual patterns, while top-performing systems often rely on computationally expensive ensembles. We present a single text-centered multimodal approach for video-level ambivalence and hesitancy recognition for the 11th Affective & Behavior Analysis in-the-Wild (ABAW) Challenge. The proposed approach combines linguistic, acoustic, facial, and scene features using text-centered multimodal fusion model. Text Residual Fusion treats text as the anchor modality and applies gated residual adjustments based on the other modalities. Experiments on the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) corpus confirm that text is the strongest unimodal modality. The Text Residual Fusion model achieves an average Macro F1-score (MF1) of 75.14% across the Development and Public Test subsets. On the Private Test subset, it reaches an MF1 of 78.24%, outperforming the text model by 4.03%. These results demonstrate that complementary multimodal information can improve recognition performance without requiring a large model ensemble.

AI.tldr: A single text-centered multimodal model (Text Residual Fusion) for video-level ambivalence/hesitancy recognition that integrates linguistic, acoustic, facial, and scene cues, achieving strong MF1 scores without large ensembles.
AI.motivation: Ambivalence/hesitancy signals are inconsistently expressed across modalities, and state-of-the-art systems rely on expensive ensembles; a compact, effective model is desirable for practical AB AW challenge settings.
AI.method: Text Residual Fusion uses text as the anchor modality and applies gated residual adjustments from other modalities (linguistic, acoustic, facial, scene features) to fuse multimodal information for ambivalence/hesitancy recognition.
AI.result: MF1 of 75.14% on Development/Public Test and 78.24% on Private Test, with the text model being the strongest unimodal baseline and the proposed model outperforming it by 4.03% on the Private Test.
AI.conclusion: A complementary multimodal approach centered on text can boost recognition performance beyond text-only models while avoiding the computational cost of large ensemble methods.

title: Human-Robot Interaction in GenAI Architectures via the Agent-Client Protocol
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary:
Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are driving robotic architectures toward agent-based high-level orchestration, in which natural-language instructions can be translated into context-aware action sequences. While the integration of these agents and robotic capabilities is increasingly converging toward standardization through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the upper Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) layer remains fragmented by proprietary, ad hoc interfaces that hinder real-time human-in-the-loop collaboration.
  To address this fragmentation, this paper proposes the adoption of the Agent-Client Protocol (ACP) -- a communication standard originally introduced for coding agents in software engineering -- as a unified communication contract for the HRI layer in agent-based robotic systems. By combining ACP at the interface-agent link and MCP at the agent-execution link, we formulate a fully decoupled three-layer architecture that separates human interaction, deliberative orchestration, and physical execution. This topology removes rigid architectural dependencies, enabling heterogeneous user interfaces to connect to the same robotic system and allowing the underlying robotic platform to be replaced without requiring client-specific integration changes. Moreover, it provides native support for collaborative HRI capabilities such as real-time observability, explicit human authorization, and immediate task interruption. We experimentally evaluate the proposed architecture on a physical mobile robot, demonstrating interoperability across three heterogeneous user interfaces and validating real-time human-in-the-loop workflows with negligible latency overhead.

AI.tldr: Proposes Agent-Client Protocol (ACP) as a unified HRI layer for agent-based robotics, combining ACP (interface-agent) and MCP (agent-execution) to create a decoupled 3-layer architecture that supports heterogeneous UIs and interchangeable robots, enabling real-time human-in-the-loop interaction.
AI.motivation: Fragmentation of the upper HRI layer due to proprietary interfaces hinders real-time, human-in-the-loop collaboration and interoperability across interfaces and robotic platforms.
AI.method: Introduce a three-layer architecture: (1) human–interface with ACP, (2) deliberative orchestration via MCP, and (3) physical execution; couple ACP at the interface-agent link and MCP at the agent-execution link; demonstrate interoperability across three heterogeneous user interfaces on a physical mobile robot and validate real-time HRI workflows with low latency.
AI.result: Demonstrated interoperability across three heterogeneous user interfaces and validated real-time human-in-the-loop workflows with negligible latency overhead on a physical mobile robot.
AI.conclusion: A decoupled ACP–MCP architecture enables standardized, interchangeable, and observable human–robot collaboration, allows seamless replacement of robotic platforms without client‑side changes, and supports collaborative HRI features such as real-time observability, explicit human authorization, and immediate task interruption.

title: Adaptive Runge-Kutta Step Control Buys Training Loss, Not Generalization: An Honest Compute-Matched Study of RK-Adam Optimizers
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code, logs, and result JSONs: https://github.com/akigogikar/RK4Optimizer
summary: Interpreting optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations has motivated applying higher-order Runge-Kutta (RK) integrators to neural networks. We build a representative Adam variant (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair, FSAL reuse, local-error step control) and evaluate it under a strict compute-matched protocol giving every method the same gradient-evaluation budget - an accounting this literature rarely enforces. Under it the RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch (RK's best-case) training. Instrumenting it shows the "adaptivity" is illusory: normalized error stays far below tolerance, the step size pins at its growth cap from step one (98-100 percent of steps), and no rtol x hmax x h0 setting makes it act; tolerances spanning 100x give bit-identical trajectories. The method is exactly fixed-step Adam with an averaged gradient at 3-4x cost. Repairing it (true reject branch; error on the applied map) reverses the full-batch result - about 40x lower training loss than tuned Adam - and a fixed-step control isolates adaptivity (an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule) as the mechanism. But the gain is fragile to the initial step size and does not reach test accuracy. A pre-registered follow-up rules out the obvious explanations: deeper minimization does not overfit, and an explicit temperature knob only hurts - leaving a trajectory effect, the controller selecting a minimum generalizing 1.3-3.4 points below first-order descent at equal depth. An n=10 study confirms one secondary effect: gradient averaging is a genuine implicit regularizer, beating lr-matched Adam and AdamW on 10/10 seeds - yet RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at a third the per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but nothing a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline does not already provide.

AI.tldr: Higher-order RK optimizers under a strict compute budget do not surpass Adam; claimed adaptive steps are illusory; fixed-step variants with corrected maps can improve training loss but not generalization; gradient averaging acts as a genuine regularizer; overall benefits of higher-order adaptive integration are limited and costlier than strong first-order baselines.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether interpreting optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations yields practical gains and whether adaptive step control provides benefits beyond traditional first-order methods under realistic compute constraints.
AI.method: Implement Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair with FSAL reuse and local-error control as a representative higher-order adaptive optimizer; compare to Adam under a compute-matched protocol (equal gradient evaluations); instrument to characterize adaptivity, including forward-error maps and reject branches; test different tol settings; perform a pre-registered follow-up to probe deeper minimization, temperature knob, and ablations; conduct n=10 experiments to assess gradient averaging and other baselines (RMSprop, NAdam, AdamW).
AI.result: Under compute-matched protocol, the RK variant loses to plain Adam in training loss for both minibatch and full-batch settings; adaptivity is illusory (normalized error well below tolerance; step size sits at max; rtol/hmax/h0 settings do not activate adaptivity; trajectory is bit-identical across wide tolerances); the method is effectively a fixed-step Adam with 3–4x cost due to gradient averaging. Correcting the map via a true reject branch reverses the full-batch result, yielding ~40x lower training loss than tuned Adam, and a fixed-step control isolates adaptivity as an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule; however, gains are fragile to initial step size and do not reach test accuracy. Pre-registered follow-ups rule out deeper minimization as overfitting, while a temperature knob hurts; the trajectory effect suggests a modest generalization benefit of 1.3–3.4 points below first-order descent at the same depth. An n=10 study confirms gradient averaging provides a genuine implicit regularizer, beating lr-matched Adam/AdamW on 10/10 seeds, though RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at substantially lower per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration offers deeper deterministic minimization and slight regularization, but offers nothing beyond what a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline provides already.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order adaptive integration yields limited gains: it can induce deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but does not outperform cost-efficient first-order optimizers like Adam in typical training, nor improves generalization reliably. Gradient averaging shows some robustness, but overall benefits of the RK-adaptivity approach are marginal under compute-constrained training.

title: VLT: A Vision-Language-Time Series Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial Intelligence
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, and 13 tables, including supplementary material. Haiteng Wang and Jingheng Yan contributed equally to this work
summary: Industrial time series serve as the foundation for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) to ensure the reliability and safety of industrial equipment such as aero-engines. However, existing approaches are typically limited to single-modality modeling, which restricts their generalization in complex scenarios. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities for multimodal learning, bridging continuous time-series signals and discrete textual semantics remains an open challenge. To this end, we propose VLT, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. A key insight is to utilize the frequency spectrum as a visual bridge to connect continuous temporal signals with discrete semantics. Specifically, a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) is designed to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics, while a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner enables joint modeling of spectral and semantic features within a shared representation space. Furthermore, a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism is introduced to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts via gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting. Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets demonstrate that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes VLT, a multimodal foundation model integrating time-series, frequency-spectrum visuals, and text; uses Time-MoE and Frequency-Text Augmented Learner with a time-centric gradient alignment; claims improved robustness and generalization in industrial PHM tasks.
AI.motivation: Single-modality models limit generalization in complex Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) scenarios. Bridging continuous time-series signals with discrete textual semantics via frequency-domain representations can enable truly multimodal learning. LLMs offer multimodal capabilities, but aligning continuous signals with discrete language remains challenging. The work introduces a frequency-spectrum bridge to connect modalities.
AI.method: Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics. Frequency-Text Augmented Learner to jointly model spectral (frequency-domain visuals) and semantic (text) features in a shared representation space. Time-centric gradient alignment with gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets show VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.
AI.conclusion: VLT provides an effective multimodal PHM foundation model that bridges time-series signals and textual semantics via frequency-domain representations. The approach demonstrates robust generalization and suggests potential for broader industrial applications and future extensions.

title: Pretraining Multiple Instance Learning Networks with Multi-Teacher Distillation from Pathology Slide Foundation Models
summary: Multiple instance learning (MIL) has become the main paradigm for whole-slide image (WSI) analysis in computational pathology. However, existing MIL aggregators are still typically trained from scratch for each downstream task, relying on limited slide-level labels to learn both aggregation mechanisms and downstream discriminative representations simultaneously. As a result, they often suffer from unstable optimization, overfitting, and limited transferability. Similar to pretrained ResNet and Vision Transformer models in natural image learning, MIL also requires reusable pretrained initialization. However, high-quality slide-level pretraining data remain scarce, and MIL models are usually lightweight and weakly supervised, making large-scale pretraining difficult in practice. To address this challenge, we propose a distillation-based pretraining framework for MIL, which leverages two slide-level foundation models, TITAN and CARE, as teachers to transfer their representational knowledge into a diverse set of MIL architectures. To effectively balance supervision from different teachers, we further introduce an angular dispersion normalized distillation loss. The distilled weights are then used as initialization for downstream adaptation. We conduct systematic evaluations on 15 benchmark datasets under both linear probing and full-parameter fine-tuning, and further validate its advantages in few-shot scenarios. Experimental results show that pretraining generally improves MIL aggregators over from scratch training, especially in linear-probing and few-shot settings, while maintaining the computational efficiency of lightweight MIL models. Code is available at https://github.com/fu0201/MIL_Pretrained.

AI.tldr: Distillation-based MIL pretraining transfers knowledge from slide-level foundation models TITAN and CARE to lightweight MIL architectures via an angular dispersion loss, improving transferability and few-shot performance across 15 WSI benchmarks; code available.
AI.motivation: MIL aggregators trained from scratch on limited slide-level labels suffer unstable optimization, overfitting, and poor transfer; slide-level pretraining data are scarce, necessitating reusable pretrained initializations through distillation from existing foundation models.
AI.method: Use two slide-level teachers (TITAN and CARE) to distill representations into MIL architectures. Introduce an angular dispersion normalized distillation loss to balance supervision from both teachers. The distilled weights initialize downstream MIL models, which are then evaluated with linear probing and full-parameter fine-tuning (and few-shot scenarios) on 15 benchmark datasets. Code at the provided repository.
AI.result: Pretraining with distillation generally improves MIL aggregators over training from scratch, with pronounced gains in linear probing and few-shot settings, while preserving the lightweight, efficient nature of MIL models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distillation-based pretraining offers an effective transferable initialization for MIL in computational pathology, enhancing transferability and data efficiency across diverse tasks; code is publicly available.

title: Steering Robustness into World Action Models via Mechanistic Interpretability and Optimal Control
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) enable semantically- and physically-informed control but are brittle under distribution shift. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability to study how robustness-relevant perturbations are represented in WAM activation space. Comparing activations across successful and unsuccessful rollouts, we find some WAM architectures exhibit low-dimensional linear separability for robustness-critical features, while others do not. This motivates the use of contrastive activation directions for training-free WAM steering. We also show that local linearity in WAM activation dynamics enables efficient feedback steering via model-based optimal control, yielding World-Action Linear Quadratic Regulator (WA-LQR), a minimally-invasive reduced-order LQR controller. Via mechanistic evaluations, we predict strong steerability in the Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT models but weak steerability in LingBot-VA, consistent with steering intervention results. On Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT, WA-LQR generalizes contrastive directions to new tasks and improves robustness to camera, gripper, and visual-noise perturbations over unsteered and prompt steering baselines.

AI.tldr: WAMs show robustness-relevant perturbations are represented in their activation space; some architectures have low-dimensional linear separability for robustness features, enabling training-free WA-LQR steering via contrastive directions; WA-LQR uses local linearity for efficient model-based control and improves robustness on certain models.
AI.motivation: Understand robustness of World Action Models under distribution shift through mechanistic interpretability and develop a minimally-invasive steering method that exploits activation-space structure.
AI.method: Compare activations from successful vs. unsuccessful rollouts to assess linear separability of robustness-relevant features; identify contrastive activation directions for steering; derive WA-LQR as a reduced-order LQR controller leveraging local linearity; evaluate steerability and robustness across models (Cosmos-Policy, DiT4DiT, LingBot-VA) and perturbations (camera, gripper, visual noise).
AI.result: Some WAM architectures exhibit low-dimensional linear separability for robustness-critical features; WA-LQR provides training-free steering and, on Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT, generalizes contrastive directions to new tasks and improves robustness to perturbations compared with unsteered and prompt-steering baselines; LingBot-VA shows weak steerability.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals interpretable, low-dimensional activation structures that enable efficient steering; contrastive activation directions can be leveraged without training; WA-LQR delivers a practical, reduced-order controller with varying steerability across models, highlighting model-dependent robustness.

title: A Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning Framework for Fine-Tuning Discrete Diffusion Models
summary: We formulate reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous time with discrete state spaces and possibly arbitrary action spaces via a stochastic control approach, where the state dynamics are modeled as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). We consider policy optimization problems and derive the corresponding policy gradient methods, leading to continuous-time variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). As a primary application, we develop a complete continuous-time RL framework for fine-tuning score-based discrete diffusion models. The proposed framework enables reward-driven optimization without requiring differentiability on the reward signals. In contrast to the existing GRPO-based approaches that only rely on terminal rewards, our formulation allows intermediate reward or advantage signals to be incorporated throughout the denoising trajectory. Importantly, when specialized to masked diffusion models (MDMs), our framework encompasses a rich class of policy parameterizations over the vocabulary simplex with analytically tractable probability ratios, providing a unified perspective on exploration and policy optimization in MDMs. For masked diffusion large language models (dLLMs), we further propose trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate computationally prohibitive trajectory likelihoods, reducing the computational cost of computing per-position probability ratios. We showcase the effectiveness of our methods on both low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and RL post-training of dLLMs on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces a continuous-time RL framework for discrete-state, continuous-action settings using controlled CTMCs; derives continuous-time policy gradient methods and continuous-time PPO/GRPO; applies to score-based discrete diffusion models and masked diffusion models (MDMs), with trajectory subsampling for large LMs; demonstrates on simple entropy-regularized problems and RL fine-tuning of dLLMs on math/coding tasks.
AI.motivation: Motivate a unified, non-differentiable reward–driven RL framework for discrete-state systems with continuous-time dynamics, and to provide principled policy optimization for diffusion-based generative models and LMs with tractable probability ratios.
AI.method: Stochastic-control formulation of RL in continuous time for a controlled CTMC; development of continuous-time proximal-style policy gradients (PPO/GRPO); specialization to masked diffusion models yielding tractable policy parameterizations on the vocabulary simplex; for large language models, introduce trajectory subsampling to estimate trajectory likelihoods.
AI.result: Enables intermediate rewards along denoising trajectories, not just terminal rewards; offers a unified policy-optimization view for MDMs with analytic probability ratios; introduces trajectory subsampling to reduce cost of computing per-position likelihood ratios; empirical validation on small entropy-regularized problems and RL post-training of dLLMs for reasoning and coding tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a cohesive, reward-driven RL framework for continuous-time control of discrete-state diffusion processes, with explicit policy-gradient methods, applicability to diffusion-model fine-tuning, and scalable estimation techniques for large vocabulary models; it broadens exploration and optimization opportunities in diffusion-based generative modeling and dLLMs.

title: RetroAgent: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured Memory for Agentic Retrosynthesis Planning
summary: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning seeks to decompose a target molecule into commercially available building blocks through a sequence of feasible reactions. The vast combinatorial search space makes this task challenging even for expert chemists. Traditional methods combine tree search with offline-trained value networks that score candidates in isolation, without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task, but relies on simple interfaces that limit exploration of the full search space. We introduce RetroAgent, an LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning through a harness with structured memory. Through memory and chemistry tools, the agent observes the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, enabling informed decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that RetroAgent delivers strong performance and generalization.

AI.tldr: RetroAgent uses a memory-enabled LLM agent to couple symbolic search with neural reasoning for multi-step retrosynthesis, leveraging full search state and chemistry tools to improve exploration and generalization.
AI.motivation: The retrosynthesis search space is vast and combinatorial. Traditional offline-value networks score isolated candidates and miss global route reasoning; LLMs offer reasoning but are limited by interface that constrains exploration.
AI.method: Introduce RetroAgent, a memory-harness that connects symbolic search with neural reasoning via a structured memory. The agent uses chemistry tools and observes the full search state (explored routes, alternatives, intermediates’ properties) to perform informed, globally aware decisions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks shows strong performance and generalization of RetroAgent.
AI.conclusion: A memory-enabled LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning improves multi-step retrosynthesis planning and generalizes beyond the training distribution.

title: Variational Inference for Bird's Eye View Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
summary: The bird's eye view (BEV) has emerged as a pivotal approach for environmental perception in autonomous driving, providing a unified spatial representation for vehicles. Nevertheless, despite BEV's significance in addressing the challenges inherent to autonomous driving, effectively fusing data from multiple camera sensors and operating in complex external driving environments remains a considerable challenge. To mitigate this issue, we recast the BEV segmentation problem within a variational inference framework. In this paper, we propose a novel transformer-based variational flow transformation network for BEV segmentation, denoted as TVB. Our architecture implicitly learns the mapping from multiple camera views to a unified canonical BEV map during training by exploiting posterior BEV supervision. TVB employs a conditional variational auto encoder (CVAE) as its backbone and produces multiple BEV map candidates. To augment the realism of the generated BEV maps, we integrate normalizing flows into the map generation process, enabling the construction of more complex and expressive probability distributions. Furthermore, we design a BEV-attention fusion (BAF) module that harnesses attention mechanisms to adaptively integrate the multiple candidate BEV maps. Experimental results, evaluated on both the nuScenes and OPV2Vdatasets, demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance in multi-camera view BEV segmentation and lane environment perception.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based variational flow network (TVB) for BEV segmentation using CVAE with normalizing flows and BEV-attention fusion to fuse multi-camera data under a variational framework; achieves state-of-the-art results on nuScenes and OPV2V.
AI.motivation: BEV segmentation requires robust multi-view fusion in complex driving environments; existing methods struggle with uncertainty and realistic map generation. A variational inference approach with flow-based distributions can better model multi-view uncertainty and produce plausible BEV maps.
AI.method: TVB uses a CVAE backbone to generate multiple BEV candidates, then augments realism with normalizing flows to form expressive distributions. A BEV-attention fusion (BAF) module adaptively fuses candidate BEV maps. The model learns a unified canonical BEV map from multiple camera views via posterior BEV supervision and transformer-based architecture.
AI.result: On nuScenes and OPV2V datasets, TVB achieves superior performance in multi-camera BEV segmentation and lane environment perception, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness due to the variational formulation and adaptive fusion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TVB framework reframes BEV segmentation as a variational inference problem, leveraging flow-based expressivity and attention-driven fusion to better integrate multi-camera data in challenging driving environments.

title: AeroAct: Action-Centered World-Action Models for Language-Conditioned Quadrotor Flight
summary: Language-conditioned quadrotor flight requires a policy to ground semantic goals, anticipate the visual consequences of ego-motion, and output control references that remain smooth and dynamically executable under rapidly changing first-person views. Existing aerial vision-language navigation and vision-language-action methods commonly use discrete actions, high-level waypoints, or instantaneous velocity commands, which provide limited supervision about how flight actions change future observations. We present AeroAct, an action-centered world-action model (WAM) for quadrotor navigation. To the best of our knowledge, AeroAct is the first WAM instantiated and demonstrated for real-world aerial flight. The model adapts a pretrained video diffusion Transformer to predict local trajectory-action chunks from egocentric visual history, proprioception, and language. Future first-person frames are used during training as dense consequence supervision, while deployment directly decodes actions without generating future video. To obtain aligned visual, state, language, and dynamically feasible action data, we build a DiffAero-based pipeline with complementary Isaac Lab and 3D Gaussian splatting renderers. We further introduce a low-cost handheld collection device that couples camera observations with motion estimates to recreate flight-like egocentric trajectories, and a self-guidance procedure that improves temporal consistency across overlapping trajectory chunks. Closed-loop simulation and real-world experiments show that temporal visual context improves target tracking and object-search performance, and that WAM-based policies can be executed on a physical quadrotor.

AI.tldr: AeroAct introduces an action-centered world-action model for quadrotor navigation that predicts local trajectory-action chunks from egocentric history and language, trained with future frame supervision, enabling real-world execution and improved visual-grounded flight.
AI.motivation: Existing aerial vision-language systems rely on discrete actions or instantaneous commands and lack supervision linking actions to future observations; a continuous, dynamically feasible action-grounding model is needed for robust, language-conditioned flight.
AI.method: Adapt a pretrained video diffusion Transformer into a world-action model that outputs trajectory-action chunks conditioned on visual history, proprioception, and language. Train with future frames as dense supervision; deployment decodes actions directly. Build a DiffAero-based data pipeline with Isaac Lab and 3D Gaussian splatting renderers; introduce a low-cost handheld data-collection device; apply self-guidance to ensure temporal consistency across overlapping chunks.
AI.result: In simulation and real flight, incorporating temporal visual context improves target tracking and object search; WAM-based policies run on a physical quadrotor.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates the first real-world instantiation of a world-action model for aerial flight, enabling grounded, dynamically feasible, language-conditioned control and providing data pipelines and procedures for future aerial WAM development.

title: xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of Transformers into $N$ parallel streams, providing a form of memory scaling beyond model width and depth. Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes this formulation at scale. The large gains from $N{=}1$ to $N{=}4$ suggest residual-stream expansion as a promising scaling axis. However, existing HC-family methods typically stop at $N{=}4$. Our experiments reveal why: scaling mHC beyond this point yields diminishing performance gains and rapidly increasing training cost. We attribute this limitation to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information for an expanding number of streams and residual-mixing generation whose cost scales cubically with $N$. To address both bottlenecks, we propose xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections), the first HC-family method to achieve meaningful expansion beyond $N{=}4$. xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only $k=4$ of the $N=16$ streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC delivers strong and consistent downstream improvements. On an 18B MoE model, xHC improves the average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC, while adding only modest training FLOPs over the vanilla baseline. Scaling-law experiments show that the vanilla and mHC require $1.50\times$ and $1.19\times$ the compute of xHC, respectively, to reach the same loss. Practical large-$N$ training also requires controlling memory traffic from the expanded residual state. We therefore introduce xHC-Flash, which reduces the per-sublayer memory traffic from $73.5C$ to $40C$, comparable to the $34C$ required by mHC at $N{=}4$, while retaining the gains of full xHC. Together, xHC and xHC-Flash make large-$N$ residual-stream expansion effective and practical for LLM pre-training.

AI.tldr: Proposes xHC, an expanded hyper-connection (HC) scheme that enables large-N residual-stream expansion in Transformers. It addresses bottlenecks (write-back information and cubic residual-mixing cost) with temporal feature augmentation and sparse updates (k=4 of N=16) plus full dense residual access. Introduces xHC-Flash to reduce memory traffic. Empirically improves 18B/28B MoE models; xHC is more compute-efficient to reach the same loss than vanilla/mHC; supports scaling-law analyses and practical large-N training for LLMs.
AI.motivation: To push residual-stream expansion beyond small N (beyond 4) in HC-family methods, which previously showed diminishing returns due to information write-back and residual-mixing costs, hindering practical large-N scaling.
AI.method: Introduce xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections) with temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back and a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only k=4 of N=16 streams while retaining dense access to the full residual. Also present xHC-Flash to reduce per-sublayer memory traffic. Validate on 18B and 28B MoE models, with scaling-law analyses.
AI.result: xHC yields strong downstream gains: ~4.0 points average improvement over mHC on an 18B MoE model, with modest training FLOPs increase over vanilla baseline. Scaling laws indicate vanilla and mHC require ~1.50x and ~1.19x the compute of xHC to reach the same loss. xHC-Flash reduces memory traffic from 73.5C to 40C, near the 34C of mHC at N=4, preserving xHC gains.
AI.conclusion: xHC and xHC-Flash make large-N residual-stream expansion practical for LLM pre-training, enabling meaningful expansion beyond N=4 with controlled compute and memory overhead.

title: WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays
summary: This study presents WrAFT, a Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool, that delivers both accurate and reliable scores and effective comprehensive feedback to argumentative essays. WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. In building the system, various Large Language Models (LLMs) have been evaluated, including LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7, through both direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning approaches. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores was utilized. Benchmark-based evaluation shows that WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring, with a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.44 against official scores on a scale of 0-5. Human evaluation of system-generated feedback also reveals high approval ratings: 96.14 percent for surface-level feedback, 93.03 percent for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69 percent for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface has been developed for the system and is publicly available and free to use.

AI.tldr: WrAFT is a modular automated writing evaluation system for argumentative essays that achieves state-of-the-art scoring (QWK 0.84, RMSE 0.44 on a 0-5 scale) and high-quality human-perceived feedback using multiple LLMs; the dataset comprises 480 TOEFL essays with official scores, and an interactive UI is publicly available.
AI.motivation: To provide both reliable scoring and effective comprehensive feedback for argumentative essays via a modular AWE system leveraging multiple LLMs and a labeled TOEFL dataset.
AI.method: Modular design with three components (scoring, surface-level feedback, deep-level feedback). Evaluation of LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7) via direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning. Training/evaluation on a proprietary 480-essay TOEFL dataset with official scores. Benchmark-based scoring evaluation (QWK, RMSE) and human evaluation of feedback. An interactive UI is developed and publicly available.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art scoring performance (QWK 0.84, RMSE 0.44) against official scores; high user approval for surface-level and deep-level feedback (96.14%, 93.03%, 94.69% respectively). UI publicly accessible.
AI.conclusion: The WrAFT framework demonstrates that a modular AWE approach using selected LLMs can deliver accurate scoring and high-quality, multi-level feedback, with an accessible public interface, indicating practical viability for argument-based writing evaluation. Limitations on dataset size and domain generalizability are not detailed in the abstract.

title: VideoSEMA: a scalable and efficient Mamba-like attention for video understanding
summary: We present for video understanding (classification) a split space-time attention model, VideoSEMA, consisting of a scalable and efficient Mamba-like attention (SEMA) block in space and a softmax temporal attention in time. In each frame, SEMA attention applies a local window attention in parallel with a global averaging in a Mamba macro-architecture, which is called Mamba-like. Under certain rank conditions, we prove that the computationally cheaper split space-time attention is equivalent to full space-time attention. On benchmark K400 data sets, VideoSEMA out-performs heavier vision transformer and Mamba models. On benchmark SSv2 data, VideoSEMA leads in top-1 accuracy among models of similar parameter sizes. As image resolution scales up from standard $224^2$ to $1024^2$ on K400 and without fine-tuning, VideoSEMA degrades much more gracefully than VideoMamba in accuracy. It is promising to extend VideoSEMA to longer videos with a dilated/sparse temporal attention.

AI.tldr: VideoSEMA introduces a scalable split space-time attention for video classification: local window plus global Mamba-like spatial attention per frame, coupled with softmax temporal attention. Under rank conditions, split attention is equivalent to full space-time attention, enabling competitive results with lighter models; it scales better with resolution and shows strong performance on K400 and SSv2, with potential extension to longer videos via dilated temporal attention.
AI.motivation: Improve efficiency and accuracy of video understanding by rethinking space-time attention to be split and scalable, reducing computation while maintaining expressive power.
AI.method: Propose VideoSEMA: per-frame a SEMA block that combines local window spatial attention in parallel with a global averaging in a Mamba-like macro-architecture, and a softmax temporal attention across frames. The authors prove equivalence to full space-time attention under rank conditions and validate on K400 and SSv2. They compare to VideoMamba and explore resolution scaling, suggesting extension to longer videos with dilated/sparse temporal attention.
AI.result: VideoSEMA outperforms heavier vision transformers and Mamba models on K400. On SSv2, it achieves top-1 accuracy among models with similar parameter counts. When image resolution increases from 224^2 to 1024^2 on K400 without fine-tuning, VideoSEMA degrades more gracefully than VideoMamba. The work suggests extending to longer videos using dilated/sparse temporal attention.
AI.conclusion: Split space-time attention can be as expressive as full space-time attention under certain rank conditions while offering computational efficiency; VideoSEMA is a strong, scalable approach for video classification with favorable scalability and promising extensions to longer sequences.

title: CosFly-VLA: A Spatially Aware Vision-Language-Action Model for UAV Tracking
summary: Dynamic target tracking is essential for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) operating in complex urban environments, where both the target and the camera viewpoint change continuously. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies can track visible targets effectively, but their performance often degrades when buildings, vegetation, or roadside objects block the line of sight. During sustained occlusion, a policy may lose the target state, execute actions toward an incorrect region, and amplify this error through subsequent observations until re-acquisition becomes impossible. To this end, we present CosFly-VLA, a spatially aware VLA model that jointly grounds the target, estimates its visibility, and generates continuous flight actions through a structured prediction interface. To train this policy, we use a large-scale recipe over diverse data sources. Spatially Grounded Continued Pretraining (CPT) on a 500k mixed pool injects UAV-view depth, distance, and 3-D spatial reasoning. A three-stage Curriculum-based Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) process then specializes the tracker through multi-head warm-up followed by two-stage curriculum learning over natural and hard / long-occlusion data. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training subsequently teaches recovery-oriented reasoning traces before structured answers. Finally, a closed-loop Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage optimizes tracking behavior with a multi-component reward covering stand-off tracking, grounding quality, collision avoidance, and task success. Relative to OpenVLA, CosFly-VLA-0.8B reduces open-loop Average Displacement Error (ADE) by 34.1% on seen-test and 35.3% on unseen-test. Closed-loop optimization improves Success Rate (SR) by 29.8% and 2.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate progress from visible-frame imitation toward spatially grounded action-closed-loop control, evaluated under a shared oracle state history.

AI.tldr: CosFly-VLA is a spatially aware VLA model for UAV dynamic target tracking under occlusion, achieving substantial ADE and SR gains over OpenVLA via CPT, curriculum SFT, CoT, and RL.
AI.motivation: Occlusion by urban structures degrades existing Vision-Language-Action policies; there is a need for spatial grounding, visibility estimation, and closed-loop control to maintain target tracking.
AI.method: CosFly-VLA grounds the target, estimates visibility, and generates continuous flight actions through a structured prediction interface. Training uses Spatial Grounded Continued Pretraining (CPT) on 500k mixed data to inject UAV-view depth and 3D reasoning; three-stage Curriculum-based Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with warm-up and curriculum over natural and hard/long-occlusion data; Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training for recovery-oriented reasoning; and a closed-loop Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage with a multi-component reward (stand-off tracking, grounding quality, collision avoidance, task success).
AI.result: Compared to OpenVLA, CosFly-VLA-0.8B reduces open-loop Average Displacement Error (ADE) by 34.1% on seen-test and 35.3% on unseen-test. Closed-loop optimization improves Success Rate (SR) by 29.8% and 2.5%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates progress from visible-frame imitation toward spatially grounded action-closed-loop control for UAV tracking, evaluated under a shared oracle state history.

title: Muse: Representation Geometry of Muon Beyond Normalized Momentum
summary: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map to matrix momentum, but their updates also depend on the representation of each parameter block before orthogonalization. We study this representation choice as a form of optimizer geometry and introduce {\method}, a family of Muon-style optimizers that shares the same momentum rule and Newton--Schulz backend across native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations. Each Frobenius-isometric representation induces a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry, in which the shorter matrix dimension determines the number of supported singular channels, the pullback scaling, and the constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. In a teacher--student model, curvature collapse and an isotropic Marchenko--Pastur spectral profile connect early-stage dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio. Pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M, together with fixed-momentum diagnostics, show that balanced non-native representations can match the performance of the native representation, whereas reducing the shorter dimension weakens the scaling and singular-channel support, leading to behavior that increasingly resembles normalized momentum.

AI.tldr: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map to matrix momentum, with a family of representations (native, nearest-square, skinny, vector) sharing the same momentum rule and Newton–Schulz backend. Each Frobenius-isometric representation induces a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry; the shorter matrix dimension controls the number of supported singular channels, pullback scaling, and stochastic nonconvex convergence constants. A teacher–student analysis links curvature collapse and Marchenko–Pastur spectra to early-stage dissipation via a norm ratio. Pretraining on LLaMA2-130M/600M with fixed momentum shows balanced non-native representations can match native performance; shrinking the shorter dimension weakens scaling and singular-channel support, drifting toward normalized momentum.
AI.motivation: Understand how parameter representation choices in Muon-style optimizers shape optimizer geometry, convergence properties, and practical performance across native and non-native representations; establish a unified framework with shared momentum backend across representations; connect spectral properties to optimization dynamics.
AI.method: Define Muon-style family with polar map and Newton–Schulz backend. Systematically analyze native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations under Frobenius-isometric constraints. Derive polar steepest-descent geometries and link short dimension to singular channels and pullback scaling. Employ a teacher–student setup to relate curvature, spectral profiles (Marchenko–Pastur), and early dissipation. Conduct pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and 600M with fixed-momentum diagnostics to compare representations.
AI.result: Each Frobenius-isometric representation yields a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry. Shorter matrix dimension sets the number of supported singular channels, pullback scaling, and constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. Curvature collapse and an isotropic MP spectral profile connect early dissipation to the represented norm ratio. Balanced non-native representations can match native performance; reducing the shorter dimension weakens scaling and singular-channel support, causing behavior to resemble normalized momentum.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer geometry in Muon-style methods is representation-dependent. Balanced non-native representations can achieve native performance, but shrinking the shorter dimension degrades scaling and singular-channel support, steering behavior toward normalized momentum. The framework generalizes momentum rules across representations via a shared Newton–Schulz backend.

title: Are LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Production-Ready? A Trace-Driven Benchmark and Optimization Agent
comment: Both artifacts are released as open source: Atrex-Bench (https://github.com/alibaba/atrex-bench) and Atrex-Kernel-Agent (https://github.com/alibaba/atrex-kernel-agent)
summary: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks draw problems from synthetic or curated sources that diverge from deployed workloads. We present Atrex-Bench, a benchmark whose 30 operators and 440 shapes are sampled directly from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Each problem carries an importance weight derived from its share of observed GPU time, weighted by application card-hours and computed separately for the serving phases in which it runs, together with a per-problem roofline ceiling, so the aggregate score emphasizes the kernels that consume the most serving time. Evaluating six frontier coding agents on Atrex-Bench shows that even the best vanilla model reaches only ${\sim}10\%$ of the hardware roofline on production operators; and correctness alone overstates capability, since much of the apparent pass rate comes from PyTorch fallbacks rather than kernels the model wrote. To close this gap, we co-release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven kernel-optimization agent that combines iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout for escaping stalled search contexts, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference-kernel files and 244 optimization-knowledge documents, plus external upstream reference projects for API/ISA lookup). In a controlled case study, the agent converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines.

AI.tldr: A production-trace–driven GPU kernel benchmark suite (Atrex-Bench) and a profile-driven optimizer (AKA) that closes the gap between frontier models and production kernels, turning zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that meet or exceed hand-tuned baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rely on synthetic or curated sources and fail to reflect deployed workloads. The benchmark emphasizes serving-time impact and aims to measure kernels that actually contribute the most GPU time in production.
AI.method: Construct Atrex-Bench by sampling 30 operators and 440 shapes from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Assign per-problem importance weights based on observed GPU time and serving-phase weight; apply per-problem roofline ceilings. Evaluate six frontier coding agents; observe that vanilla models reach ~10% of the hardware roofline and that correctness overstates capability due to PyTorch fallbacks. Develop Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA) with iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference-kernel files and 244 optimization-docs, plus external API/ISA references).
AI.result: Six frontier agents show vanilla models only reach around 10% of the hardware roofline; many apparent passes arise from PyTorch fallbacks rather than real kernels. AKA converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines in a controlled case study.
AI.conclusion: Profile-driven kernel optimization powered by a substantial knowledge base can close the gap to production performance. Atrex-Bench provides a realistic, workload-aligned benchmark, and AKA demonstrates practical capability to generate efficient kernels beyond naive models.

title: Causal-Adversarial Probing of Clinical Covariates for Prostate MRI Grading
summary: Deep learning models for prostate MRI-based cancer grading may encode clinical covariates that either reflect useful disease-related signal or non-generalising shortcut information, but their role is usually assumed. We propose a causal-reasoning framework for probing covariate dependence in MRI-based International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group prediction. Rather than treating mpMRI as a direct cause of grade, we model MRI appearance and ISUP grade as observations of latent tumour pathology, and test whether candidate clinical variables act as nuisance correlates, disease-related proxies, or irrelevant covariates in the learned representation. We implement this using an adversarial framework that suppresses the decodability of individual clinical covariate at a time while preserving MRI-based grade prediction. The approach is developed and evaluated on 2,903 prostate MRI examinations, with external validation on 576 patients. We report a set of interesting and previously under-explored imaging-to-clinical-variable interactions in the context of deep learning generalisation. For examples, in binary ISUP Grade Group $\geq2$ classification, suppressing age, BMI, and alcohol use improved AUC by 1.23%, 0.84%, and 1.42%, respectively (all p < 0.05), suggesting reduced non-generalising covariate information; In contrast, suppressing PSA and prostate volume degraded AUC by 1.91% and 7.61% (all p < 0.001), indicating that these variables carried task-relevant signal.
