These findings show that adversarial covariate suppression can provide a practical representation-level analysis for distinguishing potentially harmful dependence from informative signal in prostate MRI grading models.

AI.tldr: A causal-adversarial framework is proposed to probe how clinical covariates influence MRI-based ISUP Grade Group predictions by suppressing their decodability in the learned representation; results show some covariates act as nuisance (age, BMI, alcohol) while others carry task-relevant signal (PSA, prostate volume), guiding generalization considerations.
AI.motivation: To address whether deep learning models for prostate MRI grading rely on non-generalizable covariates or on disease-related signals, and to provide a representation-level tool to distinguish these effects.
AI.method: Model MRI appearance and ISUP grade as latent pathology observations. Use an adversarial setup to suppress decodability of each clinical covariate at a time while preserving grade prediction, effectively separating nuisance from informative covariates. Evaluate on 2,903 prostate MRI exams with external validation on 576 patients.
AI.result: Suppression of age, BMI, and alcohol use improved AUC (by 1.23, 0.84, and 1.42 percentage points, respectively; all p<0.05), suggesting reduced non-generalizing covariate information. Suppression of PSA and prostate volume degraded AUC (by 1.91% and 7.61%; both p<0.001), indicating these covariates contain task-relevant signal. External validation supported the approach and revealed interesting covariate interactions in generalisation.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial covariate suppression provides a practical, representation-level method to distinguish harmful from informative covariate dependence in MRI-based prostate cancer grading, with implications for improving model generalization and understanding covariate roles.

title: Risk-Aware Belief Control Barrier Functions over Random Finite Sets
summary: Ensuring robot safety in unknown, dynamic environments is a fundamental requirement. It involves inferring the states of an unknown and time-varying number of moving objects from noisy, incomplete measurements. We address safe control under the induced multi-object state uncertainty with a risk-aware belief control barrier function (BCBF) framework. The uncertainty is captured by a random finite set (RFS) belief, estimated by a sequential Monte Carlo probability hypothesis density (SMC-PHD) filter that represents it with a set of particles. Building directly on these particles, we construct a nonsmooth BCBF, establish forward invariance of the safe set under continuous prediction, and derive an explicit condition under which discrete updates preserve safety. Simulation and real-world underwater experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Introduces risk-aware belief control barrier function (BCBF) for safe robot control under uncertain, time-varying multi-object states represented by random finite sets; leverages an SMC-PHD filter for belief representation on particles; builds a nonsmooth BCBF directly from particles, proving forward invariance during continuous prediction and deriving a condition for discrete updates to preserve safety; validated via simulations and real underwater experiments.
AI.motivation: Safe robot operation in unknown, dynamic environments with an unknown and time-varying number of moving objects, under noisy and incomplete measurements; need guarantees that the robot remains within a safe set despite multi-object state uncertainty.
AI.method: Model multi-object uncertainty with a random finite set (RFS) belief estimated by a sequential Monte Carlo PHD (SMC-PHD) filter, representing belief as a particle set. Construct a nonsmooth BCBF directly on these particles, establish forward invariance of the safe set under continuous prediction, and derive an explicit safety-preserving condition for discrete measurement updates; validate with simulations and real-world underwater experiments.
AI.result: Demonstrates safety guarantees under multi-object uncertainty with a tractable, particle-based implementation; shows effective safe control in simulations and practical underwater experiments, highlighting computational efficiency and robustness to measurement noise.
AI.conclusion: The BCBF framework integrates RFS-based belief with barrier-based safety guarantees for multi-object systems under uncertainty. It offers a principled approach to safe control in dynamic, cluttered environments and is validated both in simulation and real-world underwater tests, with potential extensions to broader sensing modalities and more complex dynamics.

title: CASP: Learning-Augmented Offline Approximation with Verifiable Certificates and Bounded-Loss PAC Guarantees
summary: Machine-learned predictions can speed up offline NP-hard optimization, but asking a predictor what to do amounts to asking it to solve the problem, and committing an unchecked prediction forfeits every worst-case guarantee. CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) instead asks which parts of the search space may be ignored, and accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier has checked it, so correctness never depends on prediction quality. We develop the learning theory of this design. The verifier makes the induced loss class uniformly bounded, so certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples ($K$ the maximum instance size), whereas the unverified commitment class admits no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread $R$, none below $Ω(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner, with a margin we compute in closed form, and the prediction stays useful even given the LP, because it breaks ties on degenerate optimal faces, where every symmetric LP policy, meaning one whose commitments depend on the instance only through the verifiable confidence values, provably stalls. Experiments on five problems test the theory's quantitative predictions. With trained predictors, unverified pruning loses up to $26%$ of the optimum under distribution shift, while the verified deployment of the same predictions loses nothing.

AI.tldr: Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning (CASP) enables verifiable pruning decisions for NP-hard optimization, with learnable certificate parameters and favorable sample complexity; verified deployment matches or exceeds unverified pruning in robustness, while preserving optimality under distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: To provide correctness guarantees when leveraging learning for pruning, by factoring the predictor into verifiable certificates that can be checked in polynomial time, thus avoiding reliance on predictor quality for guarantees.
AI.method: Develop the learning theory of verifiable pruning: the verifier induces a uniformly bounded loss class, making certificate parameters learnable from ~O~(ε^{-2} log K) samples (K= max instance size). Compare with the unverified commit class, which has no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread R, cannot do better than Ω(R/ε^2). Show that filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner with a closed-form margin. Argue that predictions remain useful even with LPs, as they break ties on degenerate optimal faces where symmetric LP policies stall. Validate theory with experiments on five problems.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds establish sample-efficiency for learning certificates and demonstrate superior robustness of verified pruning over unverified pruning under distribution shift (up to 26% loss with unverified pruning vs. zero loss with verification). The closed-form margin for filtering and the tie-breaking role of predictions are key insights. Empirical results on five problems corroborate the theory's quantitative predictions.
AI.conclusion: Verification-augmented pruning yields robustness to prediction noise without sacrificing optimality. The learning theory provides concrete sample-complexity bounds, and empirical results confirm substantial practical gains over unverified pruning, especially under distribution shift.

title: Towards an Intention Abstraction Layer for Autonomous Industrial Systems
summary: Modern industrial environments increasingly run many autonomous subsystems at once - schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets - each pursuing its own goals while sharing the same physical resources. Because high-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded, no running component can tell whether it is still doing what was actually intended, and goal conflicts surface only after they have caused a missed target or a shutdown. We propose the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domainagnostic middleware that represents intentions as first-class, persistent, and explainable runtime objects: a large language model grounded in a formal OWL ontology parses naturallanguage goals into structured intentions, a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time, before execution, and a transparency module explains them in natural language. We report a first proof of concept in which two autonomous agents register conflicting production and energy intentions, and the IAL flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer. The result is a mechanism that shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking.

AI.tldr: IAL is a middleware that uses an LLM grounded in OWL to translate natural-language goals into structured intentions, enabling pre-execution conflict detection and explainability; demonstrated with two agents, showing conflicts are flagged before execution.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of assurance in multi-agent, resource-constrained industrial settings by moving from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution intention-level checking using a formal ontology and explainable AI.
AI.method: A domain-agnostic middleware where a large language model grounded in a formal OWL ontology parses natural-language goals into structured intentions; a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time; a transparency module explains conflicts in natural language; validated via a proof-of-concept with two agents registering conflicting production and energy goals.
AI.result: The approach flags and explains conflicts before they reach the execution layer, demonstrating pre-execution intention-level checking and improving behavioral assurance in cooperating autonomous systems.
AI.conclusion: IAL offers a persistent, explainable, domain-agnostic layer that mediates intentions, enabling safer, more reliable cooperation among autonomous subsystems by preventing misaligned goals before execution.

title: Multimodality as Supervision: Self-Supervised Specialization to the Test Environment via Multimodality
summary:
Cross-modal learning, i.e., learning to predict one modality from another, is a fundamental mechanism for self-supervision via leveraging multimodality. Many practical applications, e.g., deploying a household robot, involve devices that are equipped with a rich set of sensors that enable multimodal sensing in their test environment. This presents an opportunity to apply cross-modal learning to the multimodal data sensed by these devices to learn representations. Findings in developmental psychology also suggest that biological agents leverage it to build an effective representation of their surroundings.
  To study this, we propose a controlled setup, where we restrict a user device to just a given test environment. It results in a specialization setup where we attempt to develop a performant model for this specific test environment. Under this setup, we develop Test-Space Training (TST), which performs multimodal data collection in the test environment and performs self-supervised pre-training on it. We evaluate these models on various downstream tasks in the same environment.
  Under this setup, we find various interesting insights, such as collecting rich multimodal data only from the test environment and leveraging cross-modal learning, we can achieve competitive results with generalist models (e.g., DINOv2 and CLIP) pre-trained on large-scale internet datasets. This enables an alternative scenario where the need for external Internet-scale datasets for pre-training models is reduced. We also present a set of analyses and ablations that raise intriguing points on substituting data with (multi)modality, and how varying pre-training data enables a tradeoff between a model's abilities to specialise to a test environment, and generalize to held-out spaces.

AI.tldr: Introduces Test-Space Training (TST): collects multimodal data in a restricted test environment to perform self-supervised pretraining, achieving competitive results with generalist models pretrained on internet-scale data; analyzes specialization vs generalization tradeoffs.
AI.motivation: Leverage cross-modal self-supervision in device-constrained, environment-specific settings and reduce dependence on large external datasets for pretraining.
AI.method: Propose a controlled setup where a user device is restricted to a single test environment. Collect multimodal data in that environment and perform self-supervised pretraining (Test-Space Training, TST). Evaluate downstream tasks within the same environment and conduct ablations on data modalities and pretraining data.
AI.result: Cross-modal learning on test-environment data yields competitive performance with generalist models like DINOv2 and CLIP that were pretrained on large internet-scale datasets. Rich multimodal data from the test environment and cross-modal learning can substitute for some external data; ablations reveal tradeoffs between specialization to the environment and generalization to held-out spaces.
AI.conclusion: TST offers an environment-specialized pretraining paradigm that can reduce reliance on internet-scale datasets. It prompts questions about substituting data quantity with modality richness and highlights tradeoffs between optimal specialization for a test environment and broader generalization; warrants further exploration across environments and modalities.

title: Learning Agile Navigation in Crowded Environments for Quadruped Robots
summary: Navigating dynamic and crowded environments presents significant challenges for quadruped robots due to severe sensor occlusion and unpredictable human motion. Existing approaches face a trade-off: model-based methods, such as Velocity Obstacles (VO), theoretically guarantee safety but rely on accurate obstacle motion estimates that often fail in dense crowds, while end-to-end learning methods offer robustness but lack motion prediction capability of obstacles, leading to collisions or conservative behaviors. To solve this, we propose VOP-Nav, a novel navigation system that combines the geometric safety of VO with the agile adaptability of end-to-end learning. Using only local onboard observations, our system avoids explicit obstacle detection and tracking pipelines. The VOP-Net processes multi-frame LiDAR data to implicitly encode dynamic constraints and predict a safe velocity region derived from Velocity Obstacle theory. Importantly, the VO predictions serve a dual role: they are used as input to the navigation policy during inference and as a reward signal during training to encourage safe motion. Evaluations in Isaac Gym demonstrate that VOP-Nav achieves higher success rates than all baselines while balancing locomotion speed and collision avoidance. Real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot further validates the system's robustness and efficiency in complex indoor and outdoor dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: VOP-Nav is a navigation system that merges Velocity Obstacle safety with end-to-end learning using only local LiDAR data to predict a safe velocity region; VO serves both as input to policy and as a training reward, achieving superior simulated performance and successful real-world deployment on a quadrobot.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of model-based VO (reliance on accurate obstacle motion estimates in dense crowds) and end-to-end methods (robustness but lacks dynamic obstacle prediction). Seek a method that preserves VO safety while leveraging learning for adaptability without explicit obstacle detection/tracking.
AI.method: Use VOP-Net to process multi-frame LiDAR data to implicitly encode dynamic constraints and derive a safe velocity region based on Velocity Obstacle theory. VO predictions are used as (1) input to the navigation policy during inference and (2) a reward signal during training to promote safe motion.
AI.result: In Isaac Gym, VOP-Nav achieves higher success rates than all baselines and balances locomotive speed with collision avoidance. Real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 demonstrates robustness and efficiency in complex indoor and outdoor dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: VOP-Nav successfully fuses geometric VO safety with learning-based adaptability, enabling safe, efficient navigation in crowded, dynamic settings without explicit obstacle detection/tracking.

title: Probabilistic Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Estimating Heterogeneous Elastic Properties from Low-Resolution and Noisy Displacement Data
summary: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution displacement measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse elasticity problem because low resolution obscures spatial details needed to distinguish heterogeneous property variations, and small measurement perturbations or fitting errors are amplified through inverse estimation. Existing inverse methods often rely on high-fidelity observations and manually prespecified loss weights, limiting their adaptability and making them sensitive to noise and resolution degradation. We propose a Probabilistic Inverse Elasticity Physics-Informed Neural Network (PIE-PINN) framework for robust estimation of Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data. PIE-PINN models displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals using Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. To improve robustness, the framework combines a B-spline-guided displacement network with a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for displacement residual scales. The B-spline provides a smooth global representation of the displacement field, while the neural network correction captures local variations. The hierarchical scale model adaptively downweights severe displacement fitting errors, enabling more robust recovery of the latent mean displacement field. An alternating maximum-likelihood training strategy updates the mean through weighted residual minimization and updates the scales to adjust the loss weights. Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate the robustness of PIE-PINN.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic PINN framework (PIE-PINN) for robustly estimating Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data, using Laplace-based likelihoods, a B-spline global displacement representation with neural corrections, hierarchical half-Cauchy scales for residuals, and alternating maximum-likelihood training; demonstrates robustness to noise and resolution degradation.
AI.motivation: Ill-posed inverse elasticity problems with low-resolution observations; existing methods require high-fidelity data and manually tuned loss weights, making them sensitive to noise and resolution loss. A probabilistic, adaptive framework is needed for robust property estimation.
AI.method: PIE-PINN models displacement observations, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals with Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. It combines a B-spline-guided displacement network with a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for displacement residual scales. The B-spline provides a smooth global displacement representation, while a neural correction captures local variations. An alternating maximum-likelihood strategy updates the mean via weighted residual minimization and adjusts the residual scales to downweight outliers.
AI.result: Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate robustness: the method downweights severe fitting errors, robustly recovers the latent mean displacement field, and yields reliable estimates of Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio under noisy, low-resolution data.
AI.conclusion: PIE-PINN offers a robust, adaptive approach for inverse elasticity from imperfect data by integrating probabilistic priors, a smooth global displacement representation, and data-driven local corrections with adaptive loss weighting; it improves resilience to noise and resolution degradation compared to methods relying on high-fidelity data and fixed loss weights.

title: Seeing the End at Step Zero: Accelerating Diffusion MLLMs via MLP Sparsity-Aware Truncation
summary: Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (DMLLMs) are highly effective for multimodal reasoning, yet their inference efficiency is significantly hindered by fixed-length generation constraints. Since the actual output length is unknown, output sequences are padded to a predefined maximum length, resulting in substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. In this work, we discover that DMLLMs implicitly reveal their valid semantic boundary at the very first denoising step through a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity. Leveraging this observation, we propose Seer, a training-free framework that detects this boundary using a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-based criterion and performs one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix for all subsequent computations. To preserve these theoretical gains during batched serving, Seer incorporates a hybrid execution strategy that maximizes throughput while seamlessly accommodating dynamic sequence lengths. Experimental results demonstrate that Seer effectively eliminates padding waste, accelerating throughput by up to $\sim$31$\times$. Across 9 benchmarks, Seer robustly maintains overall performance and even improves accuracy on complex visual tasks by mitigating noise leakage (e.g., DocVQA score increases from 63.52 to 63.66), offering a highly efficient, plug-and-play solution for DMLLM acceleration.

AI.tldr: Seer is a training-free method to accelerate diffusion multimodal LLMs by detecting the semantic boundary at the first denoising step using an SNR-based criterion and truncating the redundant suffix; it yields up to 31x throughput improvement with minimal or improved accuracy across 9 benchmarks, via a hybrid batched serving strategy.
AI.motivation: To reduce padding computation in DMLLMs caused by fixed-length generation when the natural output length is unknown.
AI.method: Observe MLP activation sparsity shift at the first denoising step; use SNR-based boundary detection to determine valid output length; perform one-shot truncation for all subsequent steps; adopt a hybrid execution strategy to support dynamic sequence lengths in batched serving; plug-and-play.
AI.result: Throughput improvements up to ~31x; robust performance retention and occasional gains on complex tasks (e.g., DocVQA score 63.52 -> 63.66) across 9 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Seer provides a training-free, effective acceleration for DMLLMs by eliminating padding waste, enabling higher throughput with preserved accuracy and compatibility for real-world serving.

title: AE-UAV: An Air-to-Air Event-Based UAV Tracking Benchmark and a Real-Time Frequency-Domain Tracker
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
summary: Air-to-air (A2A) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) tracking is fundamental to airborne remote sensing of low-altitude aerial targets. However, the deployment of continuous, real-time tracking systems on UAVs presents significant challenges. In A2A scenarios, traditional frame-based cameras suffer from severe performance degradation under low illumination, overexposure, and high-speed motion owing to their limited dynamic range and fixed temporal sampling. Although event cameras offer a promising alternative with microsecond temporal resolution and a high dynamic range, current research is bottlenecked by two primary issues: 1) the absence of dedicated A2A event-based datasets, and 2) the heavy reliance of existing trackers on GPU acceleration and extensive training data, rendering them impractical for resource-constrained UAVs. To bridge these gaps, we introduce AE-UAV, an air-to-air event-based UAV tracking benchmark. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first airborne-captured event camera dataset for A2A tracking, comprising 178 flight sequences with continuous-time cubic B-spline annotations. Furthermore, we propose the Fast-Slow Frequency-domain Tracking (FSFT) method. This lightweight, training-free framework seamlessly integrates frequency-domain template matching with search region prediction and detection-based drift correction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FSFT operates at an ultra-fast 420 frames per second (FPS) on CPU-only hardware. It retains 93.97% of the accuracy of state-of-the-art GPU-dependent methods while delivering a 5.32-fold effective speedup and exhibiting superior temporal resolution generalization, thereby providing a highly efficient and robust solution for airborne remote sensing of aerial targets. The dataset and source code are available at https://github.com/MSP-xEN/AE-UAV.

AI.tldr: Proposes AE-UAV dataset and FSFT tracker for air-to-air event-based UAV tracking; enables real-time CPU-based tracking with high performance.
AI.motivation: Overcome limitations of frame cameras in A2A tracking (poor performance in low light, high-speed motion, limited dynamic range); address lack of dedicated A2A event-based datasets and reliance on GPU/training data that is impractical for resource-constrained UAVs.
AI.method: Introduce AE-UAV, the first airborne-captured event camera dataset for A2A tracking with 178 flight sequences and continuous-time cubic B-spline annotations; propose the Fast-Slow Frequency-domain Tracking (FSFT) framework, a lightweight, training-free tracker that fuses frequency-domain template matching with search region prediction and drift correction.
AI.result: FSFT runs at 420 FPS on CPU-only hardware; retains 93.97% of the accuracy of state-of-the-art GPU-dependent methods; provides a 5.32× effective speedup and shows strong temporal resolution generalization.
AI.conclusion: The AE-UAV dataset and FSFT tracker offer an efficient, robust solution for airborne remote sensing and A2A UAV tracking, enabling real-time performance on resource-constrained UAVs; code and dataset are openly available.

title: DriftWorld: Fast World Modeling through Drifting
summary: Predictive world models enable robots to plan by imagining the outcomes of their actions, but their value for control hinges on generating many rollouts quickly. This creates a bottleneck for diffusion-based world models: multistep sampling makes each rollout expensive, limiting large-scale action search at inference time. We introduce DriftWorld, an action-conditioned world model based on drifting generative models. Rather than denoising iteratively at inference, DriftWorld learns an action-conditioned drift during training, allowing it to generate future frames from the current observation and a candidate action sequence in a single forward pass at 30+ fps, which is 17x faster on average than diffusion based baselines. We evaluate DriftWorld on standard vision-based robotic manipulation benchmarks, including Bridge-V2, RT-1, Language Table, Push-T, and Robomimic. By producing rollouts that are both accurate and fast, DriftWorld achieves state-of-the-art decision-making performance with far less inference time than diffusion-based world model baselines. Beyond online control, DriftWorld can also serve as an offline simulator for ranking real-world robot policies, with rollout-based scores correlating with ground truth at up to 0.99. These results show that drifting models are a strong fit for robot world modeling, where fast, high-quality imagination directly supports planning and policy evaluation.

AI.tldr: DriftWorld uses action-conditioned drift in drifting generative models to generate future frames in a single pass, delivering 30+ fps and strong planning and offline evaluation performance, outperforming diffusion-based world models.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models require iterative denoising for rollouts, which is computationally expensive for online planning; fast, accurate, scalable world models are needed for robotics.
AI.method: Train an action-conditioned drift term within a generative model; at inference, generate a full future rollout from the current observation and a candidate action sequence in one forward pass; evaluate on standard robotic benchmarks (Bridge-V2, RT-1, Language Table, Push-T, Robomimic) and for offline policy ranking.
AI.result: Achieves 30+ fps rollout generation; ~17x faster than diffusion baselines; state-of-the-art planning performance; rollout-based scores correlate with ground truth up to 0.99 in offline evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Drifting models are well-suited for robot world modeling, providing fast, high-quality imagination that directly supports planning and policy evaluation, with potential as offline simulators.

title: Gate-Zero Growth: A Geometric Framework for Function-Preserving Continual Learning
summary: We introduce \emph{gate-zero growth}, a function-preserving (FP) operator for continual learning that adds new residual blocks through a zero-initialised gate. Under a transversality condition, gate-zero growth induces \emph{rank separation} in the functional Jacobian: old directions are unchanged, new-weight directions are exactly flat at the growth point, and new gate directions are the only first-order source of new functional variation. As gates open during continual learning, function drift is $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|^2)$ and Jacobian leakage $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|_\infty)$, giving a controlled departure from the FP locus. On a $300\mathrm{M}\to857\mathrm{M}$ Transformer adapted from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth reaches near-zero old-domain forgetting ($Δ_A < 0.1$) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) operating points, while a non-FP control ($G_{\text{stack}}$) suffers an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under the same recipe. The same geometric analysis covers LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapter constructions, establishing gate-zero growth as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in CL.

AI.tldr: A function-preserving operator called gate-zero growth enables safe capacity expansion in continual learning by adding zero-initialised gates and residual blocks, yielding rank separation in the Jacobian and controlled drift; empirically reduces old-domain forgetting on a large Transformer and generalizes to LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters.
AI.motivation: Mitigate catastrophic forgetting during continual learning while expanding model capacity, by enforcing function-preserving updates and leveraging a geometric (Jacobian) perspective to guide safe activation of new capacity.
AI.method: Introduce gate-zero growth: add new residual blocks via a zero-initialised gate; under a transversality condition this induces rank separation in the functional Jacobian (old directions unchanged, new-weight directions flat at growth, new gate directions provide first-order variation). Track function drift O(||α||^2) and Jacobian leakage O(||α||_∞) as gates open. Empirically evaluate on a Transformer scaled from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus (300M→857M) comparing exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) against a non-FP control (G_stack). Extend analysis to LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters.
AI.result: Gate-zero growth achieves near-zero old-domain forgetting (Δ_A < 0.1) under both FP operating points, while G_stack incurs ~10x more forgetting under the same recipe. The analysis generalizes to LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters, supporting gate-zero growth as the canonical local-geometry instance for safe capacity activation in continual learning.
AI.conclusion: Gate-zero growth embodies a shared local geometry that enables safe, controllable capacity expansion in continual learning, with a canonical role for rank separation in the Jacobian. It provides a unified framework that explains why certain FP adapters (LoRA, ReZero, zero-init) can grow capacity with limited forgetting and offers practical guidance for designing FP expansions.

title: Democratizing Agent Deployment Safety: A Structural Monitoring Approach
comment: Accepted in ICML 2026 Workshops: AI4GOOD and AIWILD
summary: AI software development agents are increasingly capable of modifying infrastructure and security critical systems, creating risks where an agent completes its assigned task while covertly weakening safeguards through actions such as broadening permissions, degrading logging, or introducing persistence mechanisms. While frontier laboratories may deploy sophisticated monitoring pipelines, many organizations and individual users adopting coding agents lack the resources and governance maturity required to maintain complex learned monitor ensembles. We study this problem as infrastructure level sabotage under task success in the infrastructure-as-code setting from ControlArena and compare trained and untrained monitors across synchronous and asynchronous deployment modes. We introduce an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that analyzes structural security regressions using control-flow and data-flow graph diffs alongside raw code diffs. In asynchronous evaluation, an untrained git diff monitor misses 11.6% attacks at 1% false positive rate auditing budget, our untrained IFG monitor reduces this to 3.5%, and the trained Async RF monitor achieves below 1%. Unlike the trained Async RF monitor, IFG can also operate synchronously as a pre-deployment safeguard that blocks suspicious infrastructure changes before execution or merge. In synchronous mode, IFG realtime rollback reduces joint main task and covert task success from 74.4% to 0.0% with no measurable reduction in legitimate task completion. These results suggest that untrained structural monitors provide a practical and auditable path toward democratizing deployment safety for organizations seeking trustworthy adoption of advanced AI agents.

AI.tldr: Untrained structural monitors (IFG) offer practical, auditable guardrails for AI-enabled infrastructure modifications, outperforming untrained git-diff and approaching trained monitors, with synchronous and asynchronous deployment modes enabling pre-deployment and runtime protection.
AI.motivation: Provide safe deployment of AI coding agents in infrastructure-as-code settings by detecting structural regressions and policy breaches when trained monitoring resources are scarce.
AI.method: Introduce Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that uses control-flow and data-flow graph diffs plus code diffs; compare untrained vs trained monitors under synchronous and asynchronous deployments; evaluate detection accuracy and impact on legitimate task completion.
AI.result: Asynchronous: untrained git-diff misses 11.6% of attacks at 1% FPR; untrained IFG reduces to 3.5%; trained Async RF <1%. Synchronous: IFG enables pre-deployment blocking; joint task/covert task success drops from 74.4% to 0% with no noticeable cost to legitimate task completion.
AI.conclusion: Untrained structural monitors provide a practical, auditable path to democratize deployment safety and safe adoption of AI agents in infrastructure-as-code ecosystems.

title: WorkDrive: Roadwork Chain of Causation for Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving vision-language models (VLMs) struggle in roadwork zones, where familiar visual cues such as lane markings and permanent signs are altered or absent, and temporary devices such as cones and barriers redefine the drivable corridor. VLMs can detect these objects, but without explicit guidance they anchor their reasoning on familiar elements from pre-training and fail to connect work-zone observations to correct planning decisions. We propose WorkDrive, a framework that constructs perception-grounded causal reasoning for work zones and aligns it with trajectory prediction. An automated multitask perception pipeline extracts structured scene facts and injects them into a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) annotation pipeline, redirecting the annotator's attention to domain-specific elements. The resulting reasoning labels are used for supervised fine-tuning, followed by reinforcement learning with a single reward: consistency between lateral meta-actions and the predicted trajectory. On ROADWork, the largest public work-zone dataset, the proposed roadwork CoC reduces trajectory average displacement error (ADE) by 9.0\%, and consistency-based GRPO yields a further 3.0\%, achieving progressive improvement over the trajectory-only baseline. Code and data will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: WorkDrive develops perception-grounded causal reasoning for roadwork zones to align perception with trajectory planning in autonomous driving VLMs. It uses an automated multitask perception pipeline and a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) annotation process to inject domain-specific facts, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. It achieves ADE reductions on ROADWork (9.0% with CoC; 3.0% further with consistency-based GRPO) and plans to release code/data.
AI.motivation: VLMs rely on familiar pre-training cues and struggle to adapt to altered roadwork environments where cones, barriers, and changed lane geometry require domain-specific planning cues. A perception-grounded causal reasoning approach is needed to align perception with safe trajectory planning in such zones.
AI.method: An automated multitask perception pipeline extracts structured scene facts and feeds them into a Chain-of-Causation annotation pipeline to redirect annotators toward roadwork-specific elements. The resulting reasoning labels train a model via supervised fine-tuning, followed by reinforcement learning with a single reward that enforces consistency between lateral meta-actions and the predicted trajectory.
AI.result: On ROADWork, the roadwork CoC reduces trajectory average displacement error (ADE) by 9.0% and the consistency-based GRPO adds a further 3.0% improvement, outperforming a trajectory-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating perception-grounded causal reasoning with domain-specific CoC annotations improves trajectory prediction in work zones, suggesting a viable path to bridge perception and planning for VLM-based autonomous driving. Public release of code/data will support reproducibility and further research.

title: Goal-Oriented Semantic Communication for Distributed ISAC-Enabled Vehicle Coordination
summary: Vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections relies on accurate real-time vehicle state acquisition and reliable command-and-control (C&C) signal delivery. However, existing studies typically treat sensing, communication, and control separately, which may lead to redundant transmissions, outdated state information, and unreliable vehicle coordination. In this paper, we investigate a new scenario of distributed integrated sensing and communication (ISAC)-enabled vehicle coordination at intersections, where multiple roadside units (RSUs) collaboratively transmit sensing signals for vehicle state acquisition and C&C signals for vehicle movement control under the management of a central base station (BS). To improve signaling efficiency, we propose a unified goal-oriented semantic communication (GSC) framework, which transmits sensing and C&C signals only when they are semantically important for improving intersection traffic throughput. Specifically, an extended Kalman filter (EKF) is adopted to predict vehicle states and fuse distributed sensing measurements. A masked hybrid proximal policy optimization (MHPPO) framework is then developed to jointly determine sensing transmission decisions, C&C transmission decisions, and C&C signal contents based on a value-of-information (VoI) reward. Furthermore, we propose an uncertainty-aware transmission design (UTD), including robust beamforming and VoI-based time-division power allocation, to improve sensing and communication reliability under vehicle state uncertainty and inter-RSU interference. Simulation results show that our proposed framework achieves 100% collision-free vehicle coordination with significantly reduced signaling overhead compared with predictive ISAC baselines adapted from state-of-the-art related studies and several ablation baselines.

AI.tldr: Unified semantic ISAC framework for distributed vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections, using EKF for state estimation, MHPPO for joint sensing/C&C decisions with VoI reward, and uncertainty-aware transmission design; achieves collision-free operation with reduced signaling overhead.
AI.motivation: Traditional separation of sensing, communication, and control leads to redundant transmissions, stale state information, and unreliable coordination at intersections. A distributed ISAC setup with RSUs managed by a central BS demands a unified approach to improve signaling efficiency and reliability.
AI.method: Extend Kalman filter (EKF) to predict and fuse distributed sensing measurements; propose masked hybrid proximal policy optimization (MHPPO) to jointly decide sensing transmission, C&C transmission, and C&C content based on a value-of-information (VoI) reward; develop uncertainty-aware transmission design (UTD) with robust beamforming and VoI-based time-division power allocation to mitigate state uncertainty and inter-RSU interference.
AI.result: Simulation results show 100% collision-free vehicle coordination with significantly reduced signaling overhead compared to predictive ISAC baselines and various ablation baselines.
AI.conclusion: An integrated ISAC framework with goal-oriented semantics and uncertainty-aware transmission improves signaling efficiency and reliability for coordinated vehicle movement at intersections; the combination of EKF fusion, VoI-guided MHPPO decisions, and robust UTD enables resilient coordination under uncertainty and interference.

title: Sharp Stability Threshold and Certification for Designing Stable Residual Architectures
summary: We propose \emph{the sublinear-growth principle} for deep residual architectures -- a sharp stability threshold on the input-magnitude exponent of every residual block's velocity field: $$\|v(x, t)\| \leq c\,\|x\|^q + b, \qquad q \in [0, 1].$$ The threshold $q = 1$ is established via two independent arguments. Classical ODE theory gives a global forward flow on $[0, T]$ at $q \le 1$ and exhibits divergent velocity fields at any $q > 1$. The optimal-control analysis, via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, sharpens this to a selection statement: the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so the optimum at $q > 1$ blows up while the optimum at $q \le 1$ is safe by construction. The exponent criterion $q \le 1$ is thereby a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. It clarifies architectural placements that ensure the stability of training and inference, explaining, for instance, the stabilizing role of layer normalization. The sublinear-growth velocity fields form \emph{the right function space} on which forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. An arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under the five operations that build residual blocks enables efficient certification of $q_k \le 1$ at the level of architectural primitives, in place of ad hoc trial and error in the search for stable neural architectural designs. A parameter-free modification reduces the supercritical Mamba block from $q = 5$ to $q = 1$ without layer normalization, demonstrating this point. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that the $q \le 1$ variants train stably: the criterion is the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of a normalization layer.

AI.tldr: A sharp stability threshold for residual-block velocity fields: q ≤ 1 guarantees stable training; q > 1 leads to blow-up; justified by ODE theory and HJB; provides architectural guidance and efficient certification; demonstrated on Mamba and PatchTST.
AI.motivation: Ensure training stability in deep residual architectures by bounding the input-magnitude growth of residual velocity fields; provide a principled criterion that guides architectural design and clarifies the role of normalization.
AI.method: Two main strands: (1) classical ODE forward-flow analysis to establish a global flow for q ≤ 1 and blow-up for q > 1; (2) optimal-control/HJB analysis showing bang-bang optimality on the boundary, yielding a necessary-and-sufficient condition q ≤ 1; exponent-arithmetic for composing residual blocks to certify q ≤ 1 for architectural primitives; a parameter-free modification reduces supercritical blocks (e.g., Mamba) to q = 1 without layer normalization; empirical validation on Mamba and PatchTST.
AI.result: The exponent criterion q ≤ 1 is a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. q > 1 leads to blow-up under optimal control; q ≤ 1 yields safe forward/inverse dynamics and stable training/inference. Stability is attributable to the function space of sublinear-growth velocity fields, rather than the presence of normalization layers. The framework enables efficient, architecture-level certification of q ≤ 1 and explains empirical stabilization from layer normalization as a consequence of operating within this space.
AI.conclusion: Sublinear-growth velocity fields define the appropriate function space for stable deep residual dynamics. The q ≤ 1 criterion provides principled architectural guidance, enabling stable training and inference and allowing component-wise certification. It also clarifies the role of normalization and demonstrates practical design improvements (e.g., reducing Mamba to q = 1) with empirical confirmation.

title: Alipay-PIBench: A Realistic Payment Integration Benchmark for Coding Agents
summary: Payment integration is a demanding repository-level software task: agents must select a suitable product, implement coordinated client-server flows, verify payment outcomes, and preserve consistency between transaction and business states. We introduce Alipay-PIBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on realistic Alipay payment integration. It contains nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances, each organized into Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware hardening scenarios. Scenario-specific rubrics support deterministic static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks, supplemented by LLM-assisted assessment for semantic requirements. We evaluate six coding-agent models and report rubric pass rate (RPR). Under the with-skill condition, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Access to the alipay-payment-integration skill improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points on average relative to the without-skill condition, with gains varying across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements. Alipay-PIBench provides a controlled setting for diagnosing model capability and evaluating structured guidance in payment integration.

AI.tldr: Alipay-PIBench is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on Alipay payment integration across nine products and 18 tasks, using Basic and Advanced scenarios with multi-level rubrics and LLM-assisted semantic assessment; it reports rubric pass rate (RPR) and shows skill access improves performance.
AI.motivation: Automate and diagnose coding-agent capabilities in complex, real-world payment integration tasks with domain-specific constraints.
AI.method: Nine product-specific projects; 18 task instances; Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware scenarios; scenario-specific rubrics for static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks; LLM-assisted semantic requirements; six coding-agent models; compare with/without alipay-payment-integration skill; report RPR; analyze method-level results.
AI.result: Under with-skill, mean RPR 68.58%–91.37%; access to alipay-payment-integration improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points; gains vary by model/product/scenario; results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements.
AI.conclusion: Alipay-PIBench offers a controlled setting to diagnose model capability and evaluate structured guidance for payment integration.

title: VQ-Touch: A Data-Efficient Tactile Generation Framework Across Sensors and Scenarios
summary: Tactile image generation significantly reduces the dependency on expensive and wear-prone sensors by synthesizing high-fidelity tactile data, offering an efficient solution for tactile information acquisition in robotic perception and human-machine interaction systems. However, existing methods depend on large-scale, diverse datasets from specific sensors and lack efficient data utilization and robust generalization capabilities, struggling in vision-limited environments. To address this, we introduce VQ-Touch, a tactile generation framework that supports both cross-sensor and multi-scenario applications. Specifically, to efficiently extract complex deformation and texture features from the data, we propose DM-VQGAN, an effective tactile representation learner. Furthermore, we introduce a discrete diffusion decoder with a unified conditioning interface, supporting multimodal generation tasks such as images and labels, and enhances the model's generalization capability through few-shot mixed training, thus achieving compatibility with current mainstream sensors and their variants. Experiments show that VQ-Touch surpasses state-of-the-art methods in multiple tasks.

AI.tldr: VQ-Touch enables cross-sensor, multi-scenario tactile image generation via DM-VQGAN and a discrete diffusion decoder, achieving strong generalization with few-shot mixed training.
AI.motivation: Tactile data collection is expensive and sensor-specific; there is a need for efficient data utilization and robust generalization across sensors and vision-limited environments, enabling broad applicability in robotic perception and human–machine interaction.
AI.method: Introduce DM-VQGAN as a tactile representation learner to extract deformation and texture features; develop a discrete diffusion decoder with a unified conditioning interface supporting multimodal generation (images, labels); apply few-shot mixed training to improve generalization; ensure compatibility with mainstream tactile sensors and variants.
AI.result: Empirical results show VQ-Touch surpasses state-of-the-art methods across multiple tactile generation tasks and scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VQ-Touch provides an efficient, transferable framework for tactile image generation across sensors and scenarios, with strong generalization and reduced data requirements, advancing tactile perception for robotics and human–machine interfaces.

title: Catch, Throw, Repeat: Planning for Human-Robot Partner Juggling
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Dynamic object exchange between humans and robots remains a challenging problem due to uncertainty in perception, timing, and contact-rich interaction. Human-robot juggling represents a particularly demanding instance of this problem, requiring precise real-time coordination, predictive motion planning with feedback control, and robustness to variability in human motion. Enabling such skills is of interest for advancing physical human-robot interaction and shared autonomy. We present a real-time planning and control architecture for human-robot partner juggling that enables a robot to reliably catch and throw balls in synchronized multi-ball patterns with a human partner. The system integrates predictive ball tracking, adaptive online trajectory optimization using a multiple-shooting formulation, and a state-machine-based coordination logic to enable synchronized multi-ball human-robot partner juggling. In a user study with 8 participants of varying juggling skill from beginner to expert, we demonstrate that our system can achieve three-ball cascades shared between the robot and the human. All participants exceeded previously reported best-case results within a 10-minute test session, with one participant extending the previous record for shared three-ball cascade juggling fivefold to 20 consecutive robot catches, and another participant achieving a 100% success rate with 40 consecutive catches in a single-ball catch-and-return setting. Video documentation can be found at https://kai-ploeger.com/partner-juggling

AI.tldr: A real-time planning and control framework enables a robot to co-juggle balls with a human partner, using predictive tracking and online multiple-shooting trajectory optimization with state-machine coordination to achieve multi-ball cascades and record-breaking performance in a user study.
AI.motivation: Advance physical human-robot interaction and shared autonomy by enabling reliable, synchronized, and robust manipulation in uncertainty-prone, contact-rich tasks such as human-robot juggling.
AI.method: Integrates predictive ball tracking, adaptive online trajectory optimization via a multiple-shooting formulation, and a state-machine-based coordination logic to realize real-time catching/throwing and multi-ball coordination with a human partner.
AI.result: In a user study with 8 participants of varying juggling skill, the system achieved three-ball cascades shared between robot and human. All participants surpassed prior best-case results within a 10-minute session; one participant extended the record for shared three-ball cascade juggling to 20 consecutive robot catches, and another achieved 40 consecutive single-ball catches with 100% success. Video available online.
AI.conclusion: The architecture demonstrates feasible, reliable, and synchronized human-robot partner juggling under perceptual and timing variability, highlighting potential for advancing physical HRI and shared autonomy in demanding manipulation tasks.

title: Accelerating A/B-Tests with Counterfactual Estimation: Reducing Variance through Policy Overlap
summary:
Online controlled experiments are the gold standard for hypothesis testing in online platforms. Notwithstanding their ubiquity, they are notoriously expensive to run, and issues of variance hamper statistical power in assessing treatment effects. While standard variance reduction techniques leverage model-based control variates to reduce outcome noise, they remain agnostic to potential structural relationships between competing policies.
  In this work, we identify a critical inefficiency in the standard A/B-testing protocol: when a treatment and control policy agree on an action, the resulting outcome contributes noise but no signal regarding the treatment effect -- unnecessarily inflating confidence intervals. We propose a novel experimental protocol that exploits this policy overlap to accelerate experimentation. The key insight is to frame the randomised treatment assignment mechanism as a meta-policy, and leverage $Δ$-Off-Policy Estimation methods to obtain unbiased estimates for average treatment effects. We prove analytically that our approach recovers standard A/B-testing practices in the general case, but that its variance scales with the divergence between policies rather than raw outcome variance. Hence, we dominate the standard Difference-in-Means estimator whenever policies have common support, and the improvement is strict whenever the overlap region contributes non-zero residual variance. Empirical results corroborate these theoretical insights -- holding promise for significant impact on the real-world evaluation of recommender systems, information retrieval pipelines, and large language model interfaces.

AI.tldr: A policy-overlap aware off-policy estimator for A/B testing that reduces variance by exploiting divergence between treatment and control policies; it recovers standard A/B tests in general and dominates DIF when there is policy overlap; validated theoretically and empirically.
AI.motivation: Standard A/B testing suffers from high variance and noisy outcomes, making experiments expensive. Variance reduction via model-based control variates ignores structural relations between the competing policies and unnecessary noise arising when treatment/control actions agree. The paper identifies this inefficiency and seeks to accelerate online experimentation by leveraging policy overlap.
AI.method: Frame the randomized assignment as a meta-policy and apply Δ-Off-Policy Estimation (Δ-OP) to obtain unbiased average treatment effect estimates. The approach yields an estimator whose variance scales with the divergence between policies instead of outcome variance. The authors prove that it recovers standard A/B testing in the general case and provides variance improvements when overlap exists; they compare against Difference-in-Means and establish dominance under common support.
AI.result: Theoretical results show variance bounds that improve as policy divergence decreases; the estimator matches standard A/B testing when policies differ widely but reduces variance when there is action overlap. Empirical experiments on recommender systems, information retrieval pipelines, and large language model interfaces corroborate the theory, indicating substantial potential improvements in real-world online evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Policy-overlap aware Δ-OP estimation offers a principled, faster alternative to conventional A/B testing by tying estimates to policy structure. It dominates standard estimators under overlap and recovers them generally, with practical impact on large-scale online evaluation domains. Further work may address implementation details and robustness to violations of overlap assumptions.

title: Collaborative Spatial Learning with Multi-LLM Agents in Networked Social Experiments
comment: Accepted at ASONAM 2026; to appear in the Springer proceedings
summary: Collective problem solving often requires that group members consider the tradeoff between exploitation of known solutions and exploration for new ones, where information of known solutions can be disseminated among individual members through communication networks. The Mason--Watts experiment (PNAS 2012) showed that human groups in shorter-path networks outperform those in longer-path networks on a two-dimensional search task. In this work, we focus on the investigation of such network-efficiency effects in the setting of a group of large language model (LLM) agents. Specifically, we consider groups of sixteen LLM agents playing the Mason--Watts experiment on the eight Mason--Watts network topologies. Moreover, we develop mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents such that the performance of LLM agents can be compared with both the mechanistic agents and the human experimental data. Our computational experiments indicate that the LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect when instructed to randomize their first-round choices, but not under the default initialization. In this experiment, adding a one-sentence first-round randomization instruction improves collective payoff by more than three times the estimated payoff difference across the eight network topologies. Also, the Bayesian optimization agents obtain higher payoffs than the evaluated LLM agents on this spatial search task. We further compare the agents' exploration--exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.

AI.tldr: Extends the Mason–Watts collective problem-solving framework to 16 LLM agents across 8 network topologies, showing network-efficiency only with random-first-round initialization; Bayesian optimization agents outperform LLMs; analyzes exploration–exploitation, copying, and spatial diversity.
AI.motivation: To test whether network structure and initialization strategies influence collective problem solving in groups of LLM agents, contrasting with human data and mechanistic baselines (Bayesian optimization).
AI.method: 16 LLM agents execute a Mason–Watts spatial search on 8 network topologies. Compare default vs one-sentence random-first-round instruction. Include mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents as baselines. Measure payoffs, and analyze exploration–exploitation, copying, and spatial diversity.
AI.result: LLM agents exhibit a network-efficiency effect when given a random-first-round instruction; this instruction increases collective payoff by >3x the frontier payoff difference across topologies. Bayesian optimization agents achieve higher payoffs than the evaluated LLMs on this task.
AI.conclusion: Network topology effects on collective performance depend on initialization strategies; guided randomization can unlock efficiency gains for LLM groups. Bayesian-optimization agents remain a stronger baseline. Further analysis on copying and spatial diversity informs the mechanisms behind these gains.

title: GeoDetect: Geometric Adversarial Detection for VLPs
summary: Vision-language pre-trained models (VLPs) are widely used in real-world applications. However, they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Although adversarial detection methods have demonstrated success in single-modality settings (either vision or language), their effectiveness and reliability in multimodal models such as VLPs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we study the geometry of VLP embedding spaces and observe structured anisotropy that differs from unimodal vision models. Our theoretical analysis shows that under this anisotropic structure, adversarial attacks increase the expected geometric separation between clean and adversarial examples (AEs). Specifically, we demonstrate that AEs consistently exhibit greater expected distances to randomly sampled points than their clean counterparts, indicating that AEs tend to push representations out of manifold regions. Building on these insights, we propose GeoDetect, which leverages these off-manifold deviations via geometric scores to identify AEs. Through comprehensive evaluations, we show that our approach reliably detects AEs across diverse VLP architectures and threat settings, covering unimodal and multimodal attacks as well as adaptive attacks, thereby providing a robust and practical approach to improving the safety and reliability of these models.

AI.tldr: GeoDetect leverages off-manifold deviations caused by structured anisotropy in vision-language pre-trained models to detect adversarial examples, offering robust detection across unimodal and multimodal attacks and adaptive threats.
AI.motivation: VLPs mix vision and language representations that exhibit anisotropic geometry. Adversarial examples in this space can push representations away from data manifolds. There is a need for a geometry-based, robust detection method that generalizes across architectures and threat models.
AI.method: The authors analyze the embedding geometry of VLPs, showing structured anisotropy and that adversarial examples increase expected distances to randomly sampled points, indicating off-manifold deviations. Based on this, they introduce GeoDetect, which computes geometric scores (e.g., distances to random samples within the embedding space) to discriminate clean versus adversarial inputs. A simple threshold or classifier on these scores is used for detection. The approach is evaluated across multiple VLP architectures and attack settings, including unimodal, multimodal, and adaptive attacks.
AI.result: GeoDetect reliably detects adversarial examples across diverse VLP architectures and threat settings, including adaptive attacks, demonstrating robustness and practicality for improving the safety of VLP systems.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting off-manifold deviations in the anisotropic embedding spaces of VLPs is an effective basis for detection. GeoDetect provides a practical, geometry-based defense that generalizes across architectures and attack types.

title: Assessing Physical Frailty and Fall-Risk Indicators with Social Robots: An in situ Evaluation with Older Adults
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Frailty assessments are crucial to evaluate the risk of adverse events and the health and social care needs of older adults, yet their administration remains resource-intensive and typically relies on coarse clinical outcomes, such as task completion times, which may overlook biomechanical indicators of functional decline. To address this, we present a robotic framework that guides older adults through standardised frailty and fall-risk tests while capturing clinical scores and additional frailty-related metrics, offering a deeper insight into a user's condition. The system uses a Behaviour Tree architecture that coordinates perception, decision-making, interaction, and measurement modules. Using vision-based skeleton tracking, the robot evaluates established clinical tests, including the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) and the Timed Up and Go (TUG). The framework was co-designed with healthcare professionals and evaluated in situ during six months in a rehabilitation centre's research lab with N=81 older adults. Robot-derived measurements were compared against therapist assessments and clinical reference instruments, including a gait analysis walkway and an inertial measurement unit (IMU). Results showed excellent agreement for most test completion times and gait-related parameters ($ICC > 0.9$). And, substantial agreement for the overall SPPB score comparing the robot and the therapist ($k = 0.67$) and moderate agreement comparing the robot and the IMU ($k=0.55$). The findings highlight that social robots can provide reliable and objective frailty assessments in healthcare settings while enabling the collection of relevant mobility indicators beyond conventional outcomes.

AI.tldr: Robotic framework administers frailty and fall-risk tests using vision-based skeleton tracking; shows high agreement with therapists and IMUs; handles SPPB and TUG with deep mobility metrics.
AI.motivation: To overcome resource-intensive, coarse frailty measures by extracting biomechanical indicators through robotics for objective, scalable assessment.
AI.method: A robot guides standardized tests (SPPB, TUG) using a Behaviour Tree to coordinate perception, decision-making, interaction, and measurement. Vision-based skeleton tracking evaluates tests; co-designed with clinicians; in-situ evaluation (N=81) in a rehabilitation centre. Robot measurements compared to therapist assessments and reference instruments (gait walkway, IMU).
AI.result: Most test completion times and gait-related parameters showed ICC > 0.9 with reference measures. Overall SPPB score: robot vs therapist k=0.67; robot vs IMU k=0.55.
AI.conclusion: Social robots can provide reliable, objective frailty assessments in healthcare settings and enable collection of mobility indicators beyond conventional outcomes.

title: Auditing Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs: Subpopulation-Level Effects of Fairness-Enhancing Algorithms
summary: Machine learning (ML) models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance must satisfy not only utility requirements but also fairness and privacy guarantees. While prior work has largely examined how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question-how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage-remains underexplored. We present the first comprehensive study of how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. By adapting the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, we uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations obscure. We further analyze how Differential Privacy (DP) interacts with fairness-enhancing methods across different categories, showing that DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Our results demonstrate that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. These findings reveal that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level, and we introduce the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice.

AI.tldr: Fairness interventions impact privacy risk non-uniformly across subpopulations; adapts LiRA for subgroup auditing and analyzes DP interactions, proposing a unified auditing framework.
AI.motivation: To understand how fairness-enhancing methods affect membership inference privacy at subpopulation granularity, addressing gaps where prior work focused on global metrics.
AI.method: Adapt LiRA for subgroup auditing; empirically evaluate DP interactions with fairness across model architectures, subgroup sizes, and mitigation strategies; develop a unified auditing framework.
AI.result: Findings show privacy disparities across subgroups; DP's privacy-utility trade-offs vary by subgroup; fairness interventions do not uniformly raise privacy risk; outcomes depend on architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Subpopulation-level auditing is essential; present first unified empirical framework to jointly evaluate fairness, privacy, and utility.

title: Multi-LLM Collaborative MRI Report Generation for Visual Instruction Tuning in Brain Oncology
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and their extension to vision-language models (VLMs) have made it easier to combine text and images for tasks such as report generation. Existing VLMs in medicine typically focus on 2D images (chest X-rays), and their extension to 3D imaging has been difficult because of the lack of paired 3D imaging-text data. Thus, we introduce a new method for creating a 3D image-text dataset for brain oncology using 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases. We use a cooperative system in which several LLMs work together to generate and check reports, ensuring that they are accurate and clear. By leveraging the new 3D MRI-text dataset, we further build a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions. Our VLM performed better in report generation and visual question answering tasks than other 2D and 3D methods. Our method not only improves the quality of reports but also helps with better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

AI.tldr: A 3D MRI–text dataset for brain oncology plus a cooperative LLM-driven VLM that maps MRI to text, improving report generation and VQA.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of paired 3D imaging–text data for medical VLMs and the limitations of 2D imaging in brain oncology, enabling better report accuracy and clinical utility.
AI.method: Create a 3D MRI–text dataset from glioma and meningioma cases; employ a cooperative system of multiple LLMs to draft and verify reports; develop a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions; evaluate on report generation and visual question answering.
AI.result: The proposed VLM outperforms existing 2D and 3D baselines in both report generation and VQA tasks; the dataset improves report quality and has potential to support diagnosis and treatment.
AI.conclusion: Advances 3D vision–language medical modeling in brain oncology by providing a 3D MRI–text dataset and a cooperative LLM–driven VLM, enabling better diagnostic support and treatment planning.

title: FoMoVLA: Bridging Visual Foresight and Motion Guidance for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://liauto-research.github.io/FoMoVLA
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved impressive results in visuomotor policy learning, yet remain fundamentally reactive, mapping current observations and language to actions without explicit forward prediction of world dynamics. Existing visual foresight methods predict future visual states but lack explicit motion guidance: they show where to go but not how to get there. We argue that future feature prediction and sparse point tracking are naturally complementary: the former provides the goal state, while the latter captures the continuous motion path toward it. We propose FoMoVLA, a framework that augments VLA representations with explicit spatio-temporal supervision by jointly learning future feature foresight and sparse 2D point tracking, enhancing the continuous action policy. FoMoVLA introduces compact foresight tokens to decode future feature states, decodes sparse temporal 2D point trajectories to model compact geometric motion, and couples both through a lightweight future-conditioned cross-attention module that enables consistent reasoning between anticipated states and point dynamics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboCasa GR-1 Tabletop, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and strong zero-shot generalization. Project page is available at https://liauto-research.github.io/FoMoVLA.

AI.tldr: FoMoVLA jointly learns future feature foresight and sparse 2D point tracking to enhance Vision-Language-Action policies. It uses compact foresight tokens and a future-conditioned cross-attention module to align predicted states with point dynamics, yielding state-of-the-art results and strong zero-shot generalization on multiple visuomotor benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action models are largely reactive and lack explicit forward dynamics. Prior visual foresight predicts future visuals but omits explicit motion guidance. The authors argue that future feature prediction and sparse point tracking are complementary: the former provides the goal state, the latter encodes a continuous motion path.
AI.method: FoMoVLA introduces compact foresight tokens to decode future feature states and decodes sparse temporal 2D point trajectories to model geometric motion. These signals are coupled via a lightweight future-conditioned cross-attention module that enables consistent reasoning between anticipated states and point dynamics.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on LIBERO, RoboCasa GR-1 Tabletop, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrates state-of-the-art performance and strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning future feature foresight and sparse point tracking provides explicit spatio-temporal supervision for VLA models, improving continuous action policy by aligning anticipated states with point trajectories through cross-attention.

title: Scaling Behavior Foundation Model for Humanoid Robots
summary: Humanoid control requires natural whole-body coordination, precise real-time responses to control signals, and robust generalization across diverse environmental contexts, making it a cornerstone for generalist embodied agents. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) have recently emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges by leveraging large-scale behavioral data to achieve superior expressiveness, versatility and generalization. However, despite growing interest in scaling BFMs to further improve their capabilities, it remains unclear how key factors, including the learning paradigm, behavioral data and model architecture should be coordinated to enable effective scaling. In this work, we revisit the scaling recipe for BFMs and demonstrate that substantial performance gains can be achieved through the coordination of three core components: 1) the learning paradigm of motion tracking that reformulates diverse humanoid control problems as the reproduction of integrated whole-body behaviors in the global frame; 2) the strategic synergy between on-policy rollout quantity and reference motion diversity; and 3) the expressive and scalable model architecture termed Humanoid Transformer that facilitates the natural emergence of structured behavioral representations. Through extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world deployment, we demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in control fidelity and task generalization, reducing Mean Per-Keypoint Position Error (MPKPE) on the test set by over 10% in local mode and 82% in global mode compared with existing humanoid controllers. These results establish BFM as a principled and effective foundation for scalable and general-purpose humanoid control.

AI.tldr: Scalable Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) for humanoid control achieved by coordinating: (i) motion-tracking learning paradigm; (ii) on-policy rollout vs reference-motion diversity; (iii) an expressive Humanoid Transformer, yielding strong improvements in fidelity and generalization (MPKPE: local >10% improvement, global ~82%).
AI.motivation: To determine how learning paradigm, data, and model architecture should be coordinated to scale BFMs for robust, generalizable humanoid control.
AI.method: 1) Use a motion-tracking learning paradigm that treats control tasks as reproducing integrated whole-body behaviors in a global frame. 2) Optimize the trade-off between on-policy rollout quantity and reference motion diversity. 3) Introduce Humanoid Transformer architecture to enable structured, scalable behavioral representations. Validate via extensive sim-to-real experiments.
AI.result: Significant improvements in control fidelity and generalization; MPKPE on the test set improved by over 10% in local mode and 82% in global mode compared with existing humanoid controllers.
AI.conclusion: BFMs provide a principled, scalable foundation for general-purpose humanoid control. Coordinating learning paradigm, data strategy, and architecture yields substantial gains and supports the emergence of generalist embodied agents.

title: Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Electrocardiogram Arrhythmia Diagnosis
summary: Long-tailed label distributions reduce the reliability of deep learning for electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia diagnosis, particularly for clinically important but rare abnormalities. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods mainly address class frequency while overlooking direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes. This study proposes Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis. AG-SCL integrates three components into a unified framework: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings, Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins, and tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band. The method was evaluated on the public PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset comprising 1317 hours of recordings from 141 subjects. AG-SCL achieved the best macro-level performance on both datasets.
