On PTB-XL, it obtained a balanced accuracy of 0.838, sensitivity of 0.709, specificity of 0.968, mean average precision of 0.495, and TPR at 5% FPR of 0.778. On Noc-ECG, the corresponding values were 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, and 0.900. The largest gains occurred in rare or morphologically unstable rhythm classes, while ablation studies confirmed the contributions of full-covariance modelling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Open-EXG/AG-SCL-for-Long-Tailed-ECG.

AI.tldr: Introduces Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed, multi-label ECG diagnosis, combining angular Gaussian contrastive learning, adaptive logit adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. Achieves state-of-the-art macro performance on PTB-XL and Noc-ECG, with notable gains on rare morphologies; code released.
AI.motivation: Long-tailed label distributions in ECG arrhythmia diagnosis undermine reliability, particularly for rare yet clinically important abnormalities. Prior rebalancing/logit methods focus on class frequency and neglect direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes.
AI.method: AG-SCL unifies: (1) Angular Gaussian contrastive branch modeling full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings; (2) Adaptive Logit Adjustment learning bounded, label-state-specific prior corrections; (3) tail-aware augmentation generating morphology-preserving views while preserving the 7–25 Hz QRS-dominant band.
AI.result: Evaluated on PTB-XL and Noc-ECG (1317 hours, 141 subjects). PTB-XL: Balanced accuracy 0.838; sensitivity 0.709; specificity 0.968; MA P 0.495; TPR@5%FPR 0.778. Noc-ECG: 0.918; 0.889; 0.947; 0.488; 0.900. Largest gains for rare/morphologically unstable rhythms. Ablations confirm contributions of full-covariance modeling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation.
AI.conclusion: AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by fusing prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Code available at the authors’ repository.

title: MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research
summary: Existing LLM-based theorem provers have achieved impressive results on formal mathematics benchmarks, yet they remain confined to acting as autonomous agents that prove a stated proposition. In this paper, we propose MathCoPilot, a human-in-the-loop system that embodies a new human--AI symbiotic paradigm for mathematical research, in which the mathematician steers the high-level mathematical direction while AI agents carry out the detailed formalization and proof work under continuous human guidance. MathCoPilot unifies three core capabilities: (1) an interactive workbench where the mathematician and AI agents collaborate through a living proof blueprint that decomposes a proof into navigable steps the human can directly inspect, direct, and refine; (2) automated proving skill orchestration with adaptive knowledge base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Using MathCoPilot, we systematically compare four state-of-the-art LLMs, including Gemini~3.1~Pro, GPT-5.4, and Claude~Opus~4.7, on a FormalMATH subset and on two real PDE theorems requiring deep domain expertise, evaluating their ability to produce verified Lean~4 proofs and to identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs. Our results show that while current models can handle undergraduate-level problems with high success rates under favorable autoformalization conditions, substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding.

AI.tldr: MathCoPilot introduces a human-in-the-loop system for mathematical research, combining a living proof blueprint with automated proving and knowledge-base based formalization in Lean; evaluated against four LLMs with mixed results: strong on undergraduate problems under favorable autoformalization, weak on domain-specific, deep theorems.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of autonomous LLM theorem provers by enabling human steering of high-level strategy while AI handles formalization and verification under guidance; aims to improve verification and error identification in proofs.
AI.method: Three core capabilities: (1) interactive workbench with navigable proof blueprint; (2) adaptive proof skill orchestration with knowledge-base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into Lean knowledge base; evaluation on FormalMATH subset and two PDE theorems; compare Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7; measure verified Lean 4 proofs and error detection.
AI.result: Models can solve undergraduate-level problems with high success under favorable autoformalization; significant gaps for domain-specific theorems requiring deep mathematical understanding; ability to produce verified Lean 4 proofs exists but not universal; capability to identify errors in incorrect proofs demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop symbiosis improves flexibility and verification prospects; but current state-of-the-art LLMs still struggle with deep domain knowledge; further improvements needed in autoformalization, formal verification integration, and domain expertise handling.

title: On the Disagreement in Perturbation-based xAI -- Benchmarking Perturbation Choices for Flood Detection from SAR Images
summary: Perturbation-based xAI methods are widely used to analyze the behavior and predictions of deep learning models. By altering input regions and measuring the resulting changes in class probabilities with respect to the original image, they assign relevance scores and generate heatmaps that reflect each region's contribution to the prediction. Despite their apparent simplicity, however, perturbation-based methods are sensitive to parameter choices. In this work, we focus on two key parameters of the perturbation pipeline, namely the patch geometry, including the size and shape of the perturbed regions, and the perturbation type, defined by the replacement scheme. Grounded in the use case of flood detection from Synthetic Aperture Radar imagery, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of how relevance estimation changes under different perturbation settings. Beyond visual inspection of the resulting relevance maps, we evaluate their consistency across perturbation strategies and their faithfulness to the model's reasoning. We demonstrate how different perturbation choices can steer the resulting relevance maps, yielding ambiguous and even contradictory explanations. Our findings emphasize the importance of methodological settings in perturbation-based xAI. They underscore the need to carefully inspect and evaluate perturbation choices and to treat them as an integral part when interpreting explanations, ensuring a robust understanding of both the explanations and model predictions.

AI.tldr: Perturbation parameter choices (patch geometry and replacement scheme) critically shape relevance maps in perturbation-based xAI, demonstrated on SAR flood-detection; perturbation settings must be reported and evaluated to ensure robust explanations.
AI.motivation: To reveal how perturbation design choices influence the stability, faithfulness, and interpretability of perturbation-based explanations in deep learning, especially for SAR flood detection.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study varying patch geometry (size and shape) and perturbation type (replacement scheme) in a perturbation-based xAI pipeline applied to flood detection from SAR imagery; assess visual, consistency, and faithfulness metrics of the resulting heatmaps.
AI.result: Different perturbation configurations steer relevance maps, producing ambiguous or contradictory explanations; the findings demonstrate strong sensitivity of explanations to perturbation design.
AI.conclusion: Perturbation settings are an integral part of perturbation-based XAI and must be carefully reported and evaluated to ensure robust, faithful interpretations of model predictions.

title: AHEAD: Anticipatory Hand-Driven Teleoperation via Human Intent Prediction
summary: Direct hand-driven teleoperation maps an operator's hand motion to robot end-effector commands at every frame, enabling precise control, but it requires constant monitoring and correction during approach, grasp, and placement, which can be slow and fatiguing. For repetitive pick-and-place tasks, supervisory (goal-based) teleoperation simplifies this process: the operator specifies goals/waypoints, and the robot executes the motion using planning algorithms. Yet, this introduces latency, as the robot must wait for the next command before it can plan and act. "How can we reduce robot reaction time while lowering operator workload?" To tackle this question, we present AHEAD, a real-time VR teleoperation system that anticipates operator intent to enable proactive, hand-driven control. In a digital twin, the operator performs pick-and-place naturally, using hand motion to convey high-level commands rather than a continuous robot trajectory. AHEAD processes a short window of 3D hand and head signals together with scene context through an attention-based classifier to predict the intended grasp object and placement slot. A state machine converts intent predictions into stable robot goals, enabling early motion while remaining stable under noisy predictions and corrective hand movements. AHEAD's intent prediction module achieves Top1 accuracy: 76% for grasp objects and 76% for target slots. Moreover, our user study shows AHEAD reduces robot reaction latency by 0.6 s (object) and 1.4 s (slot) relative to baselines. Participants also reported lower operator load, indicating faster robot responses while maintaining low operator effort in practice.

AI.tldr: AHEAD enables real-time intent-prediction-based VR teleoperation for hand-driven control in pick-and-place, reducing robot reaction latency and operator workload while achieving 76% Top1 accuracy for grasp objects and placement slots.
AI.motivation: Address the latency and operator workload in supervisory, goal-based teleoperation for repetitive pick-and-place tasks by enabling proactive, hand-driven control through intent prediction.
AI.method: AHEAD uses a digital twin VR interface where the operator performs natural hand motions; it processes a short window of 3D hand and head signals plus scene context with an attention-based classifier to predict the intended grasp object and placement slot. A state machine translates these predictions into stable robot goals, enabling early motion while remaining robust to noisy predictions and minor hand corrections.
AI.result: Intent-prediction module achieves Top1 accuracy of 76% for both grasp objects and target slots. User studies show reduced robot reaction latency by 0.6 s for object and 1.4 s for slot, with participants reporting lower operator load and maintained low effort.
AI.conclusion: Anticipatory, intent-prediction-based teleoperation can significantly improve responsiveness and reduce operator workload in hand-driven robotics, offering a viable path toward more efficient human-robot collaboration in repetitive manipulation tasks.

title: Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) commonly uses entropy for advantage shaping. However, entropy cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. We propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for correctness-aware advantage shaping. Both theoretical and empirical results show that this disagreement reliably indicates token-level correctness. We further show that On-policy Distillation is a special case of CPO, where the posterior distribution is instantiated by an external teacher model. CPO also resolves the zero-advantage problem. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Further analysis shows that correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, and balancing both leads to the best performance.

AI.tldr: Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO) introduces a token-level contrastive signal for advantage shaping in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, outperforming entropy-based methods and subsuming On-policy Distillation; it also resolves zero-advantage and preserves generalization.
AI.motivation: Entropy-based shaping in RL with verifiable rewards cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, producing a weak correctness signal and limiting performance. A token-level, correctness-aware signal is desired.
AI.method: CPO computes a token-level contrastive disagreement between a reference-guided distribution and a vanilla generation distribution to shape advantages. The framework supports On-policy Distillation as a special case (posterior from a teacher model) and addresses zero-advantage. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks are conducted.
AI.result: Theoretically, token-level disagreement correlates with token correctness. Empirically, CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Additional analysis shows correct responses support exploration and incorrect ones exploitation, and balancing both yields best performance.
AI.conclusion: CPO provides a principled, general improvement for RL with verifiable rewards, unifying On-policy Distillation, addressing zero-advantage, and yielding better performance and generalization by leveraging token-level contrastive signals.

title: SportD: Can VLMs Physically Strategize?
summary: Vision--language models have become increasingly capable of interpreting visual scenes, but it remains unclear whether they can use information to make strategically effective decisions. We investigate this question in soccer, where models observe the seconds preceding an on-ball decision and must choose whether to shoot or pass to a specific teammate. Unlike conventional visual-understanding tasks, soccer enables decisions to be evaluated quantitatively by estimating the value of every available action. We introduce SportD, a benchmark comprising 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each model choice is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates the action that most increases the attacking team's probability of scoring, allowing us to measure both optimal-action accuracy and the value forfeited by suboptimal decisions. Across three frontier VLMs, the best selects the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, compared with 38.9% for the professional players, and all models incur significantly greater regret. Further analysis reveals a systematic preference for lower-variance and lower-reward actions: VLMs shoot less often and select substantially less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or the real players. The models also reproduce the player's specific action above chance even when that action is suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation of familiar play patterns rather than consistent evaluation of counterfactual alternatives. SportD provides a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

AI.tldr: SportD introduces a value-grounded benchmark to assess vision–language models (VLMs) on real-time on-ball decisions in soccer, revealing current models lag behind professional players in optimal-action selection and exhibit risk-averse, pattern-imitation behavior.
AI.motivation: To close the gap between static visual understanding and strategic, value-based decision-making in dynamic environments. Soccer provides a quantitative action-value signal via a possession-value model, enabling evaluation of not just perception but optimal action choice.
AI.method: Construct SportD with 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Use a possession-value model to quantify the value of each available action. Evaluate three frontier VLMs on optimal-action accuracy and action-value regret, comparing their performance to professional players. Analyze action distributions (shoot/pass), progression, and imitation of players' actions.
AI.result: Best VLM selects the highest-valued action in 31.4% of events, versus 38.9% for professionals; all models show significantly greater regret. VLMs prefer lower-variance, lower-reward actions, shoot less, and choose less progressive passes than optimal policy or real players. Models also reproduce players’ actions above chance even when suboptimal, indicating partial imitation rather than robust counterfactual evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SportD serves as a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs and highlights the current limitations of VLMs in dynamic, strategic decision-making, pointing to avenues for incorporating explicit value-based planning and counterfactual reasoning.

title: Clean-Reference Streaming Detection of Lens Occlusion and Photometric Transitions for Camera Tamper Monitoring
summary: A surveillance camera is an image sensor whose silent physical degradation invalidates every downstream consumer of its data. In-situ integrity alarms for such vision sensors require low false-alarm rates, bounded computation, and diagnosable behavior under nuisance illumination changes. This paper studies a deliberately narrow streaming integrity monitor for two low-cost sensor-fault signatures: texture-collapsing lens occlusion and abrupt photometric scene transition. The detector compares sampled luminance and local-gradient statistics with a clean-only sliding reference, applies coarse-grid structured-light rejection and mode/rapid-brightness suppression, and emits at most one notification per tamper episode. We formalize the decision predicates and derive a consistency rule for when rapid-brightness suppression makes the scene-transition path unreachable. On 320 in-scope controlled sequences, the default state machine attains 0.800 F1 and 0.822 balanced accuracy (significantly better paired correctness than the strongest baseline, though the F1 margin is not statistically resolved); on a magnitude-swept public audit it attains the highest partial AUC under a 5\% false-alarm budget, and a separate extended-stress FPR-constrained sweep reaches 0.925 recall at 0.025 false-positive rate. Public Xiph, Bremen IoT, and UHCTD diagnostics show the fixed predicates preserve low false alarms while recall concentrates inside the declared envelope (UHCTD in-scope covered recall 0.667 versus 0.016 out of scope), and a 9.09-camera-hour verified-negative public audit records zero false alarms. The method is best interpreted as an auditable sensor-health subsystem rather than a universal camera-tamper classifier.

AI.tldr: A narrow streaming integrity monitor for surveillance cameras detects texture-collapsing occlusion and abrupt photometric transitions with auditable behavior, low false alarms, and bounded computation; achieves strong performance and public-audit validity, best viewed as a sensor-health subsystem.
AI.motivation: To enable in-situ integrity alarms for vision sensors that must operate with low false-alarm rates, bounded computation, and diagnosable behavior under nuisance illumination changes, targeting two low-cost sensor-fault signatures.
AI.method: A detector compares sampled luminance and local-gradient statistics against a clean sliding reference, applies coarse-grid structured-light rejection and mode/rapid-brightness suppression, and emits at most one notification per tamper episode. The authors formalize decision predicates and derive a consistency rule for when rapid-brightness suppression makes the scene-transition path unreachable.
AI.result: On 320 in-scope controlled sequences, F1=0.800 and balanced accuracy=0.822, outperforming the strongest baseline. In a magnitude-swept public audit, it attains the highest partial AUC under a 5% false-alarm budget, and in an extended-stress FPR-constrained sweep achieves 0.925 recall at 0.025 FPR. Public Xiph, Bremen IoT, and UHCTD diagnostics show low false alarms with recall concentrated inside the declared envelope (UHCTD in-scope recall 0.667 vs 0.016 out-of-scope), and a 9.09-camera-hour verified-negative public audit records zero false alarms.
AI.conclusion: The method should be viewed as an auditable sensor-health subsystem rather than a universal camera-tamper classifier.

title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
summary: Recent robot foundation models operate with single-step or short-history visuomotor context. We introduce Test-Time-Training Robot Policies (RoboTTT), a robot model and training recipe that scale visuomotor context to 8K timesteps, three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies, without growing inference latency. At this context length, we unlock new robot capabilities: one-shot in-context imitation from human video demonstrations, on-the-fly policy improvement, robustness to perturbations, and stronger performance on multi-stage, long-horizon tasks. We also observe, for the first time, steady gains in closed-loop performance as pretraining context length scales. At its core, RoboTTT integrates Test-Time Training into robot foundation models such as Vision-Language-Action policies, yielding a sequence model whose recurrent state consists of fast weights, parameters updated by gradient descent during both training and inference, compressing histories into weight space and retrieving contextual information for long-context conditioning. To scale training context length, the recipe combines sequence action forcing with truncated backpropagation through time. On challenging real-robot manipulation tasks, RoboTTT improves overall performance by 87% over the single-step context baseline and fully completes a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task, which no baseline ever does. RoboTTT trained with 8K-timestep context outperforms the same model pretrained with 1K timesteps by 62%, suggesting context length as a new scaling axis for robot foundation models. Videos are available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/robottt/

AI.tldr: RoboTTT scales visuomotor context to 8K timesteps using test-time training in robot foundation models, enabling one-shot imitation, on-the-fly learning, and robust, long-horizon manipulation with no latency increase; shows strong gains over short-context baselines and suggests context length as a new scaling axis.
AI.motivation: Overcome the limitations of short-context visuomotor policies by leveraging long-context information to improve imitation, learning efficiency, robustness, and performance on multi-stage tasks.
AI.method: Integrates test-time training into Vision-Language-Action robot policies, forming a sequence model whose fast-weights are updated during training and inference. Scales context via sequence action forcing and truncated backpropagation through time, achieving up to 8K timesteps while maintaining latency. Evaluated on real-robot manipulation tasks, including a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task.
AI.result: 87% improvement over a single-step context baseline; completes a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task (unmatched by baselines); 8K-context model outperforms 1K-context pretraining by 62%; steady gains in closed-loop performance with increasing context length.
AI.conclusion: Context length becomes a new scalable axis for robot foundation models. RoboTTT demonstrates significant gains in imitation, robustness, and long-horizon planning, with practical real-robot validation and accessible demonstrations.

title: PolyQ: Codesigning End-to-End Quantization Framework for Scalable Edge CPU LLM Inference
summary: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods offer either coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently on CPUs. We present PolyQ, a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design for activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation under a user-specified average-bit budget. PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from $\{2,3,4,8,16\}$, then uses a compile-time model compiler to permute and cluster channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and merge compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path. This turns fine-grained budget fitting into a practical fractional-bit deployment method for CPU-only inference. Across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2, PolyQ provides stable quality scaling from 3--6\,b and improves perplexity by 2.4--32.1\% over prior methods at a 3\,b target. End-to-end measurements on three representative CPUs -- workstation, laptop, and mobile -- show that compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8\%, prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with the configured bit budget, and energy/token overhead stays below 2\% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end. These results show that fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

AI.tldr: PolyQ enables per-channel fractional-bit quantization on CPUs by co-designing a compiler and quantization process to allocate bits from {2,3,4,8,16} under an average-bit budget, then clusters channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generating SIMD- and LUT-friendly kernels and merging permutations across operators to maintain layout regularization off the runtime path.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference on CPUs remains constrained by coarse-grained or mixed-precision quantization; a CPU-oriented, activation-aware, per-channel bit allocation that respects an average-budget can improve accuracy while preserving performance.
AI.method: Assign per-channel bit-widths from {2,3,4,8,16}; a compile-time model compiler permutes and clusters channels into bit-homogeneous blocks; generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels; merge compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path; demonstrate on Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2; measure across workstation, laptop, and mobile CPUs.
AI.result: Quality scales from 3–6 bits; perplexity improves 2.4–32.1% over prior methods at a 3-bit target; end-to-end measurements show up to 70.8% reduction in activation reorder traffic; prefill latency and decode throughput scale proportionally with the configured bit budget; energy/token overhead stays below 2% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end.
AI.conclusion: Fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

title: Action QFormer: Structured Representation Shaping under Action Supervision in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Action supervision in vision-language-action (VLA) models is often treated as a downstream objective for learning action prediction. In this paper, we study it instead as a force that shapes inherited multimodal representations. We show that this shaping has a dual effect: it is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but when action supervision is applied too directly to the inherited multimodal pathway, it can also destabilize representations that support language-side processing and object grounding. To address this tension, we introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves average closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Further analyses show that Action QFormer changes how action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations, reducing broad upstream rewriting while preserving targeted and sometimes constructive action-supervised adaptation. These results suggest that improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones, but also better ways of selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how it is shaped under action supervision.

AI.tldr: Introduces Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that reorganizes inherited multimodal information under action supervision to form action-facing representations before generation; achieves large zero-shot navigation gains and stabilizes processing; highlights the importance of selective, controlled shaping of multimodal representations.
AI.motivation: Action supervision is typically applied downstream to guide action prediction, but can destabilize language grounding and object grounding when applied too directly to the inherited multimodal path. A better mechanism is needed to harness action guidance without degrading other modalities.
AI.method: Propose Action QFormer, a query-based interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal representations into action-facing representations prior to action generation, thereby isolating action supervision from the core language/object grounding streams.
AI.result: In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, average closed-loop task success rises from 18.8% to 56.3%; fixed-instruction action-generation correctness improves from 22.5% to 75.5%; out-of-distribution instruction generations are nearly eliminated. Analyses indicate reduced broad upstream rewriting and more targeted action-supervised adaptation of representations.
AI.conclusion: Improving VLA performance requires not only stronger backbones but also principled selection and organization of inherited multimodal information, with controlled shaping under action supervision to balance action guidance and multimodal robustness.

title: Rare Concept Generation via Counterfactual Inference in Diffusion Models
comment: Comments: 17 pages, 15 figures, to appear at ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Rare concept generation focuses on synthesizing customized images conditioned on text prompts that describe objects with unusual attributes. Previous works failed to align the generated images with rare concepts, resulting in incorrect attribute rendering or inconsistent composition of concepts. Such failures, as we observed, stem from the inherent common knowledge bias in the training stage of diffusion models, where objects are strongly associated with their common attributes, making it difficult to break these associations when generating rare concepts. To address such challenges, in this paper, we propose a novel Counterfactual Inference-based Diffusion approach, dubbed CI-Diff. CI-Diff blocks the interference of the model's inherent common knowledge bias and utilizes the Natural Direct Effect to capture the independent influence of the text prompt of rare concepts on image generation so that decoupling the unusual attributes from the rare concepts. To this end, we reformulate the classifier-free guidance mechanism to highlight the atypical attributes. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to introduce causal inference into the rare concept generation task. Extensive experiments on the RareBench benchmark validate the superiority of CI-Diff over state-of-the-art diffusion models. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/200204jzy/CI-Diff.

AI.tldr: Proposes CI-Diff, a diffusion model with counterfactual inference to decouple rare concepts from common knowledge bias, using natural direct effect and redefined classifier-free guidance; achieves state-of-the-art on RareBench; code released.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between generated images and rare concepts due to diffusion models' bias to common attributes; need to accurately render unconventional attributes.
AI.method: CI-Diff employs counterfactual inference and natural direct effect to isolate the impact of rare concept prompts; blocks interference from common knowledge; reformulates classifier-free guidance to emphasize atypical attributes.
AI.result: Experimental validation on RareBench shows superior performance compared to SOTA diffusion models; code available.
AI.conclusion: First to integrate causal inference into rare concept generation; demonstrates effectiveness and provides open-source implementation.

title: TIDE: Trustworthy and Interpretable Battery Degradation Estimation with Contextual Learning and Symbolic Distillation
summary: Battery health estimation is fundamental for battery management in battery-powered systems, where inaccurate health states may affect control, maintenance, and service life. It becomes even more critical in intelligent connected systems, where estimation errors can propagate across interconnected devices and downstream decisions. In this paper, we propose TIDE, a trustworthy and interpretable battery degradation estimator for reliable battery health estimation. TIDE jointly considers accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability, which are all essential for practical deployment and downstream decision making. To realize these objectives, TIDE combines battery-domain knowledge with operational measurements in a three-component backbone. A knowledge-guided degradation prior promotes trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual component provides interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and a contextual learning component captures battery-specific operational effects for improved accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate that provides a concise model-level interpretation of its learned estimation logic. Experiments show that TIDE achieves strong estimation accuracy, improving overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. Its knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modelling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, supporting trustworthy estimation. Meanwhile, the backbone enables component-level interpretation, while symbolic distillation provides a compact model-level representation of the learned estimation logic. These results support the practical use of TIDE for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

AI.tldr: TIDE is a three-component, knowledge-guided, interpretable battery degradation estimator that achieves higher accuracy and trustworthiness, with a symbolic surrogate for model-level interpretation; shows ~19.7% fidelity improvement over baselines and reduces aging-consistency violations.
AI.motivation: Battery health estimation in BMS requires accurate, trustworthy, and interpretable models to prevent propagation of errors and to support downstream decisions in intelligent connected systems.
AI.method: A three-component backbone: (1) knowledge-guided degradation prior for trustworthiness, (2) monotone residual component for interpretable aging-consistent refinement, (3) contextual learning component for battery-specific operational effects. The backbone is distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate for concise model-level interpretation.
AI.result: Experiments show an average 19.7% improvement in estimation fidelity over representative baselines. The knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual reduce aging-consistency violations, enhancing trustworthiness. The backbone enables component-level interpretation, and symbolic distillation yields a compact model-level interpretation of the learned estimation logic.
AI.conclusion: TIDE enables practical battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems by delivering accurate, trustworthy, and interpretable health estimations, with a compact symbolic surrogate for easy deployment and interpretation.

title: Analytic Abduction: Causal Decomposition and Governed Commitment for Human--AI Coordination
summary: Abductive reasoning operates in two directions. The synthetic mode builds explanations from available hypotheses; the analytic mode, conversely, identifies the latent factors whose interaction accounts for a complex observed state. This paper develops the analytic mode as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment, in which candidate factors coexist and interact, resolving into committed conclusions only when explicit governance conditions are met. The formal core is the $κ$-$τ$ apparatus: $κ$ encodes the epistemic interaction among hypotheses, and $τ$ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to the decision's stakes. The central contribution is the causal cluster, a structured object recording which latent factors participate in a decomposition, with what weights and interaction structure, together with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster $κ^*$, inter-cluster $κ^{**}$) that guards against causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework's contribution to human-AI reasoning is the legibility of suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object, providing structural resistance to premature convergence. In practice, the decision-maker is handed not a single imposed answer but the competing explanatory scenarios, weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidence that would resolve between them, so that sound action is possible even before the ambiguity is resolved.

AI.tldr: A non-greedy analytic abductive framework using a κ-τ apparatus, causal clusters, and a two-level κ architecture to support legible, risk-aware reasoning and prevent premature convergence; validated on epidemiological crisis decomposition and cyber threat analysis.
AI.motivation: To move beyond greedy abduction by maintaining competing latent-factor decompositions under governance, enabling shared coordination and better action under uncertainty.
AI.method: Introduce κ-τ framework: κ encodes epistemic interactions among hypotheses; τ sets commitment thresholds; construct causal clusters encoding participating latent factors with weights and interactions; implement intra-cluster κ* and inter-cluster κ** to guard against misattribution; present two domain demonstrations and produce competing explanatory scenarios with supporting evidence.
AI.result: Produces a legible suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object; resists premature convergence; supports sound action before ambiguity is resolved; demonstrates applicability in epidemiology and cybersecurity.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances human-AI reasoning by offering a structured, governance-aware analytic abductive approach that yields explainable, compatible scenarios with evidentiary support, potentially generalizable to other complex domains.

title: TAMF-VTON: Texture-Aware Mask-Free Virtual Try-On via High-Fidelity Image Synthesis
summary: Recent diffusion-based virtual try-on (VTON) methods remain limited by their reliance on segmentation masks, insufficient preservation of fine-grained textures, and limited support for arbitrary multi-garment compositions. Consequently, existing approaches still face significant challenges in real-world e-commerce deployment. We present TAMF-VTON, a texture-aware, mask-free framework that enables high-fidelity image synthesis under practical unconstrained conditions. Our method requires no human parsing or inpainting masks at inference time and supports diverse garment styles, categories, and quantities, enabling the simultaneous transfer of multiple items while preserving body structure and intricate texture details. This is achieved through a unified generative pipeline with three key components: (1) a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation scheme that enables efficient fine-tuning without compromising the base model's general editing capabilities; (2) a frequency-domain supervision mechanism that explicitly optimizes high-frequency spectral consistency to preserve high-fidelity textures; and (3) a robust data curation pipeline employing an adaptive inpainting strategy to simulate the inverse VTON process for high-quality training pair generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and perceptual quality. Optimized for efficiency, the model achieves inference in under 15 seconds per image on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with INT4 quantization. By combining mask-free operation, flexible multi-garment composition, faithful texture preservation, and efficient inference on consumer hardware, TAMF-VTON demonstrates a commercially viable solution for scalable deployment in real-world digital fashion scenarios. The project is available at https://www.style3d.ai/ai-photoshoot/virtual-clothing-try-on.

AI.tldr: TAMF-VTON is a texture-aware, mask-free diffusion-based virtual try-on system that supports multi-garment transfers with high texture fidelity, using MoE-based fine-tuning, frequency-domain texture supervision, and adaptive inpainting-driven training data generation for efficient, real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion-based VTON methods rely on segmentation masks, often fail to preserve fine textures, and struggle with arbitrary multi-garment compositions, hindering real-world e-commerce deployment. A mask-free, texture-preserving, multi-garment-capable solution is needed.
AI.method: Three-part unified pipeline: (1) lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation for efficient fine-tuning without degrading the base model's general editing capabilities; (2) a frequency-domain supervision mechanism that optimizes high-frequency spectral consistency to preserve textures; (3) a robust data curation pipeline with adaptive inpainting to simulate the inverse VTON process for high-quality training-pair generation. Additional claims: no human parsing or inpainting masks required at inference, supports diverse garment styles/categories/quantities, multi-item transfer, and efficient inference (<15s per image on RTX 4090 with INT4).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show TAMF-VTON outperforms state-of-the-art methods in quantitative metrics and perceptual quality. The method is optimized for efficiency and is commercially viable for scalable deployment in real-world digital fashion scenarios.
AI.conclusion: TAMF-VTON delivers a mask-free, texture-preserving, multi-garment VTON solution with efficient inference and practical deployment potential, advancing diffusion-based virtual try-on toward real-world e-commerce applications.

title: Trajectory-Aware Flow Matching for Topology Optimisation
summary: Topology optimisation (TO) often requires repeated finite element analysis and sensitivity-based material updates, which can be costly when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying physical and design conditions. Generative TO offers a route to rapid design exploration, but existing models may rely on adversarial training, long reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance to maintain structural feasibility and physical consistency. This study develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation. Linear FMTO is first formulated as an endpoint-based baseline by interpolating between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

AI.tldr: A flow-matching topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation using trajectory-aware guidance to improve diversity, fidelity, and efficiency, outperforming diffusion baselines with fewer samples.
AI.motivation: TO is computationally expensive due to repeated FEA and sensitivity updates; generative TO offers fast design exploration but faces feasibility/physical consistency issues. A physics-informed, non-diffusion-based flow matching approach aims to enable conditional topology generation with reduced inference-time optimization.
AI.method: Baseline: endpoint flow matching between Gaussian source field and BESO reference topology. Introduce trajectory-aware FMTO: construct a probability path and target velocity field from volume-fraction-indexed BESO states, embedding optimization history into the learned transport. Analyze path--velocity mismatch to understand the effect of trajectory weighting. Evaluate on 2D and 3D problems, comparing to diffusion-based baselines, and assess trajectory-anchor density.
AI.result: FMTO yields diverse topology candidates with improved compliance, volume-fraction satisfaction, and topology fidelity, using substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Trajectory-aware weighting with moderate values offers best performance; excessive guidance over-constrains learning. Extends to 3D and demonstrates applicability beyond 2D.
AI.conclusion: Flow matching with trajectory-aware physics guidance provides efficient, diverse, and physically consistent topology generations, reducing the need for inference-time optimization and robust under limited training data; path design choices (trajectory weight, anchor density) critically influence performance and generalization.

title: MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers
summary: As Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers emerge as the core infrastructure for connecting LLMs with external tools, existing benchmarks leverage real-world MCP servers to evaluate LLM agents' tool-using capabilities. However, these benchmarks overlook the continuous evolution of tool interfaces and functionalities within MCP servers, resulting in flawed assessments that fail to capture the agent's adaptability in changing tool landscapes. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{MCPEvol-Bench}, a novel benchmark for evaluating the task-solving capabilities of LLM agents under dynamic toolset evolution. Inspired by large-scale empirical study, we propose 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution within 123 MCP servers. We benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple versions of MCP servers, revealing that even frontier models struggle to adapt to evolving tools. For instance, GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 exhibit performance declines of 13.7\% and 14.4\% in evolved MCP servers, respectively, accompanied by substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors. These findings highlight the vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows, establishing MCPEvol-Bench as a standard for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments.

AI.tldr: MCPEvol-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents’ adaptability to evolving MCP tool interfaces; it introduces 11 mutation operators across 123 MCP servers, benchmarks 12 LLMs, and shows notable performance drops under tool evolution, highlighting the need to test adaptability in dynamic tool landscapes.
AI.motivation: Existing MCP benchmarks rely on real, static tool interfaces, failing to capture how agents adapt to evolving tools and APIs; there is a gap in evaluating agent resilience in changing tool landscapes.
AI.method: Define and apply 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution across 123 MCP servers; benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple evolved server versions; analyze performance and error patterns focusing on planning and reasoning.
AI.result: Under evolved MCP servers, performance declines are observed (e.g., GPT-5.4 −13.7%, Claude-Sonnet-4-6 −14.4%), accompanied by increased planning and reasoning errors, indicating vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows to tool evolution.
AI.conclusion: MCPEvol-Bench establishes a standard for assessing agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments and demonstrates the need for more robust LLMs capable of coping with evolving tool interfaces.

title: An LLM-Based Automatic Sportscast Solution for Robot Soccer Matches
summary: RoboCup has always been a scenario to develop systems that solve real-world problems. Driven by the main goal of playing against the 2050 FIFA World Cup champions, the RoboCup Soccer leagues need to constantly measure how the research community is progressing. Computing visual statistics from match videos is a crucial way to track this evolution. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a fully autonomous, real-time sports commentator for RoboCup matches. By bridging the gap between raw kinematic tracking and natural language generation, our neuro-symbolic architecture extracts precise statistics from video streams and turns them into fluent, hallucination-free narration. The proposed system is capable of generating statistics and commentary both during live match streaming and in post-game analysis, easily adapting to the new dynamism of the league where different humanoid robots of different sizes share the field. Supplemental materials are available at https://lab-rococo-sapienza.github.io/MARIO/

AI.tldr: Autonomous real-time RoboCup commentator converts video-based robot kinematics into fluent, hallucination-free narration using a neuro-symbolic architecture; supports live and post-game analysis and adapts to varying robot sizes.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between raw kinematic tracking and natural language generation to provide quantitative statistics and commentary for RoboCup progress tracking.
AI.method: Neuro-symbolic pipeline that extracts precise statistics from video streams and generates fluent narration; designed for real-time operation and robustness across different humanoid robot configurations.
AI.result: System can generate statistics and commentary during live streams and post-game analysis; adaptable to different robot sizes; reduces reliance on manual narration; operates autonomously with hallucination-free output.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of end-to-end autonomous narration in RoboCup, linking perception directly to language, with potential impact on evaluation, viewer engagement, and analytics; supplementary materials provided.

title: Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization
summary: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware. However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: Introduces differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) to train deep continuous-time SNNs with memory efficiency, mapping irregular presynaptic spikes to fixed-time-weighted events and reducing memory from O(Nout Nin) to O(Nout M) for TTFS coding; adds synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization for stability; achieves substantial speedups and enables training of 9-layer and 20-layer conv SNNs on CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Overcome memory bottlenecks in exact spike-time computation when training deep continuous-time SNNs, while preserving accurate membrane-potential dynamics across general LIF parameters.
AI.method: Replace irregular spike-time processing with differentiable spike-time discretization: map presynaptic spikes to M fixed time intervals, yielding fixed input-dimension; use TTFS coding; apply synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization to structure firing windows and support pipeline-like processing.
AI.result: Memory for candidate activations drops from O(Nout*Nin) to O(Nout*M) (for TTFS). DSTD achieves up to ~100x memory reduction and ~20x training-time reduction over exact spike-time methods. Demonstrated training of 9-layer conv SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer conv SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: DSTD provides a scalable, memory-efficient framework for training deep continuous-time SNNs with general time constants, combining discretized differentiable spike processing and temporal regularization to enable practical deep SNNs on standard datasets.

title: TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

AI.tldr: TopoAgent introduces a self-evolving topological framework for autonomous scientific reasoning in multimodal LLMs, replacing linear planning with dynamic, state-isolated DAGs and adaptive atom splitting to improve robustness and performance on science benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of monolithic, linear planning in multimodal LLMs (visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, brittle execution under fixed task granularity) by enabling context-aware, noise-resistant reasoning.
AI.method: Use a front-end decomposer to split queries into visually-grounded atoms, organize them into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to enforce context isolation, and apply adaptive atomic fission to dynamically split bottleneck nodes into finer sub-atoms at runtime when tool capabilities are exceeded.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks shows TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agents, with enhanced robustness, reduced noise impact, and self-correction.
AI.conclusion: Topology-based, self-evolving reasoning (TopoAgent) provides a robust, noise-resistant framework for autonomous scientific reasoning that surpasses linear-agent baselines.

title: Blurring Modal Boundaries: A Unified Survey from Single- to Multi-Modal Person Re-ldentification
summary: Person re-identification (ReID) serves as a critical component in intelligent surveillance systems, aiming to match identities across disjoint camera networks. While traditional methods primarily rely on single-modal RGB imagery, they are often constrained by environmental challenges such as low illumination and occlusion. To overcome these limitations, the field is rapidly evolving toward cross-modal and multi-modal paradigms. This survey presents a comprehensive overview of this transition, systematically reviewing key cross-modal tasks including visible-infrared (VI-ReID), text-image (TI-ReID), sketch-based (Sketch-ReID), and the emerging Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) ReID, which extends perception beyond direct visibility. Furthermore, we examine tri-spectral and multi-modal fusion ReID, discussing how complementary information from diverse sensors enhances robustness. Beyond summarizing datasets, challenges, and methodologies, we propose a Transformer-based baseline framework for visible-infrared ReID, designed to effectively capture modality-invariant features. Finally, based on the current landscape, we outline several promising directions for future research.

AI.tldr: Survey of cross-modal and multi-modal person ReID, proposing a Transformer-based baseline for visible–infrared ReID; covers VI/ TI/ Sketch/ NLOS ReID, tri-spectral fusion, datasets, challenges, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Overcome limitations of single-modality ReID (e.g., low illumination, occlusion) by leveraging cross-modal and multi-modal information; address robustness through fusion across sensors and modalities.
AI.method: Systematic survey of existing cross-modal ReID tasks (VI-ReID, TI-ReID, Sketch-ReID, NLOS-ReID) and tri-/multi-modal fusion; discussion of datasets, challenges, and methodologies; proposal of a Transformer-based baseline for VI-ReID.
AI.result: Comprehensive synthesis of current methods and datasets; introduction of a Transformer-based baseline for VI-ReID to capture modality-invariant features; summarized challenges and potential future research directions.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal/multi-modal ReID is a promising trajectory to enhance robustness; Transformer-based baselines show potential for learning modality-invariant representations; further work needed on datasets, alignment, efficiency, and new modalities (e.g., NLOS).

title: Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

AI.tldr: Introduces GradDist and Grad2Fair to assess and achieve graph fairness without demographic data, using gradient distributions to quantify bias and guide debiasing.
AI.motivation: Fairness in GNNs often relies on access to demographic attributes. When demographics are unavailable or unreliable, there is a need for demography-free fairness techniques. The authors observe that gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information and leverage this for fairness.
AI.method: Propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes of gradient distributions. Propose Grad2Fair, a gradient-guided approach that debiases graphs using gradients without predicting demographics, enabling stable fairness performance.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets show Grad2Fair achieves superior fairness performance compared to baselines in most cases, with code released at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: Demography-free fairness in GNNs is feasible; gradient-based analysis (GradDist) can quantify bias, and the proposed Grad2Fair method effectively debiases without demographic predictions, yielding robust fairness improvements.

title: SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

AI.tldr: On-device SmartRAG decomposes on-device intelligence into Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking to run a 1.7B LLM on smartphones with EvoNER and MRGraph for competitive multi-hop QA against much larger models, using selective LLM calls to label, plan, and answer.
AI.motivation: Privacy, low latency, offline availability, and edge-budget constraints make giant models impractical on mobile devices; compression alone cannot resolve the compute-cost gap.
AI.method: Four coordinated modules (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking). EvoNER for continual learning: an on-device NER that expands labels via teacher-distilled updates without retraining the backbone. MRGraph as a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph. Retrieval combines graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. LLM invoked only for high-value semantic tasks (labeling, planning, answer synthesis). Evaluation on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) with a 1.7B quantized backbone.
AI.result: SmartRAG achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to ~18× larger while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.
AI.conclusion: On-device intelligence can approach the capabilities of much larger models by distributing work across specialized on-device modules and limiting LLM usage to high-value tasks, enabling private, fast, offline QA on mobile hardware.

title: Physics-Informed Diffusion for Biomechanically Plausible 3D Sign Language Generation
summary: Sign language production, which generates continuous 3D skeletal motion from spoken language input, must simultaneously satisfy two constraints: semantic fidelity, so that a deaf viewer can recognize the intended sequence of glosses, and biomechanical plausibility, so that the generated skeleton respects anatomical constraints. Existing approaches optimize semantic reconstruction through coordinate-based objectives that treat the skeleton as an unstructured vector, thus allowing for bone length drift, joint angle violations, and temporarily locked fingers. We introduce PIDiffSign, a physics-informed diffusion model for gloss-to-pose translation that incorporates anatomical constraints into both the architecture and training objective. The model uses a Transformer encoder-decoder, where the decoder is conditioned on the diffusion time step through adaptive zero-initialized layer normalization and cross-attends to gloss representations. A differentiable geometry module enforces bone length consistency and biologically valid joint angles throughout generation. Training combines anthropomorphic, kinematic, angular, and finger-joint constraints with a contrastive gloss-pose alignment loss and classifier-free guidance for semantically conditioned sampling. Experiments on the PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily benchmarks show consistent improvements over a strong diffusion baseline in pose accuracy, joint-angle correctness, distributional realism, and back-translation quality. These results demonstrate that physics-informed diffusion improves both motion realism and semantic fidelity for sign language generation.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed diffusion model (PIDiffSign) translates glosses to pose for sign language by enforcing anatomical constraints during both architecture and training, yielding improved motion realism and semantic fidelity vs a diffusion baseline on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily.
AI.motivation: Sign language synthesis must satisfy semantic fidelity and biomechanical plausibility. Coordinate-based objectives without anatomy enforcement permit bone-length drift, implausible joint angles, and awkward finger motion.
AI.method: A Transformer encoder-decoder with a diffusion-time-conditioned decoder (adaptive zero-initialized layernorm) and gloss-conditioned cross-attentions. A differentiable geometry module enforces bone-length consistency and biologically valid joint angles. Training includes anthropomorphic, kinematic, angular, and finger-joint constraints, plus a contrastive gloss-pose alignment loss and classifier-free guidance for semantically conditioned sampling.
AI.result: PIDiffSign achieves consistent improvements over a strong diffusion baseline in pose accuracy, joint-angle correctness, distributional realism, and back-translation quality on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed diffusion improves both motion realism and semantic fidelity for sign language generation; integrating anatomical constraints into both architecture and loss yields more natural, semantically faithful sign language motion.

title: MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits
summary:
We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

AI.tldr: MESHA is a mechanism-forced BAI algorithm for strategic linear bandits that uses uniform sampling and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition to mitigate misreports; it provides a theoretical upper bound on failure probability and shows OD-based sampling fails under strategic reporting; experiments show MESHA outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: In strategic linear bandits, arms may misreport their feature vectors to influence BAI outcomes; designing robust algorithms under strategic behavior is essential.
AI.method: Proposes MESHA with uniform sampling and epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC). Analyzes Nash equilibria where arms may attempt to pass GTC; derives an upper bound on MESHA's failure probability under budget T; contrasts with G-optimal/design-based sampling; uses simulations.
AI.result: Theoretical bound on failure probability under budget T; demonstration that OD-based sampling can starve the true best arm; empirical results showing MESHA outperforms OD-based and feature-agnostic baselines.
AI.conclusion: MESHA provides a robust mechanism-forced approach to BAI in strategic linear bandits, leveraging GTC to curb misreports and achieving better practical performance; the work highlights vulnerabilities of OD-based strategies in strategic settings.

title: Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications
summary: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

AI.tldr: Kaleidoscope provides an integrated, human-in-the-loop workflow for contextual functional evaluation to achieve reliable automated scoring, combining persona-based test generation, contextual rubrics, human annotations, and LLM-based scoring gated by agreement thresholds; early pilot indicates practical benefits.
AI.motivation: Public-sector AI deployments face policy, governance, and context gaps that limit traditional benchmarks; there's a need for end-to-end, context-aware evaluation that can be reviewed and governed.
AI.method: Integrated workflow: generate persona-based tests; apply contextual rubrics; collect human labels; use LLMs to score only when agreement with labels crosses a configured threshold; iterative, inspectable process; pilot across four use cases; 108 Q&A pairs, four domains, 14 evaluation dimensions.
AI.result: Early evidence from a three-week pilot suggests Kaleidoscope enables end-to-end reliable, automated scoring and yields useful features for scalable evaluation; 108 annotated items across domains; 14 dimensions; 4 domains; custom rubrics tested.
AI.conclusion: Kaleidoscope offers a practical, auditable pipeline for contextual evaluation suitable for product teams; further validation across more domains and longer timescales is warranted.

title: Rotational Motion-Induced Error Compensation for Phase-Shifting Profilometry-Based Eye Reconstruction
summary: With the proliferation of immersive Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) for Virtual and Augmented Reality (VR/AR), reliable and high-precision eye tracking has become increasingly important. Conventional 2D image-based methods offer low system complexity but remain limited in stability, accuracy, and robustness. Three-dimensional ocular surface reconstruction can provide richer geomet-ric information, and structured light profilometry is particularly attractive because it enables dense and accurate surface measurement. However, Phase-Shifting Profilometry (PSP), which estimates phase from sequentially acquired fringe images, is highly susceptible to motion-induced errors when the eye rotates between frames. This study proposes a rotational motion compensation framework for PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction. Relative eye rotation is estimated from image-based motion cues using a user-specific 3D eye model in a spherical-coordinate domain. The estimated motion is then used to compensate for camera-pixel mismatch and phase-shift errors caused by inter-frame rotation. A region-wise optimization strategy is further introduced to reduce residual artifacts by inde-pendently refining the compensation strength in different ocular regions. Experiments with a rotating fake eye under non-uniform motion demonstrate that the proposed method substantially suppresses motion-induced deformation and improves reconstruction accuracy. An additional experiment with a non-spherical rigid object indicates that the compensation principle is not restricted to spherical eye geometry. These results establish a practical basis for stable PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction toward future high-precision eye tracking in immersive environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a rotational motion compensation framework for PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction to mitigate motion-induced phase errors from inter-frame eye rotations. Uses a user-specific 3D eye model in spherical coordinates to estimate relative rotation from image cues, applies compensation for camera-pixel mismatch and PSP phase errors, and employs region-wise optimization to reduce artifacts. Validated on rotating fake eyes and non-spherical objects, showing improved accuracy and robustness for high-precision eye tracking in VR/AR.
AI.motivation: Eye tracking in VR/AR requires high-precision, stable 3D reconstruction. PSP offers dense surface info but is sensitive to inter-frame eye rotation, causing deformation and errors. A robust compensation framework is needed to enable reliable dynamic 3D eye reconstruction under realistic motion.
AI.method: A rotational motion compensation framework for PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction. Relative eye rotation is estimated from image-based motion cues using a user-specific 3D eye model formulated in a spherical-coordinate domain. The estimated motion corrects camera-pixel mismatch and phase-shift errors due to inter-frame rotation. A region-wise optimization refines compensation strength independently across ocular regions to suppress residual artifacts.
AI.result: Experiments with a rotating fake eye under non-uniform motion show substantial suppression of motion-induced deformation and improved reconstruction accuracy. An additional experiment with a non-spherical rigid object indicates the compensation principle generalizes beyond spherical eye geometry.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a practical basis for stable PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction in immersive environments, contributing toward future high-precision eye tracking in VR/AR.

title: Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering
summary: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

AI.tldr: VoICE offers a Voronoi-based counterfactual explainability framework for feature-weighted k-means that yields valid, cost-efficient, actionable explanations by projecting into the target cluster's weighted Voronoi region.
