AI.motivation: Counterfactual explanations are standard in supervised learning but difficult for clustering because cluster IDs are unlabeled and governed by the partition geometry; there is a need for local, interpretable explanations of cluster assignments that respect feature weights.
AI.method: Define weighted Voronoi regions for a feature-weighted k-means; generate counterfactuals by projecting onto the target cluster's region; incorporate feature weights into both geometry and the counterfactual objective; intersect target regions with data-derived bounds and contract toward the centroid to limit extrapolation and boundary sensitivity.
AI.result: VoICE consistently yields valid target-cluster membership across benchmark datasets, whereas a leading pairwise centroid baseline often fails to do so.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides parsimonious, least-cost explanations under actionability constraints and improves interpretability and reliability of clustering explanations.

title: Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026, Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA)
summary: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

AI.tldr: Perception-RFT with GRPO enables direct perception-based policies for multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens; results show substantial inference savings and that reasoning-based RL underperforms; identifies Grounding Divergence on OOD benchmarks and an effective early SFT→RL transition that reduces training data by 65%.
AI.motivation: Explicit visual grounding in multimodal document QA is hindered by the need for large annotated datasets (SFT) and costly, verbose RL traces; it remains unclear whether explicit reasoning is necessary for effective grounding and efficient inference.
AI.method: Introduce Perception-RFT applying Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA; bypass intermediate reasoning tokens; construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings for comparison; conduct analysis on Qwen3-VL-4B; examine optimization dynamics and grounding performance; explore early SFT→RL transition.
AI.result: Reasoning-enabled models suppress reasoning traces and converge to direct perception-based policies at 4B parameters; per-query token length reduced by >60%; reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training; Grounding Divergence observed: a trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on OOD samples (4,828); early SFT→RL transition achieves comparable precision with ~65% less training data.
AI.conclusion: Direct perception-based policies can outperform reasoning-based RL in multimodal document QA, achieving similar or better grounding with substantially lower inference cost and data requirements. The findings reveal transfer of text-domain SFT saturation and RL instability to multimodal settings, uncover Grounding Divergence, and suggest cautious, data-efficient transition strategies.

title: Selectivity Drives Efficiency: Dataset Pruning for Visual Place Recognition
summary: Recent visual place recognition (VPR) studies have increasingly relied on large-scale datasets to train more robust and discriminative models. Although this trend significantly improves recognition performance, it also introduces substantial storage and training costs, especially when new architectures or training strategies need to be repeatedly developed and evaluated. Dataset pruning (DP) provides a promising way to improve data efficiency by retaining only informative training data. However, conventional DP methods mainly follow the sample-wise classification paradigm, which overlooks the relation-dependent training nature of VPR, where supervision is typically formed by image pairs rather than independent images. To address this issue, we propose a place-wise dataset pruning framework tailored for VPR. Instead of pruning individual images, our method treats each place as the basic pruning unit and introduces two complementary novel metrics, i.e., intra-place diversity (IPD) and inter-place similarity (IPS), to evaluate the training value of each place. By jointly considering these two metrics, our method ranks all places and constructs a compact yet informative coreset, thereby allowing the pruned dataset to still support the training of robust and discriminative VPR models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DP baselines under different pruning ratios while reducing selection and training costs. Moreover, by pruning a merged dataset roughly 3.5$\times$ the size of GSV-Cities to a comparable scale, our coreset maintains highly competitive performance, achieving 94.5\% R@1 on MSLS-val and 97.0\% R@1 on Nordland with only NetVLAD. Codes will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Place-wise dataset pruning (DP) for visual place recognition (VPR) introduces IPD (intra-place diversity) and IPS (inter-place similarity) as joint criteria to rank and prune data by places rather than individual images. The resulting coreset preserves training efficacy while reducing data and training costs, outperforming sample-wise DP baselines and remaining competitive when merging datasets (e.g., ~3.5× smaller than GSV-Cities).
AI.motivation: Large-scale VPR datasets boost accuracy but create heavy storage and training costs. Conventional sample-wise DP fails to capture the pair-based supervision inherent in VPR (image pairs), motivating a place-wise approach.
AI.method: Treat each place as the pruning unit. Compute intra-place diversity (IPD) to quantify within-place variability and inter-place similarity (IPS) to measure similarity between places. Jointly rank places by IPD and IPS to form a compact, informative coreset. Train VPR models (NetVLAD) on the pruned dataset and evaluate on standard benchmarks.
AI.result: The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DP baselines across pruning ratios. It maintains strong performance even when pruning a merged dataset to about 3.5× smaller than GSV-Cities, achieving 94.5% R@1 on MSLS-val and 97.0% R@1 on Nordland with NetVLAD.
AI.conclusion: Place-wise pruning with IPD and IPS yields a data-efficient coreset for VPR that preserves discriminative capability while reducing data size and training costs. The approach demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization and will have publicly released code.

title: SUFLECA: Scaling Up Feature Learning for CAD-to-image Alignment
summary: CAD-to-image alignment aims to estimate an object's 9D pose (rotation, translation, and anisotropic scale) from a single RGB image, enabling applications in robotics and augmented reality. Recent zero-shot methods use visual foundation models to match image regions to CAD models, yet typically their correspondences are appearance-driven and degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. To address these limitations, we introduce SUFLECA (Scaling Up Feature LEarning for CAD Alignment), a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD alignment with two key contributions. First, SUFLECA scales up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations through Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images spanning 12 real and synthetic datasets, learning compact geometry-aware features that generalize across domains. Second, we propose a geometrically consistent matching algorithm that establishes reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences. Together, these contributions enable accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement. On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy, outperforming, with a smaller computational footprint, the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and, for the first time on this benchmark, even surpassing fully supervised methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/snt-arg/SUFLECA

AI.tldr: SUFLECA is a weakly-supervised, zero-shot CAD-to-image alignment method that learns geometry-aware features via NOCS supervision on 674k images and uses a geometrically consistent matching algorithm to obtain fast, one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on ScanNet25k and even surpassing some supervised methods without iterative pose refinement.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot CAD alignment with appearance-driven correspondences degrades under occlusion and sim-to-real shifts; need scalable, geometry-grounded representations that generalize across domains.
AI.method: Two main components: (1) large-scale geometry-grounded feature learning with NOCS supervision across 12 real/synthetic datasets (674K images); (2) a geometrically consistent one-to-one CAD-to-image matching algorithm; no pose refinement; sub-second inference.
AI.result: On ScanNet25k, achieves 33.4% category and 42.3% instance accuracy; outperforms strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3 and 12.2 percentage points; for the first time on this benchmark, surpasses fully supervised methods; code released.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that scalable geometry-grounded learning and principled geometric matching enable accurate, fast zero-shot CAD alignment with strong cross-domain generalization and competitive accuracy.

title: What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity
summary: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

AI.tldr: Bounded second-order heterogeneity explains Local SGD efficiency for general convex objectives; the paper proves improved convergence guarantees, tightens lower bounds (nearly tight), and extends the principle to serial SGD with replacement.
AI.motivation: Explain when and why Local SGD benefits from local updates under data heterogeneity, extending Patel et al.’s bounded second-order heterogeneity from strongly convex to general convex objectives to provide a sharper theory.
AI.method: Prove an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under the bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption; derive new, tighter lower bounds for Local SGD; apply the technique to obtain a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement to capture the impact of rare high-curvature clients.
AI.result: An improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD under the assumption; improved lower bounds (nearly tight) for Local SGD; a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement that demonstrates the role of second-order heterogeneity in rare high-curvature client effects.
AI.conclusion: Provides a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD; shows second-order heterogeneity as a key control parameter; extends understanding to the impact of rare high-curvature clients via serial SGD bounds.

title: InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring
summary: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

AI.tldr: InCarEmo is a multimodal in-cabin emotion dataset that fuses RGB/IR video, audio, and dialogue text to support emotion recognition, fatigue, and distraction tasks, with Chinese data and an auxiliary English benchmark for cross-lingual evaluation, plus extensive unimodal/multimodal baselines and noise/low-light analyses.
AI.motivation: Public in-cabin affective datasets are largely visual and lack conversational data, hindering capture of linguistic and interactive cues essential for robust driver emotion understanding and safe HVI (human-vehicle interaction).
AI.method: Collect scripted in-cabin scenarios under diverse lighting and driving contexts; record RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text; provide Chinese data with an auxiliary English benchmark; define three tasks (multimodal emotion recognition, fatigue detection, distraction monitoring); evaluate unimodal and multimodal methods with modality-missing and noise tests; benchmark cross-lingual performance.
AI.result: Demonstrates benefits of multimodal fusion over unimodal baselines; identifies performance gains and remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions; provides extensive baseline results and a unified benchmark for future research.
AI.conclusion: InCarEmo establishes a comprehensive, interpretable, and robust foundation for in-cabin affective understanding, enabling safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction and highlighting remaining challenges to be addressed in real-world deployments.

title: FlashDecoder: Real-Time Latent-to-Pixel Streaming Decoder with Transformers
summary: Real-time video generation demands fast decoding as much as fast denoising, yet current latent video diffusion models rely on 3D convolutional decoders that are slow and memory-intensive at high resolutions or for long video. We introduce FlashDecoder, a fast, memory-efficient pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes latents to pixels frame by frame. At each step, the current frame attends only to a fixed-size window of past frames through a rolling KV cache. The fixed temporal window keeps decoding fast and memory bounded regardless of video length, enabling constant-latency streaming. Because frames are processed sequentially, temporal causality is enforced without explicit attention masks, enabling training at resolutions up to 1080p and matching the reconstruction quality of convolutional decoders. On the Wan2.1 and Wan2.2 latent spaces, FlashDecoder matches each convolutional decoder in reconstruction quality (e.g., 41.55dB vs. 41.49dB PSNR at 1080p) while decoding 3.6x-4.7x faster with up to 11x less memory on a single H100 GPU. With architecture-aware inference optimizations, the speedup widens to 12x.

AI.tldr: FlashDecoder is a fast, memory-efficient pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes frames sequentially with a fixed-size rolling KV cache, enabling real-time, constant-latency video decoding with comparable quality to 3D convolutional decoders at up to 1080p and significant speed/memory gains.
AI.motivation: Real-time video generation demands fast decoding and low memory usage. 3D convolutional decoders are slow and memory-intensive at high resolutions or long videos, hindering streaming and latency requirements. A streaming, causally-consistent decoder is needed.
AI.method: Introduce FlashDecoder, a pure-Transformer video decoder that processes frames sequentially, with each frame attending only to a fixed-size window of past frames via a rolling key-value cache. This fixed temporal window ensures constant-latency decoding and bounded memory regardless of video length. The model enforces temporal causality through sequential processing without explicit attention masks. Training is performed at 1080p, with architecture-aware inference optimizations.
AI.result: On Wan2.1 and Wan2.2 latent spaces, FlashDecoder matches each convolutional decoder in reconstruction quality (e.g., 41.55 dB vs 41.49 dB PSNR at 1080p) while decoding 3.6x–4.7x faster and using up to 11x less memory on a single H100 GPU. With architecture-aware optimizations, the speedup increases to 12x.
AI.conclusion: A streaming, pure-Transformer decoder with a fixed temporal window can deliver real-time, high-resolution video decoding with reconstruction quality comparable to 3D convolutional decoders, enabling constant-latency streaming and substantial efficiency gains.

title: BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong
summary: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

AI.tldr: BadWAM reveals two WAM-specific adversaries—action-only and imagination-preserving—demonstrating that the coupling between imagined futures and executed actions can be hijacked, significantly reducing task success and exposing limits of future-imagination regularization.
AI.motivation: Question the robustness and safety guarantees of World-Action Models by analyzing potential adversarial misalignment between imagined futures and actual actions.
AI.method: Introduce BadWAM framework; define attack surface by attack strength and stealthiness; instantiate two attack types (action-only and imagination-preserving); evaluate across WAM variants in closed-loop settings; report impact on task success and imagination drift.
AI.result: Attacks substantially degrade performance: action-only attack reduces success from 96.5% to 43.1%; imagination-preserving attack shows that future-regularization can suppress drift while enabling strong action disruption, revealing a WAM-specific vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: World-Action Models are vulnerable to drift attacks that align imagination with misexecuted actions; defenses must address WAM-specific attack modes; interpretation and safety guarantees are not automatically robust under adversarial perturbations.

title: GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

AI.tldr: Proposes GAttNHP, a unified framework for Temporal Knowledge Graphs that integrates a self-attention-based continuous-time Hawkes process, a semantic soft-grouping mechanism to share excitation via latent groups, and a non-crossing quantile regression head for calibrated time predictions, achieving state-of-the-art on six datasets, notably for long-tail chains.
AI.motivation: Three core challenges in forecasting on Temporal Knowledge Graphs: (i) capturing long-range temporal dependencies; (ii) modeling cross-chain interactions where events on one chain excite or inhibit others; (iii) heavy-tailed inter-arrival times that render deterministic time predictors unreliable.
AI.method: 1) Self-attention encoder turns each subject–relation chain into a continuous-time point process to capture lingering history. 2) Semantic soft-grouping converts global Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, enabling chains to share excitation patterns via latent group memberships rather than all pairwise computations. 3) Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head predicts calibrated, monotonically ordered time quantiles, robust to heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on six benchmark TKG datasets shows that GAttNHP surpasses state-of-the-art baselines for both entity prediction and time prediction. Ablation studies indicate the largest performance gains occur on long-tail event chains where existing models struggle the most.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses long-range dependencies, inter-chain excitations, and heavy-tailed timing in TKGs by combining a continuous-time Hawkes-based attention model with group-wise excitation sharing and calibrated quantile time prediction, yielding strong overall performance and stability, especially for rare events.

title: AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery
summary: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

AI.tldr: VLMs can infer building typologies from Google Street View images with about 70% accuracy, approaching expert labeling, with Chain-of-Thought prompting improving stability; analysis of AI explanations reveals visual cues dominate, while human experts rely on broader context; results support AI as a scalable, complementary tool for urban analysis.
AI.motivation: Assess the viability of large vision-language models to automate building-typology classification in urban contexts and to understand their reasoning relative to domain experts.
AI.method: Evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) on GSV images; compare against human expert ground-truth; apply scaling strategies and various prompting techniques (notably Chain-of-Thought); analyze AI explanations by keyword probability to uncover reasoning patterns.
AI.result: Average accuracy ~70%; CoT prompts yield more stable performance; AI focuses on visual indicators; experts rely on broader contextual/domain knowledge; VLMs demonstrate potential for scalable approximation of expert capabilities.
AI.conclusion: VLMs can serve as complementary, scalable tools for urban analysis and automation, leveraging visual pattern recognition; potential to integrate into workflows and support reasoning transparency through explanation analysis.

title: TanGO: Training-Free 3D Editing via Tangent-Space Guidance and Optimization
summary: While recent flow-matching 3D generative models (e.g., VecSet) adopt structured representations, their tokens share global context, causing conventional training-free editing to suffer from semantic artifacts such as collapsed preserved regions or incomplete transformations. To address this, we propose TanGO, a training-free framework that enables adaptive per-token steering in the tangent space of generative dynamics. To realize this selective control, we formulate a one-step optimal control rule and determine the strength of each token's control signal using a von Mises-Fisher inspired directional discrepancy derived from the source and target velocity fields. Experiments show that TanGO substantially reduces structural artifacts and achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing 3D editing baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/siw00-lim/TanGO.

AI.tldr: TanGO enables adaptive per-token editing in flow-matching 3D generative models by a one-step optimal control in tangent space, reducing artifacts and achieving state-of-the-art editing without training.
AI.motivation: Training-free editing in flow-matching 3D generators suffers from semantic artifacts due to shared global token context; selective per-token control is needed to separate source and target semantics and avoid collapsed regions or incomplete transformations.
AI.method: Formulate a one-step optimal control rule; determine per-token control strength using a von Mises–Fisher inspired directional discrepancy between source and target velocity fields; apply control in the tangent space of the generative dynamics for adaptive steering.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial reduction of structural artifacts and state-of-the-art performance compared to existing 3D editing baselines; code is publicly released.
AI.conclusion: TanGO provides effective, training-free per-token control for 3D editing with fewer artifacts, enabling more faithful transformations in flow-matching models.

title: ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation
summary: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

AI.tldr: Proposes ChronoQG, a temporally expressive, hop-bounded benchmark for temporal KGQG, with four datasets totaling 16k questions; shows current methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints.
AI.motivation: Static KGQG benchmarks ignore temporal scope, hindering evaluation of temporal validity, event ordering, and time-sensitive constraints in generated questions.
AI.method: ChronoQG framework combines a temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to produce temporally faithful questions; creates four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal KGs (16,011 questions).
AI.result: Evaluation indicates existing LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines fail to consistently preserve temporal constraints, especially with multiple constraints and complex constraint types.
AI.conclusion: ChronoQG establishes temporally faithful QG as a distinct, challenging testbed and highlights the gap between static KGQG and TKGQG.

title: Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report
summary: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

AI.tldr: GIRAI 2026 evaluates how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections using 38 indicators across five dimensions, across 135 countries; data from Nov 2023 to Sep 2025; finding: governance expanding but often non-binding; few require disclosure of government algorithms; 35 countries deployed unacceptable-risk AI; conclusion: shift from framework adoption to enforceable rights-based protections and resourced oversight.
AI.motivation: Assess the degree to which high-level AI ethics commitments translate into concrete, rights-based protections and redress mechanisms in governance structures.
AI.method: Global network of 135 researchers; 68,138 data points; 38 indicators across three pillars (government policy/implementation 17; civil society engagement 5; enabling conditions 15) and documented cases; score 0-100; data timeframe; five dimensions and 38 indicators; ranking by score.
AI.result: 126/135 countries have at least one government policy/initiative across 17 policy indicators; many frameworks are non-binding: Global South contributed 203 of 306 new cases; 78% non-binding vs 42% in Global North; transparency frameworks exist in 58% of countries, but only 18% require public disclosure of government algorithms; 35 countries show credible evidence of deploying unacceptable-risk AI.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI governance should move beyond formal adoption toward enforceable protections, adequately resourced oversight bodies, and accessible redress mechanisms.

title: Benchmarking Face Recognition without Real Faces
summary: Synthetic face datasets have become effective enough to train face recognition models with accuracy rivaling that of models trained on real photographs. This progress sidesteps the ethical and legal burdens of collecting real biometric data, yet evaluation has not kept pace. Even studies that train entirely on synthetic images still rely on real-face benchmarks to measure performance, leaving the privacy problem only half solved. We ask whether synthetic datasets can replace real benchmarks for face recognition evaluation. We test 12 synthetic datasets against 7 established real benchmarks using 24 pre-trained models that span both convolutional and transformer architectures. Our evaluation covers biometric verification metrics, similarity score distributions, cross-model ranking consistency, and the underlying distributional properties of each dataset. Benchmarking fidelity varies widely across the synthetic candidates, but the two strongest, MorphFace and Vec2Face, reproduce the relative behavior of real benchmarks and reach agreement levels that fall within the natural disagreement already observed among the real benchmarks themselves. These results establish that well-constructed synthetic datasets can support reliable comparative evaluation for face recognition, moving the field closer to a fully synthetic and privacy-preserving pipeline for both training and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: Well-constructed synthetic face datasets can replicate real benchmark behavior and support reliable evaluation for face recognition, enabling privacy-preserving benchmarking alongside training.
AI.motivation: Reduce privacy and legal concerns of real biometric data by substituting synthetic data for both training and benchmarking, and assess whether synthetic benchmarks can replace real ones.
AI.method: Evaluate 12 synthetic datasets against 7 real benchmarks using 24 pre-trained models (CNNs and Transformers). Analyze biometric verification metrics, score distributions, cross-model ranking consistency, and dataset distributional properties.
AI.result: Benchmark fidelity varies across synthetic datasets; MorphFace and Vec2Face most closely reproduce real benchmark behavior and agree with real benchmarks within the natural disagreement observed among real benchmarks themselves.
AI.conclusion: Well-constructed synthetic datasets can support reliable comparative evaluation for face recognition, moving toward a fully synthetic and privacy-preserving pipeline for training and benchmarking.

title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning
summary: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

AI.tldr: A decision-theoretic analysis of epistemic uncertainty reframes evaluation around regret (reducible error) and selective prediction. It derives that the Bayes-optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, exposes weaknesses in standard disentanglement metrics, and proposes risk/coverage/ regret surfaces as diagnostic tools. Empirical benchmarking shows decision-theoretic rankings can diverge from proxy-task rankings, including pairwise inversions.
AI.motivation: Current uncertainty evaluations (e.g., out-of-distribution detection, active learning) rely on scores that do not align with Bayes-optimal strategies. The authors argue for a decision-theoretic framework centered on regret (reducible error) to assess epistemic uncertainty and to ensure the selected predictions align with operational utility.
AI.method: Formalize selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret within the epistemic reject-option framework. Prove that the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. Propose evaluating the achievable risk, regret, and coverage surface as diagnostics for joint disentanglement and utility.
AI.result: A theoretical unification showing that the optimal decision rule blends aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty with a threshold. Standard correlation metrics for disentangled components may fail to predict real-world utility. The authors advocate using the risk/regret/coverage surface to diagnose joint disentanglement and utility, and they demonstrate, on datasets with dense annotations, that ranking across decision-theoretic criteria can invert relative performance compared to proxy-task rankings.
AI.conclusion: Decision-theoretic evaluation is essential for meaningful epistemic uncertainty assessment. The framework reveals discord between proxy-task metrics and operational utility, and provides diagnostic tools (risk, regret, coverage surfaces) for evaluating joint disentanglement and practical usefulness of uncertainty decompositions.

title: Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models
summary: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

AI.tldr: Per-layer transcoders (PLTs) analyzed with attribution graphs reveal a dictionary of deception-related features in Qwen3-4B; these features causally influence deceptive outputs, enabling circuit-level deception analysis and monitoring.
AI.motivation: Investigate mechanistic interpretability of deceptive behavior in LMs and assess whether transcoders can reveal internal features and circuits driving deception, for safety and security monitoring.
AI.method: Pre-trained per-layer transcoders (PLTs) applied to Qwen3-4B to construct feature-activation attribution graphs and inter-feature dependency networks; perform feature steering and circuit-level analysis to identify deception-related feature sets.
AI.result: Identified a defined set of deception-related features that exert stronger influence on deceptive outputs; observed predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses when these features are steered; supports that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and can be monitored via transcoders.
AI.conclusion: Transcoders show promise for behavioral monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to deceptive or malicious behaviors in language models; the approach could generalize to other problematic behaviors and aid safety interventions.

title: Still image and spatial-temporal tomato data enabling detection, segmentation, tracking, and video-instance segmentation using strong and weak labels
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Two novel datasets released - link to repository in document
summary: In this manuscript we release two datasets for visual sensing of tomato plants grown in commercial-like settings and acquired using a robot. The first is BUTom21 which consists of still images and manual annotations. The second is BUTom-ST21 which consists of video-based data and semi-automated annotations through AI-based methods, referred to as pseudo-labels. In both cases, we provide pixel-level labels for the ripeness of the fruit. The aim is to provide the research community a challenging set of real-world imagery to explore methods to sense and estimate the state of tomato plants and their fruit, which is an important horticultural crop. Importantly, the spatial-temporal dataset provides individual fruit count and ripeness information enabling researchers to push the boundaries of field-based phenotyping.

AI.tldr: Two datasets for tomato plant phenotyping: BUTom21 (static images with manual pixel-level ripeness labels) and BUTom-ST21 (video with AI-generated pseudo-labels); provide pixel-level ripeness, enable fruit counting and ripeness estimation in real-world, robotics-enabled settings.
AI.motivation: Address real-world field phenotyping challenges in tomato crops by providing annotated datasets collected in commercial-like settings with robotic sensing, to advance sensing, counting, and ripeness estimation methods.
AI.method: Data gathered with a robot in commercial-like settings. BUTom21 comprises still images with manual pixel-level annotations of fruit ripeness. BUTom-ST21 comprises video data with semi-automated annotations (pseudo-labels) generated by AI-based methods for the same task.
AI.result: Dataset release offering pixel-level ripeness labels, and a spatio-temporal dataset enabling individual fruit count and ripeness information, facilitating research on field-based phenotyping.
AI.conclusion: The work provides real-world, challenging datasets for sensing and estimating the state of tomato plants and fruit, supporting development of robust field-based vision methods and phenotyping pipelines.

title: Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting
summary: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.

AI.tldr: APAL is an asymmetric peak-aware loss for time-series forecasting that prioritizes under-prediction penalties and peak regions, paired with a peak-critical evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: In many operational forecasting tasks, under-prediction risk and peak events are more consequential than average errors; symmetric losses (MSE/MAE) fail to capture tail and timing failures, harming decisions during spikes.
AI.method: Introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), model-agnostic, which weights peak regions higher and penalizes under-predictions more heavily. Pair with a peak-critical evaluation protocol evaluating channel-wise tail errors (Top-10%/Top-1%), and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, peak timing error). Evaluate across five backbones on long-horizon multivariate forecasting, using City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly counts subset and a beach visitor count dataset, plus additional benchmarks to test generality.
AI.result: APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across peak-critical datasets and settings, with a controllable trade-off against aggregate error; the gains are demonstrated across multiple backbone models and datasets.
AI.conclusion: APAL offers a practical, model-agnostic solution for peak-focused forecasting, enabling improved handling of peak events with a tunable balance between peak accuracy and overall error.

title: CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, IAPR Intl. Conf. on Document Analysis and Recognition Workshops (ICDARw), 2026
summary: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: A CrimeNER Demo platform offering domain-specific NER for crime documents with pretrained models, user-specific fine-tuning, and an end-to-end extraction pipeline; publicly available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: To support research and law enforcement by providing ready-to-use, domain-adapted NER for crime-related information and enabling customization with user-annotated data.
AI.method: Two-level granularity crime entity types; pretrained models on CrimeNER database; optional fine-tuning on user data; automated pipeline to extract and annotate entities; demo platform with tutorial and video; GitHub repository.
AI.result: A functional demonstrator platform delivering pretrained models and a fine-tuning workflow, plus an automatic extraction pipeline; public availability on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: The platform promotes crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool for researchers and law enforcement.

title: VideoChat3: Fully Open Video MLLM for Efficient and Generalist Video Understanding
summary: Recent advances in video understanding have spanned motion, long video, and streaming interaction, driving this field toward real-world applications. Despite this progress, current open-source models remain limited in several ways. They often struggle to generalize across diverse video types, making them effective only in specific domains. High computational demands further restrict their efficiency and scalability. Moreover, most models are only partially open, with key components such as training code, strategy, or datasets unavailable, which hinders reproducibility and slows community-driven development. To address these issues, we introduce VideoChat3, a fully open, efficient, and generalist video-centric MLLM. VideoChat3 advances video understanding through two complementary designs. For efficiency, we introduce Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception, which enables efficient spatiotemporal representation and reduces the cost of processing video inputs during training and inference. For effectiveness, we develop a scalable video data synthesis pipeline that curates three diverse, high-quality training datasets: VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, and VideoChat3-OL617K, covering general, long-form, and streaming video scenarios, improving the model's generalization across domains. By integrating these designs, VideoChat3 achieves a rare balance of broad generalization and computational efficiency. Experiments across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks demonstrate that VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts with only 4B parameters and higher efficiency.

AI.tldr: VideoChat3 is a fully open, efficient, generalist video-centric MLLM that uses I3D-ViT and adaptive frame resolution for efficiency, coupled with a scalable data synthesis pipeline and three diverse training datasets, achieving strong generalization across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks with 4B parameters and high efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current open-source video-language models struggle with cross-domain generalization, high computational cost, and limited openness (training code, strategies, datasets). A fully open, efficient, and generalist model is needed to advance reproducibility and applicability in real-world video understanding.
AI.method: Introduce Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception to enable efficient spatiotemporal representation; develop a scalable video data synthesis pipeline; curate three datasets—VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, VideoChat3-OL617K—covering general, long-form, and streaming scenarios; train and evaluate VideoChat3 as a 4B-parameter model.
AI.result: VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts using only 4B parameters and higher efficiency across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A rare combination of broad generalization and computational efficiency is achieved in an open, generalist video LLM framework, driven by an efficient I3D-ViT backbone, adaptive frame strategies, and a scalable, domain-diverse data synthesis pipeline.

title: PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance
summary: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

AI.tldr: Presents a positive learning result for decentralized, privacy-preserving PAC learning of reachability in turn-based stochastic games, via a game-theoretic generalization of ECD and a polynomial sample complexity bound.
AI.motivation: Reachability is a fundamental objective but difficult to learn in reinforcement learning. PAC learning is impossible for MDPs without extra assumptions, and this difficulty extends to turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs). Prior PAC results assume public/shared information or centralized learning. The work aims to relax these to private information and decentralized learning.
AI.method: Introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter. Propose a learning framework that allows private (non-shared) information and decentralized learners with potentially different algorithms. Derive a polynomial-sample complexity bound as a function of the number of states, actions, the ECD parameter, and the inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.
AI.result: Establishes a polynomial-sample complexity bound for learning in TBSGs with reachability under private information and decentralized learning. Claims to be the first positive result achieving these conditions in this setting.
AI.conclusion: Provides the first positive result for decentralized and private-information learning in TBSGs with reachability objectives, generalized ECD to a game-theoretic context, and a concrete polynomial-sample complexity guarantee; lays groundwork for practical decentralized learning in competitive stochastic environments.

title: Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

AI.tldr: RAPTOR introduces a self-supervised pretraining for RL-based multi-hop reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs by learning reachability to guide action exploration, improving training efficiency and predictive performance on ICEWS datasets.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning (RL) based multi-hop reasoning on temporal knowledge graphs suffers from sparse rewards and enormous, time-evolving action spaces, leading to inefficient exploration and limited performance.
AI.method: A self-supervised pretraining framework that learns a reachability predictor for candidate actions to the target entity, biasing the RL agent toward promising paths and providing a strong initialization for downstream fine-tuning.
AI.result: Empirical results on ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 show that RAPTOR pretraining improves training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines for RL-based TKG reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Reachability-aware pretraining is an effective inductive bias that enhances RL-based multi-hop reasoning in temporal knowledge graphs and can be integrated with existing RL methods to boost performance.

title: Frequency-Structured Field Learning for Light-Field Disparity Estimation
summary: Light-field disparity estimation requires global consistency in smooth or textureless regions and local precision near occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and abrupt depth transitions. Existing methods address these requirements through EPI matching, cost-volume or focal-stack construction, view aggregation, or direct convolutional regression, often relying on local windows, discrete disparity hypotheses, memory-intensive volumes, or attention-based aggregation. We instead formulate disparity estimation at the field level, predicting disparity from globally and locally updated EPI-derived latent features without explicitly constructing a disparity volume. We introduce FreqLF, an EPI-guided Fourier-local framework that encodes angular parallax cues from horizontal and vertical EPI stacks together with central-view appearance features. These cues are projected into a latent field and updated through stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers. Fourier low-mode updates enable global feature interaction, while local convolutions preserve spatial variations needed for fine disparity detail. A coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder then predicts disparity, using the mixture mean as the final estimate. Experiments on the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark show that FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines while avoiding explicit cost-volume construction in the base model. Ablations confirm the complementary roles of the Fourier and local branches, and scaling experiments demonstrate practical behavior across spatial resolutions. These results suggest that Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation. The code will be published soon.

AI.tldr: FreqLF: an EPI-guided Fourier-local latent-field method for light-field disparity estimation that avoids explicit disparity volumes and achieves near-supervised accuracy.
AI.motivation: Global consistency in smooth regions and local precision near occlusions requires bridging global and local reasoning; traditional volume and multi-view methods have trade-offs and memory costs. A field-level representation can unify global parallax cues with local detail.
AI.method: Encode angular parallax from horizontal/vertical EPI stacks and central-view features into a latent field; update using stacked Fourier-local layers (Fourier low-mode global interactions + local convolutions); decode disparity with a coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture model; use mixture mean as final estimate; no explicit cost volume.
AI.result: On HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark, FreqLF matches strong supervised baselines while avoiding cost-volume; ablations confirm the complementary roles of Fourier vs local branches; scaling shows robustness across resolutions; code forthcoming.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-local latent-field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation, effectively combining global coherence with local detail without constructing disparity volumes.

title: Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs
summary: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control
comment: 48 pages, 10 figures, 29 numbered tables. Preprint v1
summary:
Autonomous coding agents increasingly execute multi-step software work, but lifecycle states such as reviewed, tested, DONE, and ready-to-merge remain claims unless supported by current evidence. We present Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control, a method that permits lifecycle transitions only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies the relevant gate. The method treats agent outputs as claims rather than lifecycle state, and uses proof operationally to mean gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model, not semantic program correctness.
  We evaluate an open-source implementation through mechanism tests, a powered control-policy ablation, and operated self-application evidence. The unattended-loop engine passed 10 of 10 scenarios with zero false-DONE, and local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, the pre-registered A4 versus A2-prime comparison reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31 of 1,800 injected cells under a compute-budgeted naive loop to 2 of 1,800 under the gated loop, a 1.6 percentage-point improvement in not-amplified rate with a 95 percent confidence interval of [0.8, 2.5]. A near-compute A3 versus A4 comparison, 14 of 1,800 versus 2 of 1,800, indicates that the gain is associated with enforcing review as a lifecycle gate rather than merely adding a reviewer. The self-application corpus contains 565 stories and 1,007 review findings, with 94.8 percent resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit. These results support Proof-or-Stop as a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on. The evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

AI.tldr: Proof-or-Stop yields gate-based lifecycle control for autonomous coding agents, requiring fresh, source-bound, verifiable evidence to advance lifecycle states, treating outputs as claims subject to mechanism-level proof. Evaluation shows strong gating performance and reduced amplification in a self-application setting, with limitations in scope.
AI.motivation: Lifecycle states like DONE or ready-to-merge are only claims unless verifiable evidence supports them; need a mechanism to ensure evidence-backed transitions under a trust model to prevent unsafe automation.
AI.method: Treat agent outputs as claims; define proof as gate-admissible evidence tied to current source state; gate transitions on such evidence; evaluate via mechanism tests, ablations, and self-application data.
AI.result: Unattended-loop engine passed 10/10 scenarios without false DONE; local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts; 9,240-cell ablation shows A4 vs A2-prime reduces visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31/1800 to 2/1800; near-compute A3 vs A4 shows gains mainly from enforcing review as a lifecycle gate; self-application corpus: 565 stories, 1,007 reviews, 94.8% resolved; 68-row cross-vendor exhibit.
AI.conclusion: Proof-or-Stop is a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on; evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

title: Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. 20 pages, 7 figures. Project page: https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/
summary: State-of-the-art flow based text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit remarkable generative abilities but remain vulnerable to producing unsafe content. Prior safety efforts range from concept erasure and prompt filtering to classifier-based gating. However, simple techniques like parameter efficient adaptations of the models easily bypass such guardrails. We introduce a unique principled approach that achieves safety by regulating the model's attention dynamics through inference-time introspection, exhibiting intrinsic robustness. Our method analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. This introspective control ensures safety of deployed models. Across standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, our approach achieves remarkable safety scores while maintaining or even improving alignment and perceptual quality. Our results reveal that attention-space regulation offers a considerably more promising path to safer diffusion transformer based image generation than the existing concept erasing mechanism.Our code can be accessed at https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/

AI.tldr: Proposes inference-time attention regulation to improve safety in diffusion T2I models by introspection, yielding robustness to unsafe content while preserving quality and outperforming concept erasure.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of static safety defenses (e.g., prompt filtering, concept erasure, gating) that can be bypassed by small changes; seek a principled, robust mechanism integrated into the model's inference dynamics.
AI.method: Inference-time introspection that analyzes and rebalances attention activations during image synthesis to steer generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment.
AI.result: On standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, achieves strong safety scores while maintaining or improving alignment and perceptual quality; attention-space regulation offers advantages over concept erasure.
AI.conclusion: Attention-space regulation is a promising, robust path to safer diffusion-based image generation with released code for reproducibility.

title: Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set
summary:
This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

AI.tldr: Analyzes optimal linear combination of binary classifiers via truth-table based structuring; derives conditions for existence/uniqueness of the convexified empirical risk minimum; provides closed-form weights for Exponential and Logistic losses; studies three-classifier configurations; introduces φ-frontiers for data quality.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous, convex-analytic framework for ensembling binary classifiers and to obtain non-iterative weight formulas, while characterizing when a minimizer exists as the number of classifiers grows; and to assess data quality through φ-frontier.
AI.method: Partition data into equivalence classes using truth tables; analyze a multidimensional extension of classification-calibrated functions; derive sufficient conditions for a global minimum of the convexified empirical risk; enumerate three-classifier configurations; obtain explicit weight formulas for exponential and logistic losses; introduce φ-frontiers.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of the global minimum; complete classification of three-classifier configurations into unique/minimum/infimum/non-unique; closed-form optimal weights for Exponential and Logistic losses; φ-frontiers as a diagnostic for stability and data quality.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled framework for designing and analyzing optimal linear classifier ensembles with provable guarantees and introduces a practical data-quality diagnostic (φ-frontier).

title: Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach
summary: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

AI.tldr: LLM-based two-mode detection of online firestorms: retrospective thread-level classification and sequential early warnings with three indicators; strong results on Reddit data; demonstrates LLMs as context-aware estimators for social media monitoring.
AI.motivation: To improve detection of online firestorms by capturing contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads, beyond volume signals and static sentiment features, and to enable timely warnings.
AI.method: Two operating modes. Global mode retrospectively classifies complete Reddit threads by aggregating local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. Early-warning mode processes threads sequentially with a sliding window, issuing warnings when calibrated thresholds are exceeded. The LLM estimates three indicators—negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count—on a balanced Reddit dataset.
AI.result: Global mode achieves strong classification performance; early-warning mode attains high recall and detects escalating threads after few comments and distinct contributors.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that LLMs can function as repeated, context-aware estimators for monitoring social media discourse, not just for static judgments.

title: DINE: Distance Is Not Enough -- Learning Global Deformation Priors for Robust Soft-Tissue Point Cloud Registration
summary: Non-rigid point cloud registration is central to soft-tissue shape analysis, but large deformations, noise, and outliers make correspondence estimation challenging. Most learning-based methods rely on local objectives such as Chamfer distance, which encourage point-wise proximity but do not constrain the global plausibility of the predicted deformation field. We address this limitation with DINE, a maximum a posteriori framework that augments distance-based registration with a learned statistical prior over displacement vector fields.
