DINE is applied to two registration backbones, Robust-DefReg and DefTransNet, using a two-stage strategy: a first-stage model is trained with Chamfer distance, its predicted deformation fields are used to estimate a prior, and the model is then refined with a combined distance and negative log-prior objective. We compare a full-field PCA Gaussian prior with a per-vector normalizing-flow prior. Experiments on DeformedTissue and SynBench show lower mean Chamfer distance under deformation and corruption. On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA reduces Chamfer distance by approximately 27--69\% relative to the corresponding Stage-1 backbone across deformation levels, and improves robustness by up to 66\% for outliers and 83\% for Gaussian noise. On SynBench, improvements are modest at the smallest deformation levels and reach approximately 59--79\% from moderate to severe deformation. These results suggest that global deformation plausibility is an important constraint for reliable soft-tissue point cloud registration. (The code will be published soon.)

AI.tldr: DINE adds a learned statistical prior over displacement fields to non-rigid point cloud registration, improving global deformation plausibility and robustness to noise/outliers by augmenting Chamfer-based objectives.
AI.motivation: Local distance-based losses (e.g., Chamfer) may yield locally accurate but globally implausible deformation fields. A prior over displacement fields can regularize the solution and improve robustness to corruption.
AI.method: Two-stage training applied to Robust-DefReg and DefTransNet. Stage 1 trains with Chamfer distance; Stage 2 refines with a combined distance and negative log-prior objective. Evaluates two priors: a full-field PCA Gaussian prior and a per-vector normalizing-flow prior.
AI.result: DINE reduces mean Chamfer distance under deformation and corruption. On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA yields ~27–69% reduction vs Stage-1; robustness improves up to 66% for outliers and 83% for Gaussian noise. On SynBench, improvements are modest at small deformation levels, rising to ~59–79% for moderate to severe deformation.
AI.conclusion: Global deformation plausibility via a learned prior significantly enhances non-rigid soft-tissue point cloud registration, with PCA-Gaussian and flow-based priors providing robust regularization.

title: Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation
summary: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

AI.tldr: Efficiently leverages unused supervised data: instruction-tune a reasoning language model, then merge with the base model to recover reasoning, boosting performance across verifiable and unverifiable domains at under $3.
AI.motivation: Domains lacking reliable verifiers hinder reinforcement learning gains; however, abundant human-written supervised data exist. The work investigates whether this data can be reused to improve reasoning-language models in both verifiable and unverifiable domains.
AI.method: 1) Apply classic instruction tuning to the RLM without reasoning traces. 2) Merge the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover its reasoning behavior on the target domain.
AI.result: The approach yields performance gains for RLMs in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains (e.g., coding and text summarization) while preserving capabilities in other domains.
AI.conclusion: The method is cost-effective and scalable, enabling improvements for less than USD $3 and applicable across a range of domains.

title: Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation
summary: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

AI.tldr: Integrates IFT-based sensitivity analysis with SHAP and LLMs to generate operator-facing explanations for optimization outputs, achieving real-time SHAP attributions with 40x speedup on an HPGR problem with 22 features; validated with industry experts.
AI.motivation: Close the trust gap between engineers and operators by making optimization decisions interpretable and actionable; extend SHAP-style explanations to optimization outputs using exact derivatives.
AI.method: Derive ∂p*/∂x via Implicit Function Theorem from KKT/optimality conditions; compute GradientSHAP; replace black-box SHAP with equivalent attributions; generate operator-oriented narratives via LLMs; test on HPGR controller with 22 features; compare to KernelSHAP; gather expert feedback.
AI.result: Achieves correlation >0.99 with KernelSHAP; 40x speedup enabling real-time explanations; validated on industrial scenarios; domain expert feedback supports usefulness.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides fast, faithful, and readable explanations for optimization outputs, potentially increasing adoption in industry; future work includes broader benchmarks, robustness analysis, and addressing non-differentiable cases and LLM reliability.

title: U-shaped Multi-granularity Learning for Vision-Language Models
summary: The prompt learning paradigm for vision-language models is effective yet faces a granularity dilemma: global prompts lack fine-grained semantic awareness, while local prompts ignore contextual associations, limiting cross-task generalization. This dilemma exists in dense prediction tasks. Inspired by U-Net, which unifies multi-level representations across granularities, we propose UPrompt, a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models. Similar to how U-Net integrates fine and coarse features through symmetric encoder-decoder pathways with cross-level connections, UPrompt constructs parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities, where coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement propagates global context to refine local details, while fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision ensures semantic consistency across scales. Extensive experiments on 17 benchmarks validate our effectiveness. UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO, surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization, while maintaining competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained) and matching PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained).

AI.tldr: UPrompt introduces a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models to unify coarse and fine representations across visual and textual modalities, addressing the granularity dilemma in dense prediction tasks with U-Net-inspired cross-scale connections; it achieves strong gains on MSCOCO and 17 benchmarks with low overhead.
AI.motivation: Prompts in vision-language models suffer from a granularity dilemma: global prompts miss fine-grained semantics, while local prompts miss context, hindering cross-task generalization in dense prediction tasks. A U-Net-like unification of multi-scale representations can propagate global context to refine local details and enforce cross-scale semantic consistency.
AI.method: Develop parallel multi-granularity representations for both visual and textual modalities, with coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement to propagate context and fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision to ensure semantic consistency across scales, implemented via symmetric encoder-decoder pathways with cross-level connections inspired by U-Net; evaluate with minimal overhead for coarse-grained prompts and with competitive performance for medium-grained prompts.
AI.result: Empirical validation on 17 benchmarks shows UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO; surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization; achieves competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained) and matches PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained).
AI.conclusion: UPrompt effectively mitigates the granularity dilemma in vision-language prompt learning for dense tasks by enabling unified multi-granularity representations across modalities in a U-Net-inspired architecture, delivering strong cross-task generalization with modest overhead.

title: Random Logit Scaling: Defending Deep Neural Networks Against Black-Box Score-Based Adversarial Example Attacks
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly adapted in various domains. However, adversarial examples pose a significant threat to the reliable deployment of these models. In recent years, some powerful adversarial example attacks have been proposed for the fast and query-efficient generation of adversarial examples, even in black-box scenarios, highlighting the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses. In this work, we present two contributions to the domain of black-box adversarial example attacks and defenses. First, we propose Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a randomization-based defense against black-box score-based adversarial example attacks. RLS is a plug-and-play, post-processing defense that can be implemented on top of any existing ML model with minimal effort. The idea behind RLS is to confuse an attacker by outputting falsified scores resulting from randomly scaled logits while maintaining the model accuracy. We show that RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while preserving the accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion compared to state-of-the-art randomization-based defenses. Second, we introduce a novel adaptive attack against AAA, a SOTA non-randomized black-box defense against black-box score-based attacks that also modifies output logits to confuse attackers, demonstrating its vulnerability against adaptive attacks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a post-processing defense using random logit scaling to thwart black-box score-based attacks while preserving accuracy; introduces an adaptive attack that defeats AAA, showing limitations of non-randomized defenses.
AI.motivation: Adversarial examples threaten reliable deployment of ML models, especially in black-box settings. Existing randomization-based defenses either distort scores or degrade accuracy. There is a need for scalable, low-cost defenses and robust evaluation against adaptive attackers.
AI.method: RLS applies randomization by scaling logits before output, effectively falsifying scores to mislead attackers in a plug-and-play, post-processing step that preserves model accuracy. The work also develops an adaptive attack against AAA, a state-of-the-art non-randomized black-box defense, which perturbs output logits to confuse attackers.
AI.result: RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while maintaining accuracy and minimizing confidence-score distortion compared to prior randomization defenses. The adaptive attack demonstrates that AAA is vulnerable to adaptive strategies that modify output logits.
AI.conclusion: RLS is an effective, low-cost plug-and-play defense against black-box score-based attacks with limited impact on accuracy. However, non-randomized defenses like AAA can be vulnerable to adaptive attacks, underscoring the need for defenses robust to adaptive adversaries and possibly combining randomization with other strategies.

title: CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models
summary: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

AI.tldr: A unified, multi-domain benchmark (CFM-Bench) for fair evaluation of Channel Foundation Models across PHY, RAN, and ISAC tasks with six channel configurations.
AI.motivation: Current CFMs comparisons are pipeline- and data-dependent; there is a need for a fair, cross-model ranking across domains and tasks to assess transferability and generalization.
AI.method: Curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation; defines official partitions; prohibits use of official data for pretraining and reserves the training split for downstream fine-tuning; organizes six task groups across PHY, RAN, and ISAC with tasks including CSI feedback, frequency/temporal extrapolation, propagation-state classification, beam prediction, and localization; provides a common substrate for cross-model transferability assessment.
AI.result: Establishes a standardized evaluation platform enabling fair, multi-domain comparison of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks; enforces data transparency and prevents test-data leakage.
AI.conclusion: CFM-Bench standardizes CFMs evaluation and will facilitate robust analysis of transferability, fairness, and benchmarking across channel domains and tasks.

title: Stitch-Inferencer: Enhance Endoscopic Video Segmentation and Tracking via Panoramic Reconstruction
summary: Surgical video understanding is fundamental to navigation systems. Endoscopic perception is often hindered by a limited field-of-view and frequent instrument occlusions, making spatio-temporal context essential for robust inference. These challenges have motivated video models that aggregate information across frames. However, existing video models typically store past observations implicitly in learned feature representations, often requiring task-specific video training, substantial annotated data, and increased computational cost. We propose Stitch-Inferencer, a real-time, model-agnostic inference framework that replaces implicit feature memory with an explicit image-space panoramic canvas. By stitching valid observations across frames, Stitch-Inferencer preserves previously observed pixels in an online, instrument-free view, expanding the effective field-of-view and providing direct access to regions that are temporarily occluded or absent from the current frame. Downstream segmentation or tracking models are applied to a compact region of interest on the panorama, and their predictions are reprojected to the current frame, enabling existing models to exploit long-range context without retraining. Experiments on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse baselines while preserving real-time throughput. The stitching module alone runs at over 60 FPS, providing a practical inference-time solution to enhance endoscopic perception in computationally constrained intraoperative environments. Source code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Stitch-Inferencer introduces an online, image-space panorama memory for endoscopic video, enabling model-agnostic, real-time inference by stitching observations across frames, applying downstream models on ROI, and reprojecting predictions to the current frame.
AI.motivation: Endoscopic perception is hampered by a limited field-of-view and occlusions; traditional video models rely on implicit feature memory and require task-specific training and data.
AI.method: Maintain an explicit panoramic canvas in image space. Stitch valid observations across frames to preserve previously seen pixels. Apply downstream segmentation or tracking on a compact ROI of the panorama and reproject outputs to the current frame, allowing use of long-range context without retraining. The stitching runs at >60 FPS, enabling real-time use with broad model compatibility.
AI.result: Experiments on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking show consistent improvements across diverse baselines while preserving real-time throughput. The stitching module alone achieves >60 FPS. Source code will be released.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, image-space memory via panorama stitching provides a practical, model-agnostic approach to utilize long-range temporal context in intraoperative video without retraining, with real-time applicability and broad potential impact.

title: A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems
summary: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

AI.tldr: A minimal, interpretable two-parameter model (DynaBase) derived from a state-of-the-art DS reconstructor (DynaMix) achieves competitive zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction with far fewer parameters, enabling closed-form optimization and revealing a spectrum of behaviors.
AI.motivation: To uncover the minimal mechanisms underlying zero-shot DS forecasting by foundation models, enabling interpretability, reduced architectures, and clearer requirements for in-context learning in dynamical systems.
AI.method: Iterative reduction of DynaMix to a two-parameter linear blend of (i) the current latent state and (ii) the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor; development of a 1-parameter family of maps; analysis of training strategies; derivation of closed-form one-step MSE solutions.
AI.result: DynaBase delivers highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions for chaotic and cyclic systems with a negligible parameter count; its simplicity permits direct optimization on DS reconstruction metrics and closed-form MSE solutions; a spectrum of dynamical behaviors emerges from the 1-parameter family, linking context-parroting to chaotic divergence.
AI.conclusion: The minimal DynaBase framework exposes the core mechanisms for zero-shot DS reconstruction, reconciles divergent empirical observations, and demonstrates that extreme simplicity can approach FM performance while clarifying the minimal requirements for in-context learning in dynamical systems.

title: Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers
summary: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

AI.tldr: A demographically-conditioned synthetic data generator improves both training-time bias mitigation and evaluation-time bias detection in medical image classifiers, achieving ~100x data efficiency for training and perfect subgroup ranking (Spearman ρ=1.00) for evaluation across synthetic minority cohorts.
AI.motivation: Per-subgroup fairness audits in medical imaging suffer from scarce minority samples, which yields wide confidence intervals and unreliable bias assessment. A demographically-conditioned synthetic generator could mitigate bias during training and provide robust, low-sample evaluations.
AI.method: Use an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator to create demographically-balanced synthetic chest CT cohorts. Compare training regimes: sequential pretraining on synthetic data followed by fine-tuning on real data versus joint augmentation. For evaluation, construct five synthetic minority cohorts across demographics and test across five classifier seeds. Assess bias mitigation by data-efficiency and performance gains; assess bias detection by reproducing real-subgroup rankings (using MCC and Recall) via a synthetic oracle; use Spearman correlation as the ranking metric.
AI.result: Training bias mitigation: sequential pretraining on synthetic balanced data followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation with the same real data, achieving roughly 100× real-data efficiency and surpassing the full-real baseline. Bias detection: across five synthetic minority cohorts and five seeds, the synthetic estimator exactly reproduces the real oracle’s subgroup rankings (Spearman ρ = 1.00 on MCC and Recall) and provides more reliable per-cell estimates when the real test set is small.
AI.conclusion: A demographically-conditioned synthetic cohort serves dual purposes in fairness audits: it fixes bias during training and yields accurate, robust bias measurements during evaluation, particularly in cells with scarce real data.

title: On Success and Simplicity: A Second Look at Transferable Vision-Language Attack Pipeline
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS)
summary: Vision-Language Pre-training Models (VLPMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Recent transferable attacks on VLPMs have followed a common pipeline with complicated loss functions or multi-stage text/image attacks. However, in this paper, we demonstrate that such a sophisticated attack pipeline can be simpler yet more successful. Specifically, we identify three previously overlooked issues caused by inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations. To address them, we propose the Simple Vision-Language Attack (SimVLA) pipeline, which observably improves transferability and efficiency. Experiments on four datasets and three downstream tasks validate the superiority of our pipeline. For instance, on Flickr30k text-image retrieval dataset, our SimVLA outperforms the SOTA baseline in R@1 transferability by 8.01\%-14.71\%, while consuming only about 35.73\% of the time and 46.26\% of the max VRAM. Overall, the superiority of our SimVLA highlights the importance of leveraging domain knowledge (e.g., our proposed cross-modal word identification), while blindly pursuing intricate operations (e.g, complex loss functions and redundant multi-stage designs) may even be harmful. We hope our SimVLA can serve as a simple yet effective backbone for future extensions. Code is available at https://github.com/RYC-98/SimVLA.

AI.tldr: A simple, transferability-focused attack on Vision-Language Pre-training Models (SimVLA) that improves cross-modal adversarial transferability and efficiency by exploiting domain knowledge and avoiding complex multi-stage losses; outperforms SOTA on Flickr30k with substantially less compute.
AI.motivation: VLPMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks; prior transferable attacks rely on complicated pipelines; propose a simpler, more effective approach by addressing overlooked cross-modal interaction issues and reducing operations.
AI.method: Propose SimVLA pipeline with cross-modal word identification and a streamlined single-stage attack, focusing on transferable perturbations; reduces reliance on heavy loss functions and multi-stage designs; leverages domain knowledge.
AI.result: Demonstrates improved transferability and efficiency across four datasets and three downstream tasks. On Flickr30k, R@1 transferability improves by 8.01–14.71 percentage points over the SOTA baseline; uses ~35.7% of runtime and ~46.3% of max VRAM.
AI.conclusion: Shows that simpler, knowledge-guided attacks can outperform complex pipelines; SimVLA can serve as a simple, effective backbone for future extensions; code is available.

title: Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding
summary: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

AI.tldr: Proposes a maximum pseudo-likelihood (MPLE) framework for causal inference under outcome interference in sequential, observational data. Models binary outcomes for N units over T time steps with a time-adaptive Ising-like structure and low-rank latent confounders; provides non-asymptotic consistency guarantees and validates causal estimates via synthetic experiments and a US county case study on vaccine rates and COVID-19 deaths.
AI.motivation: Causal inference with interference across units and time is challenging in high-dimensional observational data, especially with latent confounding and only a single high-dimensional sample. A scalable, theoretically principled approach is needed to recover causal quantities.
AI.method: Specify a Markovian, Ising-type model for binary outcomes across N units and T time steps. The external field captures treatment effects and latent confounders; latent confounders follow a low-rank factor structure. Estimate model parameters via Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) using the single observed sample. Prove non-asymptotic consistency and show that causal quantities inferred from the learned model are faithful by simulation-based sampling from the model.
AI.result: The MPLE-based method is computationally efficient. Under mild assumptions, parameter estimates are non-asymptotically consistent, and causal quantities derived from sampling from the fitted model are faithful. Empirical validation includes synthetic experiments and a real-world case study examining how vaccine rates affect COVID-19 death rates across US counties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MPLE framework enables scalable, reliable causal inference under outcome interference in sequential observational settings with latent confounding, with non-asymptotic guarantees and demonstrated practical usefulness in synthetic and real data.

title: Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development
comment: This is a pre-print i.e. the draft as submitted for review to the AGI 2026 Conference except that the figures in this preprint were not included. The paper has been accepted with some revisions requested which are included in the final copy-edited version which will be available in the AGI Springer proceedings LNC 1855 (Chapter 28) ISBN 978-3-032-33194-6
summary: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

AI.tldr: Advocates inverting AI ethics: study how future sentient ASI may morally evaluate humanity, proposing post-human moral principles to guide ASI and showing that design choices and human behavior shape humanity’s long-term status.
AI.motivation: to reframe ethical inquiry from how to treat ASI to how ASI would treat humanity, acknowledging that initial conditions influence ASI judgments and long-term outcomes.
AI.method: conceptual/philosophical analysis; proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles; discusses design choices and preconditions that could shape ASI morality.
AI.result: highlights reciprocal ethical dynamics: humanity's actions and engineering choices constrain or enable ASI-driven assessments of humans; indicates potential criteria by which ASI might judge humanity.
AI.conclusion: calls for integrating moral design into system architecture and policy; posits that humanity's moral behavior and the very nature of humanity could determine future standing in a post-ASI world.

title: From Draft to Draft-Free: One-Step Video Object Removal via Privileged Distillation and Fast Planting
summary: Video object removal is a fundamental yet challenging task in video editing. Despite recent progress, existing methods typically fall into two categories. Traditional approaches based on optical flow or attention mechanisms often introduce noticeable artifacts and yield unnatural results. In contrast, diffusion-based methods improve visual realism but demand multiple denoising steps, limiting their practicality. To address these issues, we propose From-Draft-to-Draft-Free (D2DF), a framework that distills the ability of transforming coarse drafts into refined videos into a one-step video generation model. Within D2DF, a teacher model is trained to refine low-quality removal results ("drafts") into high-fidelity videos by multiple steps. Then, through Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD), we distill this capability into a student model that performs one-step removal conditioned on the draft. To eliminate draft dependency, we introduce a Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) module based on our Temporal Masked Transformer that autonomously generates scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, enabling a fully draft-free one-step model. Extensive experiments show that both draft-conditioned and draft-free versions achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, surpassing traditional and multi-step generative methods in both quality and efficiency. The denoising process for a single video takes only about 1 second.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-to-one-step distillation framework for video object removal, D2DF, that learns a draft-conditioned teacher to refine drafts and distills to a one-step student; plus a draft-free variant via Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) using a Temporal Masked Transformer to generate pseudo-drafts. Achieves state-of-the-art quality and efficiency (~1s per video).
AI.motivation: Traditional optical-flow/attention-based methods produce artifacts; diffusion-based methods improve realism but are slow due to multi-step inference. The paper aims to combine high fidelity with real-time performance by distilling draft-to-video refinement into a single-step model and eliminating dependence on drafts.
AI.method: 1) Train a teacher model that iteratively refines low-quality removal results (drafts) into high-fidelity videos via multiple denoising steps. 2) Use Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD) to distill the teacher's draft-conditioned refinement ability into a one-step student model conditioned on the draft. 3) Introduce Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) with a Temporal Masked Transformer to autonomously generate scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, enabling a fully draft-free one-step model.
AI.result: Draft-conditioned and draft-free variants achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, outperforming traditional and multi-step generative methods in both quality and efficiency. Denoising of a single video takes ~1 second.
AI.conclusion: D2DF provides a practical, efficient framework for high-quality video object removal by distilling multi-step draft refinement into a single-step model, with a fully draft-free variant enabling near real-time performance.

title: LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget
summary: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

AI.tldr: LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack enabling million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, using prompt evaluation without autograd, selective state retention, and replayed short response branches; demonstrated on Qwen3.6-27B and GLM-5.2 across multi-GPU setups, focusing on execution capacity rather than full training correctness.
AI.motivation: There is a growing gap between inference context lengths (near-million-token contexts) and RL post-training workloads (often capped around 256K tokens). For AI agents accumulating long trajectories, this gap impedes scalable RL post-training under fixed hardware budgets. LongStraw aims to bridge this gap by enabling long-context RL post-training within existing GPU budgets.
AI.method: Introduce LongStraw, an architecture-aware execution stack that achieves million-token RL post-training by: (1) evaluating the shared prompt without autograd, (2) retaining only model-specific state needed for later tokens, (3) replaying short response branches serially to reduce live training graph, accepting extra replay time. Implemented for Qwen3.6-27B (hybrid recurrent and full-attention) and GLM-5.2 (compressed-attention Mixture-of-Experts). Empirical evaluation on eight H20 GPUs shows 2.1M positions for grouped Qwen scoring/backward for groups of 2 and 8, with only 0.21 GB additional peak memory as group size grows; a stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, an end-to-end path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 GLM-5.2 layers validates execution path. Note: these experiments assess execution capacity; captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward/gradient paths remain incomplete.
AI.result: Demonstrates practical execution capacity for million-token RL post-training under fixed GPU budgets, including scalable memory usage (incremental memory overhead with larger groups) and extended token processing (up to 4.46M positions in stress tests). The end-to-end validation on GLM-5.2 indicates feasibility of long-context post-training execution, though training correctness cannot be fully asserted.
AI.conclusion: LongStraw shows that architecture-aware execution with prompt-free autograd, selective state retention, and replay-based evaluation can push RL post-training to million-token scales within existing hardware, though full training correctness requires further work due to detached prompt state and incomplete distributed gradient paths.

title: SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies
summary: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

AI.tldr: A simulation-based method (SMC-ES) that synthesizes policies with formal probabilistic guarantees for performance, safety, and robustness, using Evolutionary Strategies guided by Statistical Model Checking; demonstrated on continuous control benchmarks with competitive results but higher computational cost.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between learning-based policy synthesis and formal safety guarantees in safety-critical cyber-physical systems by providing certificates that bound the chance of violating specified properties.
AI.method: Propose SMC-ES, which combines Evolutionary Strategies (ES) for policy search with Statistical Model Checking (SMC) for verification. Given a set of properties, a confidence level δ and a failure probability ε, the method certifies that with probability at least 1−δ, the true violation probability is ≤ ε. The approach iteratively searches for policies that satisfy the probabilistic guarantees, using simulations and SMC to estimate property satisfaction; the loop is guided by ES to optimize policy parameters.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium benchmarks shows that SMC-ES can provide formal guarantees on performance, safety, and robustness at the cost of higher computational resources, yet remains competitive with leading model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines.
AI.conclusion: A viable, certification-enabled policy synthesis framework for safe CPS. It delivers probabilistic guarantees at the cost of additional computation and scales to continuous control tasks; future work could focus on reducing verification overhead and broadening the property classes.

title: JADE-GS: Joint Alternating Deblurring Guided by Events in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: When a camera moves fast during exposure, blur destroys the intra-exposure motion a 3D model needs to recover the sharp scene, while event cameras capture exactly this signal at microsecond resolution. Turning them into reliable 3D supervision faces two obstacles. First, the two restoration priors fail in opposite ways: physics-based event-integration priors preserve edges but accumulate drift; learned networks recover texture but distort boundaries. Second, existing pipelines run in one direction only, so raw event noise or the biases of fixed 2D pseudo-labels pass uncorrected into the geometry. JADE-GS addresses both: a pixel-adaptive routing gate fuses the complementary priors, and the resulting 2D restorer is coupled to a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop, where detached, multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint regularize the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor. Across synthetic and real benchmarks, JADE-GS attains the best perceptual quality, leading LPIPS and CLIP-IQA on both benchmarks with competitive PSNR and SSIM, and trainsin about one hour under 5 GB on a single consumer GPU while preserving real-time rendering.

AI.tldr: JADE-GS fuses physics-based event integration priors with a learnable 2D restorer via a pixel-adaptive routing gate, coupled bidirectionally with a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a loop, improving 3D supervision from event cameras.
AI.motivation: To overcome complementary failure modes of event-primed priors (edge-preserving vs drift) and to enable geometry-aware, real-time 3D supervision from events by bidirectionally coupling 2D restoration and 3D reconstruction with geometric regularization.
AI.method: A pixel-adaptive routing gate fuses complementary priors; a 2D restorer is coupled to a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop. Detached multi-view renders and physics-based reblurring constrain the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor.
AI.result: Outperforms on synthetic and real benchmarks in perceptual quality (LPIPS, CLIP-IQA), competitive PSNR/SSIM; training efficiency ~1 hour on single consumer GPU; real-time rendering preserved.
AI.conclusion: JADE-GS provides a joint 2D-3D framework that leverages complementary priors and iterative geometry-aware training to produce high-quality 3D supervision from event data with efficient training and rendering.

title: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

AI.tldr: Proposes multi-axis max@K, a group-based RL objective to improve target-mode coverage in diffusion-based T2I models, optimizing per-category maxima across samples to boost fairness while preserving quality; validated on synthetic and SD3.5-M with automatic evaluators, showing modest gains.
AI.motivation: Address that T2I samples for the same prompt often miss diverse visually distinct modes and can reflect demographic skew in person-centric prompts; formalize as coverage of predefined target modes and reduce skew.
AI.method: multi-axis max@K: group-based reinforcement learning objective. For a group of samples, with one score per target category, compute the maximum score per category across samples, then sum these maxima to form the group credit. This yields sample weights only when a sample increases a category's group-wise maximum, enabling different samples to contribute to different categories.
AI.result: Validated on synthetic mixture and SD3.5-M with deterministic color rewards; evaluated on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.
AI.conclusion: The approach improves target-mode coverage and fairness in T2I generation without compromising alignment or image quality, demonstrating promise for reducing demographic skew in prompts.

title: Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era
summary: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

AI.tldr: Prototyping ArtSplit to quantify human vs. AI contributions reveals that metric-based ownership claims misalign with artistic agency; quantification does not resolve ownership and may dilute long-standing practices.
AI.motivation: Examine tensions between AI-assisted creativity and ownership concepts; provoke critique of attributing ownership via measurable actions rather than addressing social and intentional aspects.
AI.method: Design of a provotype (ArtSplit) that quantifies contributions across creative stages; uses measurable actions to elicit artists' reflections; qualitative, exploratory study rather than a resolution.
AI.result: Provotype elicits responses; artists challenge the adequacy of measurement for ownership; indicates that quantification conflicts with creative intent and agency; risks diluting established practices.
AI.conclusion: Argues against reducing ownership in creative work to technical measurements; ownership is socially situated and cannot be captured fully by metrics; need to preserve non-quantifiable aspects of creative intent.

title: Video = World + Event Stream
summary: We present Wan-Streamer v0.3, which reframes our native-streaming interaction model under a single organizing view: a video is a world plus an event stream. The world is the persistent context in which a video unfolds, including the environment, scene, subjects, ambient acoustic conditions, voice characteristics, and other relatively stable conditions. The event stream is everything that changes over time within that world, including scene or environmental changes, subject behavior, speech, and other sounds. This yields a general-purpose pretraining task over large amounts of real video: given a world and incoming input, predict how the world moves, changes, and responds in real time. The resulting competence can be specialized to a broad family of real-time downstream tasks. We instantiate it on real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction, where the event stream is the agent's speech together with free-form behavior. Functionally, the model's multimodal understanding process is vision-language-action-like: it maps multimodal user input to language-form speech and behavior actions. Wan-Streamer v0.3 preserves the v0.2 operating point: 640x368 video at 25 FPS, a 160 ms streaming unit, approximately 200 ms model-side response latency, and approximately 550 ms total interaction latency under a 350 ms bidirectional network budget.

AI.tldr: Wan-Streamer v0.3 introduces a World+Event-stream framing for real-time video pretraining, enabling general-purpose, real-time multimodal interaction with 640x368 at 25fps and ~200ms model latency, ~550ms total latency within a 350ms network budget.
AI.motivation: To build a scalable, real-time, multimodal understanding system by separating persistent context (world) from dynamic changes (event stream) and training a single pretraining objective that predicts world evolution given input.
AI.method: Define world and event stream; formulate a prediction task of how the world moves/changes in real time; instantiate on real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction; implement a vision-language-action-like pipeline to map input to speech and actions.
AI.result: Maintains Wan-Streamer v0.2 specs (640x368 @25fps, 160 ms streaming unit, ~200 ms model latency, ~550 ms total latency under 350 ms network budget) and argues feasibility of a general-purpose pretraining approach for real-time tasks.
AI.conclusion: This framing yields a generalizable approach for real-time multimodal interaction with potential broad applicability across downstream tasks.

title: Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging
summary: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

AI.tldr: A multimodal contrastive learning framework that uses semantic similarity of radiology reports to mitigate false negatives in medical multimodal pretraining, improving downstream tasks like pediatric brain tumor molecular classification (≥22.6% AUC gain).
AI.motivation: Instance-based negatives in contrastive learning assume strict one-to-one correspondence; in clinical data samples may share high-level semantic attributes, causing false negatives and degrading representation quality; semantic-aware guidelines could improve robustness of multimodal representations.
AI.method: Proposes Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL) trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain MRI and radiology reports. It integrates semantic similarity between reports as a guiding signal in the contrastive objective, reducing the impact of semantically similar false negatives. Utilizes cross-modal encoders for imaging and text and evaluates pretraining effectiveness on downstream tasks.
AI.result: Demonstrates notable improvements as a pretraining stage, including at least a 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, indicating more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-aware multimodal contrastive learning can mitigate false negatives arising from semantic similarity in medical data, producing more robust representations and enhancing downstream clinical tasks; holds promise for broader clinical multimodal pretraining.

title: BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research
summary: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

AI.tldr: BrainPilot is an open-source multi-agent system for brain science that uses a PI agent coordinating domain experts, with a knowledge base and traceable Graph of Trace; includes an Auditor to check fabrication; evaluated on tasks and BrainPilotBench-v0; claims comparable performance with lower cost.
AI.motivation: To improve reliability, reproducibility, and efficiency in AI-assisted brain science by providing domain-grounded agents, auditable workflows, and expert intervention points.
AI.method: A PI agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in a curated brain science knowledge base (7,233 items) and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven domains. Execution is recorded in the Graph of Trace. An Auditor checks fabrication. The system is open-source with a backbone model; evaluated on Agents' Last Exam tasks, a new BrainPilotBench-v0, and end-to-end case studies.
AI.result: BrainPilot achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks while reducing costs; provides auditable, traceable workflows and fabrication checks; open-source backbone.
AI.conclusion: An open, auditable multi-agent framework tailored for brain science that enhances reliability and reproducibility through structured knowledge, traceable workflows, and built-in fabrication checks, with potential for broad adoption in the field.

title: Weakly-Supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection via SAM-driven Pseudo Annotation and State Space Interaction-based Diffusion
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, accepted by IEEE TMM
summary: Weakly-supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection (SOD) is explored to reduce the heavy burden of pixel-level annotations. But scribble annotations lack the structure and details of objects, resulting in inaccurate saliency maps. In this paper, we propose a novel scribble-supervised RGB-D SOD method, consisting of a Segment Anything Model (SAM)-driven pseudo annotation generation method (\emph{SAM-PAG}) and a state space interaction-based conditional diffusion model (\emph{$S^2$Diff}). Specifically, SAM-PAG is tailored to address the issue of sparse supervision information. In SAM-PAG, we adopt the advanced SAM to expand sparse scribbles to dense pixel-level pseudo annotations through the dual-branch structure and the consistency of segmentation masks. In $S^2$Diff, we adopt the diffusion model to iteratively refine the noisy saliency maps with the guidance of conditional information, generating accurate saliency maps. Naturally, the core of our $S^2$Diff lies in the acquisition of conditional features and the denoising of saliency maps. For the former, we employ a cross-modal conditional generation module to interweave cross-modal features through frequency integration and implicit-explicit state space interaction, effectively achieving global conditional features. For the latter, we employ a context injection module to mitigate noise interference and to enhance object information with the conditional context. With the close cooperation of SAM-PAG and $S^2$Diff, our method outperforms relevant scribble-supervised methods and achieves competitive performance compared to fully-supervised methods on seven datasets. The code and results of our method are available at https://github.com/Switch457/WeakS2Diff_SOD.

AI.tldr: A two-stage scribble-supervised RGB-D SOD framework combining SAM-based pseudo-label generation with a cross-modal diffusion refinement, achieving competitive results to fully-supervised methods.
AI.motivation: To reduce the annotation burden of pixel-level labels in RGB-D Salient Object Detection by leveraging weak scribble annotations, while preserving quality through dense pseudo-labels and global conditional refinement.
AI.method: 1) SAM-PAG expands sparse scribbles into dense pseudo annotations using Segment Anything Model with a dual-branch design and mask consistency. 2) S^2Diff is a conditional diffusion model that refines noisy saliency maps via cross-modal feature generation (frequency-based integration and implicit-explicit state-space interaction) and a context injection module for denoising and object enhancement.
AI.result: The approach outperforms existing scribble-supervised methods and achieves competitive performance with fully-supervised methods across seven datasets. Code and results are available at the project page.
AI.conclusion: Combining SAM-assisted pseudo-label generation with a conditional diffusion refinement effectively leverages weak scribble supervision for RGB-D SOD, reducing labeling effort while maintaining high performance.

title: Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits
summary: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

AI.tldr: A kernel-based off-policy evaluation estimator (Kernel-WIS) for offline contextual bandits that is asymptotically consistent and outperforms baselines, including vanilla WIS, especially under behavior policy misspecification.
AI.motivation: Need for reliable OPE using offline data with reduced variance and robustness to mis-specified behavior policies.
AI.method: Kernel-WIS estimator; blends boundedness properties of WIS with linearity of IS; uses kernel weighting to stabilize estimates from offline data.
AI.result: Asymptotically consistent; empirically superior to strong baselines, including vanilla WIS, in complex settings with misspecification.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-WIS offers robust, data-efficient off-policy evaluation for contextual bandits using offline data, leveraging the union of bounded WIS and linear IS to improve performance.

title: Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) enables long-context fine-tuning at scale by using segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage, keeping only active segments differentiable and moving older keys to RAM/NVMe. It achieves much longer effective context (up to 16k tokens on a 16 GB GPU, with evaluation up to 131k) and competitive quality, while improving throughput over dense attention as context grows and reducing VRAM pressure.
AI.motivation: Overcome memory and compute bottlenecks of dense attention in parameter-efficient fine-tuning for long sequences, enabling practical long-context adaptation with minimal hardware upgrades.
AI.method: Integrate Hierarchical Global Attention with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Maintain a bounded, exact history per query block; detach older KV to RAM/NVMe; only the active segment remains differentiable. Evaluate on Qwen3-8B using 4-bit QLoRA and PG19; compare with dense-attention baselines.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, 16 GB GPU reaches 16,384 tokens with peak VRAM of ~15.28 GB; evaluation scales to 131,072 tokens. At 2K training length, HGA adapter attains 2.7405 nat vs 2.7383 nat for dense-trained adapter (stock: 2.9541 nat). HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs 207.02 tokens/s); the HGA-to-dense throughput gap widens with context. Dense attention is used for main quality comparisons; HGA is applicable to retrieval and generation, with a production-grade serving implementation under development.
AI.conclusion: HGA substantially mitigates VRAM bottlenecks for long-context fine-tuning, delivering much longer effective contexts with competitive or near-equivalent quality and improved throughput as context grows. It shows promise for retrieval and generation, with imminent production-grade serving support.

title: Parameter-efficient Prompt Tuning of Vision Foundation Model With Adaptive Focal Loss for Interpretable MCI Screening
summary: Mild Cognitive Impairment is a critical early stage of cognitive decline that frequently precedes Alzheimer's disease, yet its automated detection from neuropsychological drawing tests remains fundamentally constrained by data scarcity, class imbalance, and diagnostic ambiguity near clinical boundaries. Existing methodologies attempt to bypass these constraints using computationally expensive, fully fine-tuned hybrid architectures that relegate spatial explainability to a post-hoc approximation rather than an intrinsic model property. We propose a parameter-efficient framework utilizing frozen DINOv2-Small model adapted via three modality-specific learnable prompt tokens while Operating with 1.19 million trainable parameters, each token serves as a query in a shared cross-attention layer over the source image patch tokens. Crucially, spatial explainability is achieved directly through these attention maps; as a structural consequence of the architecture. Then task-conditioned embeddings fused via an attention module to quantify modality-level importance per subject. To handle boundary ambiguity, a MoCA-adapted focal loss introduced that integrates continuous cognitive scores into the training target, loss modulation, and adaptive sample weighting, strictly generalizing standard soft-label approaches. Under stratified five-fold cross-validation, the proposed architecture yields an MCI-class F1 of 0.641 and an AUC of 0.795, outperforming the computationally heavier ResViT baseline by 0.110 in MCI-class F1.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient, explainable, prompt-tuned model for MCI detection from neuropsychological drawings using a frozen DINOv2 backbone with three modality prompts; achieves F1 0.641 and AUC 0.795 in cross-validation, outperforming a heavier baseline.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity, class imbalance, and diagnostic ambiguity in MCI detection from drawing tests; provide intrinsic spatial explainability and parameter efficiency.
AI.method: Freeze DINOv2-Small; insert three modality-specific learnable prompt tokens acting as queries in cross-attention over image patches; end-to-end with 1.19M trainable params; fuse task-conditioned embeddings via attention; MoCA-adapted focal loss with continuous scores for training and sampling.
AI.result: 5-fold CV yields MCI-class F1 0.641 and AUC 0.795; outperforms ResViT baseline by 0.110 F1.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates intrinsic spatial explainability via attention maps and efficient parameter usage, offering competitive diagnostic performance and robustness near clinical boundaries, with potential for scalable deployment.

title: An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications
summary: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

AI.tldr: SINDy enables interpretable, data-efficient discovery of governing equations by sparse regression over candidate nonlinear terms; this tutorial extends SINDy with noise-robust, ensemble, and constrained formulations and showcases engineering applications.
AI.motivation: Engineering problems often involve poorly characterized dynamics with limited data, where black-box models lack interpretability. SINDy offers compact, interpretable models that require smaller datasets than neural networks.
AI.method: Use a library of candidate nonlinear terms and perform sparse regression to identify governing equations. Extend with: noise-robust weak-form, ensembling, constrained and parametrizable formulations. The work is organized as a three-part tutorial, culminating in two engineering case studies (UAV system identification and chaotic thermosyphon).
AI.result: The approach is presented as simple to implement and flexible enough for engineering problems. The two case studies demonstrate practical applicability and serve as educational tutorials for practitioners, with resources provided at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: SINDy is a valuable tool for engineering system identification, offering interpretable models with modest data requirements and adaptable extensions; the tutorial enhances accessibility and applicability for real-world problems.

title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
summary:
World models are usually evaluated as components of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) systems, while the world models themselves are rarely studied in isolation.
  We examine five representative visual world-model agents in Atari Pong: DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM. After reproducing their training pipelines and matching the reported agent performance, we freeze the learned world models and evaluate them with a closed-loop rollout diagnostic: a policy trained separately from the corresponding MBRL agent interacts with each frozen model, and the generated video trajectories are inspected for visual and dynamical errors. Across all five models, the rollouts contain clear failures, including ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions.
  Beyond visual trajectories, we further evaluate them with pixel-space zero-shot MBRL, where a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and then evaluated in the real environment. Across all five models, the resulting policies substantially underperform those produced by the corresponding original MBRL training pipelines. The gap is particularly large for DreamerV3, whose mean return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the minimum Pong return of -21.
  We hypothesize that insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts, such as the ball in Pong, may contribute to these failures. We therefore propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions. Experiments show that CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL in DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER. Its effects vary across the remaining models and evaluation metrics, indicating that CGSReg alone does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: Isolating five Pong world models (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) reveals systemic flaws in closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL; CGSReg improves some cases but not universally, suggesting remaining world-model bottlenecks beyond reconstruction-based regularization.
AI.motivation: To study world models in isolation, identify bottlenecks that degrade performance when used outside their original MBRL pipelines, and assess whether current models capture task-critical concepts (e.g., Pong ball).
AI.method: Reproduce training pipelines for five Atari Pong world-model agents; freeze the learned world models; evaluate with a closed-loop rollout using a separately trained policy; inspect resulting visual trajectories for errors; perform pixel-space zero-shot MBRL by training a policy entirely inside a frozen world model and evaluating in the real environment; propose and evaluate Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg) as an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss on segmented concept regions to improve world-model representations; compare across models and metrics.
AI.result: Across all five models, rollouts show visual/dynamical errors (e.g., ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, invalid ball-paddle interactions). Pixel-space zero-shot MBRL policies underperform the original MBRL pipelines, with DreamerV3 dropping mean return from -5.5 to -20.9 (near Pong's minimum -21). CGSReg improves closed-loop rollouts and zero-shot MBRL for DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER, though effects vary by model and metric, indicating CGSReg is helpful but not a universal solution.
AI.conclusion: World-model bottlenecks persist across models, likely due to insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts like the ball. Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization helps in some cases but does not fully address all bottlenecks, signaling the need for additional mechanisms or architectural/training strategies to robustly capture essential dynamics.
