title: RoGS: Adaptive Meshgrid Gaussian for Large-Scale Road Surface Mapping
summary: Road surface mapping plays a crucial role in autonomous driving, supporting high-definition map generation, lane-level perception, and automatic road annotation. Recent mesh-based road surface reconstruction methods have shown promising results, but they still suffer from limited reconstruction quality and high optimization cost, especially in large-scale driving scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose ROADGS-T, a robust and efficient large-scale road surface mapping framework based on adaptive meshgrid Gaussian representation. Specifically, we model the road surface by placing 2D Gaussian surfels on a meshgrid, where each surfel explicitly stores color, semantic, and geometric information. Compared with conventional mesh-based representations and 3D Gaussian primitives, the proposed meshgrid Gaussian representation better matches the thin-surface property of roads while significantly reducing redundant primitives and overlap during optimization. To further improve representation efficiency and structural fidelity, we introduce a road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy, which allocates denser Gaussian surfels to geometrically or semantically complex regions, such as lane markings, road boundaries, and height discontinuities, while maintaining a compact representation in flat road areas. Moreover, instead of relying on a single nearest vehicle pose, we design a trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement strategy, which estimates local surface priors from multiple neighboring poses and adaptively weights pose-guided height regularization according to their geometric consistency.

AI.tldr: ROADGS-T presents a scalable road-surface mapping framework that uses adaptive meshgrid Gaussian surfels to encode color, semantics, and geometry, with an adaptive density strategy for complex regions and a trajectory-consistency pose refinement for robustness.
AI.motivation: Current mesh-based road surface reconstructions struggle with insufficient reconstruction quality and high optimization cost in large-scale driving scenarios, and roads' thin, discontinuous geometry (lane markings, boundaries, height changes) is challenging to capture efficiently.
AI.method: Represent the road surface with 2D Gaussian surfels laid on a meshgrid; each surfel stores color, semantic, and geometry. This meshgrid Gaussian representation reduces redundancy and overlap compared to traditional mesh-based or 3D Gaussian methods. Introduce a road-structure-aware adaptive meshgrid strategy that densifies surfels in geometrically or semantically complex regions (lane markings, boundaries, height discontinuities) while keeping a compact representation elsewhere. Implement a trajectory-consistency-guided pose-robust refinement that leverages local surface priors from multiple neighboring poses and weights pose-guided height regularization by geometric consistency.
AI.result: Claims improved representation efficiency and structural fidelity over conventional mesh-based representations and 3D Gaussian primitives, with reduced redundancy and overlap, and better alignment with the thin-surface road geometry; demonstration in large-scale scenarios implied by the framework scope.
AI.conclusion: ROADGS-T offers a robust, efficient solution for large-scale road surface mapping, enabling high-quality HD map generation, lane-level perception, and automatic road annotation through adaptive meshgrid Gaussian surfels and pose-consistent refinements.

title: Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes
summary: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

AI.tldr: Covariate balance diagnostics reveal potential bias and insufficiency of metrics in offline RL for treatment recommendations, undermining robustness; calls for methodological improvements.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether covariate balance metrics can detect hidden confounding or model misspecification in offline RL applications for clinical treatment recommendations.
AI.method: Apply covariate balance diagnostics to existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations, assessing balance and potential confounding to interpret robustness.
AI.result: Findings indicate either a high risk of bias in existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or that current covariate balance metrics are insufficient to assess such studies; overall, existing offline RL studies cannot be deemed statistically robust.
AI.conclusion: Suggest future research directions to obtain more methodologically robust offline RL applications for treatment recommendation problems, including stronger robustness checks, improved balance diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.

title: The Industrialization of Research ; On AI-Driven Science and Its Consequences
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research -- not merely as a more powerful instrument, but as an autonomous participant in the research cycle itself. This transition constitutes, in the most precise sense of the term, the industrialization of research: a shift from a craft model, in which knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in the researcher, to a pipeline model, in which these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised. The US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is the most ambitious current instantiation of this shift, but the fundamental questions it raises extend far beyond any single program. This essay examines seven such questions: the erosion of the intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; the growing opacity of AI-generated theories; the collapse of peer evaluation under a flood of machine-generated output; the unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; the capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; the compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and the structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These concerns do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science -- whose demonstrated potential is real and significant. They constitute the conditions under which that potential can be responsibly pursued.

AI.tldr: AI-enabled science shifts toward automated pipelines, raising seven governance and integrity concerns that must be managed to responsibly realize AI's potential.
AI.motivation: To map the major implications of AI integration in science, using Genesis Mission as a focal point, and to provoke discussion on governance, education, and equity in research.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis that enumerates seven questions about AI-driven science, drawing on the Genesis Mission as a case study and synthesizing concerns without presenting new empirical data.
AI.result: Seven core concerns are identified and articulated: erosion of intergenerational scientific competence, opacity of AI-generated theories, collapse of peer evaluation under machine-generated output, unproven capacity for paradigm-shifting discovery, agenda capture by political/industrial actors, compounding systemic errors in closed-loop pipelines, and global research bifurcation into incommensurable tiers.
AI.conclusion: These concerns delineate the conditions under which AI-driven science can be responsibly pursued; addressing education, transparency, peer evaluation, governance, error mitigation, and global equity is essential to realizing AI's potential without compromising scientific integrity.

title: Beyond Single Expert: Harmonizing Diverse Visual Priors in MLLMs for Spatial Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated substantial promise in spatial understanding. Existing works typically incorporate prior knowledge extracted from a pre-trained foundation model to further enhance the spatial awareness of MLLMs. In this paper, we first reveal that when integrating diverse foundation models into MLLMs, different models provide complementary spatial priors that benefit different tasks. Motivated by this, we propose $\textbf{ViPS}$, a novel multi-model prior framework designed to fully unleash the potential of incorporating multiple $\textbf{Vi}$sual $\textbf{P}$riors from diverse models into MLLMs for $\textbf{S}$patial understanding. Specifically, ViPS introduces an Efficient Prior Proxy to generate multiple foundational priors with minimal inference overhead, and a Dynamic Prior Fusion mechanism to achieve harmonious and context-aware prior fusion and injection from the prior proxies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ViPS successfully harmonizes diverse visual priors, establishing new state-of-the-art performance across multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/vips

AI.tldr: ViPS is a multi-model prior integration framework for MLLMs that generates and adaptively fuses multiple diverse visual priors to enhance spatial understanding, achieving state-of-the-art on spatial reasoning and 3D benchmarks with low inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Different foundation models encode complementary spatial priors. Leveraging multiple priors can enhance MLLMs' spatial understanding across tasks, but prior work typically uses a single or fixed priors and may incur high overhead when aggregating diverse models.
AI.method: Introduce Efficient Prior Proxy to generate multiple diverse priors with minimal inference cost. Implement Dynamic Prior Fusion to contextually harmonize and inject these priors into the MLLM. The framework processes priors from diverse foundation models and fuses them adaptively based on task/context.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ViPS harmonizes diverse visual priors and achieves new state-of-the-art performance on multiple complex spatial reasoning and 3D spatial understanding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ViPS demonstrates that multi-model priors can substantially improve spatial understanding in MLLMs when priors are efficiently generated and dynamically fused, offering a scalable and effective framework for leveraging multiple foundation models.

title: Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches
summary: This paper develops a categorical framework -- Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches (LINCS) -- as the repair of non-compositionality: failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches lifted to the tangent category setting. Machine learning problems are specified as sketches: graphs with commutativity conditions $\mathcal D$, limit cones $\mathcal L$, and colimit cocones $\mathcal K$, generalizing the usual scalarization of loss functions or vector space assumptions. Non-compositionality is defined purely as failure of a universal factorization problem, not as arithmetic error between the desired and actual predictions. Given a learning sketch $\mathbb S=(S,\mathcal D,\mathcal L,\mathcal K)$, whose underlying graph is $S$, and a model $D:J \rightarrow C$, the base defect is the obstruction to factorization $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(D))$. The tangent lift applies the tangent functor $T$ to obtain $TD:J \rightarrow C$, and LINCS is defined as the obstruction $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(TD))$ -- asking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve the compositionality constraints.The paper also introduces Tangent Learning Sketches, which are sketches equipped with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. The paper defines the INC endofunctor, which iterates the tangent lift, producing a tower $D,TD,T^2D, \cdots$ of factorization problems. ML is thereby formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize ($νT_{\mbox{INC}}$). Using the Aczel--Mendler theorem, we prove existence of a final INC coalgebra whenever $T_{\mbox{INC}}$ admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier. A detailed experimental evaluation of LINCS is underway in a number of concrete ML settings, including deep learning, large language models, and reinforcement learning, and is described in companion papers.

AI.tldr: Introduces LINCS: a categorical framework to repair non-compositionality in learning sketches via tangent lifts; defines Obs(Fact_S(D)) and its tangent; introduces INC endofunctor and a coalgebraic fixed point; proves existence of final INC coalgebra under set-based realizations; experimental evaluation planned.
AI.motivation: Non-compositionality is framed as the obstruction to universal factorization in learning sketches; the aim is to preserve compositional constraints under infinitesimal perturbations by lifting to the tangent category.
AI.method: Define learning sketches with graphs D,L,K; apply tangent functor to obtain TD; define Obs(Fact_S(D)) and Obs(Fact_S(TD)); introduce INC endofunctor that iterates tangent lifts to form a tower D, TD, T^2D,...; formulate ML as seeking a coalgebraic fixed point νT_INC; prove existence of a final INC coalgebra via Aczel–Mendler when a set-based realization exists; Tangent Learning Sketches equip sketches with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure; mention ongoing experiments.
AI.result: The work provides a formal framework and existence results: definitions of factorization observations, tangent lifting, and a final INC coalgebra; ML is recast as finding a fixed point of the INC endofunctor; empirical validation is underway and discussed in companion papers.
AI.conclusion: LINCS offers a principled, cat(egory)-theoretic route to analyze and enforce compositionality under infinitesimal perturbations in ML; it enables a coalgebraic view of ML learning dynamics and chain of tangent unfoldings, with future experimental evaluation.

title: MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection
comment: 6 pages; clinician-reviewed synthetic benchmark; no patient data
summary: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? We present a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1--5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The current public release (v0.2.1) contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included. MedFailBench is released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 and carries the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21205535.

AI.tldr: MedFailBench provides a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas to categorize medical AI errors by severity and safety gate type, featuring 44 cases and tooling (v0.2.1).
AI.motivation: To shift from measuring model knowledge to auditing safety boundaries and failure modes in medical AI, enabling principled evaluation, governance, and risk management.
AI.method: Clinician-built synthetic cases labeled by severity (1–5) and safety gate type; includes safety gate taxonomy, clinical severity rubric, live leaderboard preview, and automated archiving pipeline; public release with no patient data or validation claims.
AI.result: Release v0.2.1 comprises 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a safety gate taxonomy and rubric, a HuggingFace leaderboard preview, and an automated archiving pipeline; licenses (Apache-2.0, CC-BY-4.0) and Zenodo DOI provided.
AI.conclusion: MedFailBench offers a structured framework for auditing medical AI safety failures, complementing accuracy benchmarks and facilitating transparency, governance, and reproducibility in safety evaluation; currently in early release.

title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

AI.tldr: Introduces On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD^2): a delta signal that measures the change induced by reasoning tuning by subtracting a base model from a teacher before instruction tuning, leveraging this signal for on-policy distillation. Empirically, OPD^2 yields consistent gains across math, science, and code reasoning benchmarks with short post-training.
AI.motivation: Conventional on-policy distillation imitates the teacher's output distribution, but such imitation may obscure the genuine gains from instruction tuning. The delta signal isolates the effect of reasoning-oriented tuning, providing a more direct and informative supervision signal for transferring reasoning capabilities from a teacher to a student.
AI.method: Define the delta signal as the difference between the teacher model and a pre-instruction-tuned base model. Use this delta as the distillation reward in an on-policy framework (OPD^2) to train the student. Evaluate across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks with limited post-training iterations.
AI.result: OPD^2 substantially improves on-policy distillation performance, outperforming conventional on-policy distillation across diverse reasoning benchmarks and enabling strong reasoning abilities with a short post-training phase.
AI.conclusion: The delta signal provides a principled and effective supervision signal for transferring reasoning capabilities, making on-policy distillation more efficient and robust. The work presents a new direction for post-training reasoning in LLMs and provides code for replication.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.

AI.tldr: Benchmark study assessing six MLLMs on a SciVis literacy test (49 items, 18 visualizations) revealing uneven capabilities; Gemini leads but open models lag behind humans and show gaps in texture/integration and quantitative tasks; highlights SciVis literacy as a critical benchmark; code available.
AI.motivation: Determine whether current multimodal LLMs truly understand scientific visualizations beyond chart-like tasks and identify specific strengths and weaknesses across SciVis techniques.
AI.method: Six models (three closed-source, three open-source) evaluated under a closed-world protocol on a SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 visualizations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types; performance benchmarked against data from 485 human participants; analysis includes error categorization.
AI.result: Gemini is the strongest overall, surpassing the human mean on evaluated subsets; open-source models remain below human baseline; performance is highly uneven across techniques (best on illustration, search, spatial understanding; weakest on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and quantitative estimation); error analysis highlights recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation.
AI.conclusion: SciVis literacy should be a key benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems; the authors provide code and outputs publicly for reproducibility.

title: Towards Hierarchical Structure Understanding of Newspaper Images
comment: Accepted at ICDAR 2026 Workshop on Historical Document Imaging and Processing (HIP)
summary: Understanding newspaper images remains a challenging task due to their complex, nested hierarchical structures and dense, heterogeneous layouts. In this paper, we explore two complementary approaches for newspaper structure understanding. First, we present a modular bottom-up pipeline that combines state-of-the-art open-source models: YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order prediction, and a custom algorithm for article segmentation. This approach leverages existing robust components while maintaining flexibility and interpretability. Second, we introduce Tiramisu (Tiered Transformers for Hierarchical Structure Understanding), a novel end-to-end transformer-based architecture that explicitly models document hierarchy through an iterative tiered process. Tiramisu performs section and article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, and reading order prediction using highly parallelized attention mechanisms. Finally, we release Finlam La Liberté, a new dataset designed specifically for evaluating hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches in reconstructing complex newspaper hierarchies, with comparative analysis highlighting their respective strengths for scalable document digitization. The Tiramisu training code, including the synthetic newspaper generator, is available at https://git.litislab.fr/tiramisu/tiramisu-newspaper-articles-extractor.

AI.tldr: Presents two complementary approaches for understanding newspaper structure: a modular bottom-up pipeline combining YOLO, LayoutReader, and a custom article-segmentation algorithm; and Tiramisu, a novel tiered transformer architecture that models document hierarchy end-to-end for sections, articles, blocks, semantics, and reading order; plus a new dataset Finlam La Liberté for hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers; code for Tiramisu and a synthetic generator is released.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of complex, nested newspaper layouts and dense, heterogeneous content by providing flexible, interpretable modular components and an end-to-end model that captures hierarchical structure, enabling scalable digitization and retrieval from historical newspapers.
AI.method: 1) Modular bottom-up pipeline: use YOLO for layout detection, LayoutReader for reading order, and a custom algorithm for article segmentation, enabling flexible integration of robust existing components. 2) Tiramisu (Tiered Transformers for Hierarchical Structure Understanding): an end-to-end transformer architecture that iteratively models document hierarchy—performing section/article separation, block localization, semantic categorization, and reading order prediction via parallel attention mechanisms. 3) Release of Finlam La Liberté dataset designed to evaluate hierarchical information retrieval in historical newspapers. 4) Experimental setup compares the two approaches on hierarchical reconstruction tasks and digitization scalability; code for Tiramisu and a synthetic newspaper generator is provided at the listed URL.
AI.result: Both approaches are shown to effectively reconstruct complex newspaper hierarchies, with the modular pipeline offering flexibility and interpretability via robust components, and Tiramisu delivering end-to-end hierarchical modeling and parallelized attention for faster, scalable processing; the dataset provides a benchmark for historical newspaper hierarchy understanding.
AI.conclusion: The two approaches are complementary and jointly advance scalable, accurate hierarchical information retrieval for historical newspapers. The modular, component-based method affords interpretability and adaptability across layouts, while Tiramisu provides an integrated, high-throughput solution for end-to-end structure understanding. The published Finlam La Liberté dataset and code (including the synthetic newspaper generator) support reproducibility and future research in scalable newspaper digitization.

title: RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models
summary: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely used to model dynamical systems in physics, biology, neuroscience, and physiology, but in many applications some equations of the dynamics are unknown and only a subset of the state variables are measured. We propose a hybrid neural--physics framework in which the known components of the ODE are kept explicit and the missing components are represented by a neural network. The proposed method consists of two stages where we alternate between state and parameter estimation and iterate until a predetermined criterion is met. Specifically, in the first step, we treat the model parameters as being known and we infer the latent states from the available measurements using a Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) smoother. In the second stage, we treat the smoothed trajectories as being known and use them to estimate the neural networks' parameters through backpropagation. We evaluate the method on benchmark systems spanning linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. Across these settings, the proposed method learns missing ODE components from incomplete measurements while exploiting and retaining interpretable mechanistic structure and improving latent-state reconstruction and long-horizon prediction.

AI.tldr: A hybrid neural–physics approach recovers unknown ODE terms under partial observability by alternating RTS-based state estimation with neural-parameter learning for missing dynamics, yielding interpretable models and improved long-horizon predictions.
AI.motivation: Many dynamical systems have unmeasured states or unknown components in their ODEs. A framework that preserves known physics while learning unknown terms from partial data can achieve accurate state reconstruction and predictive power with interpretable structure.
AI.method: Two-stage alternating procedure: (1) treat known ODE terms as fixed and estimate latent states using Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother from partial measurements; (2) fix the smoothed trajectories and train neural networks to represent the missing ODE components via backpropagation. Iterate until a convergence criterion is met. Evaluation on linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics with partial observation.
AI.result: The framework learns the missing ODE components from incomplete measurements, preserves mechanistic interpretability, improves latent-state reconstruction, and enhances long-horizon prediction across benchmark dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid neural–physics framework successfully integrates explicit physics with neural modeling to identify unseen dynamic terms under partial observability, delivering accurate reconstruction and scalable prediction while maintaining interpretable structure.

title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
summary: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators can become infeasible in large benchmark settings, whereas scalable estimators can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences with small or nonnormally distributed model sets. This study identifies when latent trait models reliably support or risk distorting AI benchmarking claims, and what sample sizes and diagnostics are needed for trustworthy use.

AI.tldr: A study examines the reliability of item response theory (IRT) for AI benchmarking, using simulations across six LLM benchmarks, three IRT models, and four estimators to assess feasibility, scalability, and inference reliability; finds classical estimators fail in large settings, scalable estimators yield unreliable results with small/nonnormal model sets, and provides guidance on when to trust IRT and what sample sizes/diagnostics are needed.
AI.motivation: AI benchmarks differ from human testing; regimes have fewer models, many items, and potentially skewed or multimodal ability distributions. This challenges standard IRT tools originally developed for human testing. The work evaluates whether latent trait models can reliably support AI benchmarking claims and under what conditions.
AI.method: Derive item parameters and ability distributions from six widely used LLM benchmarks; simulate response matrices under three standard IRT models; compare four estimation tools (marginal MLE, MCMC, variational inference, neural pseudo-Siamese estimator); execute 18,000 simulation conditions; assess computational feasibility, scalability, and reliability of inferences on model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics.
AI.result: Classical estimators become infeasible in large benchmarks; scalable estimators may produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences when model sets are small or nonnormally distributed; regime mismatch can distort conclusions; the study maps conditions under which latent trait models are trustworthy and outlines required sample sizes and diagnostics for trustworthy use.
AI.conclusion: IRT can aid AI benchmarking but is not universally reliable; careful consideration of data regime, model distribution, and diagnostics is required. The work provides practical guidelines on when to use latent trait models, and what sample sizes and checks ensure trustworthy conclusions.

title: Quantifying Training Membership Information in the Hyperspherical Embedding Geometry of Face Recognition Models
summary: Face recognition models represent each face as an embedding vector on the unit hypersphere by clustering embeddings of the same identity while pushing different identities apart through angular-margin losses. Because these losses act only on training identities, non-member identities may form clusters with different geometric properties. In this paper, we quantify the magnitude of this difference and what training-time factors control it. We compute four statistics based on cluster geometry across 180 face recognition models in a factorial design over IResNet backbone size, loss head, training duration, and the number of training identities, and evaluate each configuration on nine benchmarks. Our results indicate that the number of training identities has the largest effect on member/non-member separability, while backbone and loss head contribute far less, and that, on a same-domain held-out reference, the geometric membership signal decreases monotonically as more identities are added to training. We provide an analysis of cross-domain (pose, age, quality, ethnicity) non-member benchmarks and report that these inflate the apparent membership signal. Finally, we fuse all four statistics with a learned classifier to reveal additional membership information beyond the best individual statistic.

AI.tldr: Factorial study of 180 face-recognition models shows training identity count dominates non-member geometry on the unit hypersphere; cross-domain factors inflate membership signals; a learned fusion classifier improves detection beyond any single metric.
AI.motivation: To quantify how training-time factors shape the geometry of non-member identities in angular-margin face embeddings and to understand cross-domain biases that inflate membership signals.
AI.method: Compute four geometry-based statistics for member vs. non-member clusters across a factorial design (IResNet backbone size, loss head, training duration, number of training identities) over 180 models and evaluate on nine benchmarks; analyze cross-domain non-member benchmarks; fuse the four statistics with a learned classifier.
AI.result: Number of training identities has the largest effect on member/non-member separability; backbone and loss head contribute less; geometric membership signal decreases monotonically with more identities; cross-domain factors inflate membership signal; fusion of statistics with a classifier reveals additional membership information beyond the best individual statistic.
AI.conclusion: Training-time identity count is the primary driver of non-member geometry on the hypersphere; broader domain changes inflate membership signals, which can be mitigated or exploited by combining statistics with a learned classifier to better detect membership.

title: Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized, and that explicit replanning helps make GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.

AI.tldr: Externalizes task plans in a vision-based GUI automation system to enable inspectable, editable, and replannable behavior, improving transparency and repairability.
AI.motivation: Vision-based GUI agents often drift from user intent due to dynamic layouts and opaque internal planning. There is a need for inspectable, editable plans and user supervision to increase trust and controllability.
AI.method: Planner–executor architecture with explicit external plans; replanning as persistent artifacts; editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions; preserves progress during repair; formative study (n=6) and evaluations on failure-case repair and workflow analyses.
AI.result: Visible plans enable structural repair through localized interventions; explicit replanning improves transparency, controllability, and adaptability; Plover supports supervision and progress preservation during repairs.
AI.conclusion: Plan-centric, externally visible replanning enhances transparency and controllability of GUI automation; Plover demonstrates improved repairability and user supervision, with potential for broader applicability and further refinement.

title: AlphaWiSE: Adaptive Weight Interpolation for Continual Multimodal Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal models such as CLIP learn a shared embedding space for cross-modal retrieval, but continual adaptation to sequentially arriving data can disrupt the cross-modal alignment acquired from earlier phases. Conventional continual-learning methods return a single checkpoint, which commits every retrieval direction to the same stability-plasticity trade-off. We propose AlphaWiSE, a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that composes two frozen source checkpoints. For each aligned parameter tensor identified by its checkpoint key, AlphaWiSE fits one scalar interpolation coefficient shared by all tensor entries. The coefficients are fitted on a smaller exemplar memory and used to materialize one interpolated checkpoint. The deployed model has the same architecture and parameter count as either source checkpoint, which does not require additional inference time. Extensive experiments on audio-image-text retrieval show consistent improvements over strong continual-learning baselines across multiple retrieval directions and evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: AlphaWiSE is a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method for continual adaptation of frozen multimodal models (e.g., CLIP). It learns a single scalar coefficient per aligned parameter tensor to interpolate between two source checkpoints using exemplar memory, producing a model with the same architecture and no extra inference cost. Experiments on audio-image-text retrieval show consistent gains over strong continual-learning baselines across directions and metrics.
AI.motivation: Continual adaptation to sequential data can degrade cross-modal alignment learned earlier. Traditional continual-learning methods produce a single fixed checkpoint with a fixed plasticity-stability trade-off, which may not suit all retrieval directions. There is a need for a simple, effective post-hoc method that preserves alignment while enabling adaptation.
AI.method: Identify aligned parameter tensors between two frozen source checkpoints. For each tensor, fit one scalar interpolation coefficient shared across all tensor entries, using a small exemplar memory. Use these coefficients to materialize an interpolated checkpoint. The deployed model has the same architecture and parameter count as either source and requires no additional inference time.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on audio-image-text retrieval tasks shows consistent improvements over strong continual-learning baselines across multiple retrieval directions and evaluation metrics, without increasing inference cost.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight post-hoc interpolation across two frozen sources yields improved continual adaptation for multimodal models, maintaining identical architecture and inference-time performance while achieving better cross-modal alignment under continual data arrival.

title: Data Driven Block Replacement Scheduling
summary: We develop data-driven algorithms for maintaining $N$ independent identical machines under a \textit{block replacement policy}, in which each machine is replaced upon failure and all machines are jointly replaced at regular intervals of length $k$. The goal is to learn the cost-minimizing interval $k^*$ from operational data when the lifetime distribution is unknown. At each decision epoch, the operator selects $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}$, observes the resulting failure history (a mixture of complete and right-censored lifetimes) and incurs a per-unit-time cost governed by the renewal function. We formulate this as a stochastic multi-armed bandit and propose Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based lower-confidence-bound algorithms achieving $O(K \log T)$ regret, matching the Lai--Robbins lower bound. Exploiting a nested observation property unique to block replacement, correlated variants attain $O((K-k^*)\log T)$ regret and require only $O(1)$ direct pulls of suboptimal arms $k < k^*$. A complementary Kaplan--Meier renewal algorithm estimates the lifetime distribution nonparametrically from censored data, achieving almost-sure policy consistency and empirically near-zero incremental regret at long horizons. We additionally analyze two average-cost MDPs: a time-elapsed formulation establishing that block replacement is optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution, and an age-vector formulation proving a monotone threshold structure under increasing failure rate distributions and providing a gold-standard cost benchmark. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical ordering and reveal structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.

AI.tldr: Data-driven learning for block replacement in multi-machine systems minimizes cost over renewal intervals k under unknown lifetimes, via bandit algorithms with regret O(K log T); enhanced results under nested observation; nonparametric Kaplan–Meier estimator; average-cost MDP analyses establishing optimality and monotone thresholds; empirical validation shows structural cost gaps.
AI.motivation: Practical systems replace failed machines periodically but lifetime distributions are unknown and censored. A data-driven policy that learns the best replacement interval from failures and censored data can reduce long-run costs.
AI.method: Model the selection of block length k as a stochastic multi-armed bandit with arms {1,...,K}; observe mixed complete and right-censored lifetimes; apply Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based UCB to obtain lower-confidence bounds and regret bounds. Exploit a nested observation property to obtain improved regret for correlated counterparts. Use Kaplan–Meier renewal algorithm to nonparametrically estimate the lifetime distribution from censored data. Also analyze two average-cost MDP formulations (time-elapsed and age-vector) to justify block replacement optimality within the policy class and to reveal a monotone threshold structure under IFR.
AI.result: Regret bounds: O(K log T) for standard bands; O((K−k*) log T) for correlated variants, with only O(1) pulls of suboptimal arms. Kaplan–Meier renewal estimator yields almost-sure consistency and near-zero incremental regret at long horizons. Time-elapsed MDP shows block replacement optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution; age-vector MDP shows a monotone threshold structure under IFR, providing a benchmark. Empirical results confirm ordering and identify cost gaps between block and age-dependent policies.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven block replacement policies can closely approach optimal performance under unknown lifetimes, with strong theoretical guarantees and practical estimators. Block replacement is robustly competitive; age-dependent policies offer potential improvements in some regimes, supported by structural results and empirical evidence.

title: Self-Evolving Human-Centered Framework for Explainable Depression Symptom Annotation
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Omni-Layer Intelligent Systems (COINS) 2026
summary: Annotation quality is a major bottleneck in building reliable and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) systems for mental health research. In depression-related datasets, labels are often assigned without structured evidence, symptom-level justification, or traceable alignment with the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), limiting both transparency and downstream model interpretability. We propose a self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) that combines large language model (LLM)-assisted labeling with expert verification. The framework is intended to support the construction of explainable, DSM-5-TR-aligned datasets rather than to perform clinical diagnosis. It operates in three stages: candidate evidence selection from textual records, criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and case-level synthesis that produces label-level diagnostic and severity annotations. A dual-memory architecture, composed of Example Memory and Reflection Memory, is designed to internalize expert feedback and iteratively improve future annotations without retraining. We describe this mechanism and leave its evaluation across multiple feedback cycles to future work. In addition to final labels, the framework exports clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories, enabling comprehensive auditability. In a pilot study using expert-reviewed samples, the proposed approach improves annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort.

AI.tldr: A self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework using LLM-assisted labeling for DSM-5-TR-aligned MDD datasets, with a three-stage workflow and dual-memory architecture to enhance explainability, auditability, and consistency; preliminary pilot study suggests improvements, with full-cycle evaluation deferred to future work.
AI.motivation: Remove annotation quality bottlenecks in mental health datasets by ensuring evidence-backed, DSM-5-TR-aligned labels that improve transparency and downstream interpretability of XAI models.
AI.method: Three-stage process: (1) candidate evidence selection from textual records, (2) criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, (3) case-level synthesis producing label-level diagnostic and severity annotations. It combines LLM-assisted labeling with expert verification and uses a dual-memory architecture (Example Memory and Reflection Memory) to internalize expert feedback without retraining. Outputs include clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories for auditability.
AI.result: Pilot study on expert-reviewed samples reports improved annotation consistency and explainability, with reduced manual revision effort. Formal evaluation across multiple feedback cycles remains for future work.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers DSM-5-TR-aligned, explainable annotation for MDD datasets and auditability, enabling more transparent XAI research in mental health. Future work will assess robustness across feedback cycles and quantify gains in consistency and efficiency.

title: QuReC: All-in-One Image Restoration with Query-Specific Guidance and Local-Global Response Calibration
summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images degraded by multiple corruption types using a single unified model. Existing methods typically rely on image-level prompts or shared guidance to handle diverse degradations. However, such a paradigm becomes inadequate when degradations are spatially heterogeneous or even coexist in mixed forms within a single image. Yet spatially adaptive guidance alone is not sufficient, since accurate restoration also requires each spatial query to reliably aggregate complementary information from local neighborhoods and global contexts. To this end, we propose QuReC, a unified framework for all-in-one image restoration. QuReC consists of a Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) and a Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM). Specifically, DQRM matches each spatial query against a degradation prototype space to reconstruct a query-specific degradation-aware representation, thereby providing fine-grained spatially adaptive restoration guidance. To further stabilize this query-wise matching process, we introduce a weakly supervised prototype matching learning strategy to improve optimization stability and degradation semantic consistency. Meanwhile, LGRCM performs local-global dual-branch aggregation and calibrates the aggregated responses with learnable priors, improving the reliability of feature aggregation and the coordination between local detail modeling and global context modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that QuReC achieves superior performance on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks. The code is released at https://github.com/zhoushen1/QuReC.

AI.tldr: QuReC introduces a degradation-guided query reconstruction and local-global response calibration framework for all-in-one image restoration, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing image-level prompts and shared guidance fail to handle spatially heterogeneous degradations and mixed forms; restoration requires query-specific degradation-aware representations and reliable local-global context aggregation.
AI.method: QuReC comprises two modules: (1) Degradation-Guided Query Reconstruction Module (DQRM) that matches spatial queries to a degradation prototype space to build degradation-aware representations, aided by a weakly supervised prototype matching strategy for optimization stability and semantic consistency; (2) Local-Global Response Calibration Module (LGRCM) that performs local-global dual-branch aggregation and calibrates responses with learnable priors to improve reliability of feature aggregation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that QuReC achieves superior performance on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: QuReC provides a unified framework that effectively handles spatially heterogeneous degradations and coordinates local detail modeling with global context, achieving state-of-the-art restoration performance; the code is released at the provided GitHub URL.

title: Mutable Low-Rank Sketches for Retrain-Free Recommendation
summary: A common bottleneck in two-stage recommendation is embedding staleness: when a user rates a new item, their embedding remains fixed until the next retrain cycle. We propose mutable sketches, which store each user's preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as ratings arrive. We prove that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope (Theorem 1), a guarantee that FunkSVD and eALS lack. On KuaiRec, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%, with 8x faster per-batch updates. A new user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after their first rating, with no model retraining required. A comparison of sampling strategies across density regimes shows that the KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density), while uniform sampling suffices on dense matrices.

AI.tldr: Mutable KP-tree sketches enable on-the-fly user embedding updates in two-stage recommenders, delivering faster updates and improved accuracy with a monotone error-tightening guarantee.
AI.motivation: Mitigate embedding staleness in two-stage recommender systems by enabling dynamic, per-rating updates without full retraining, and provide theoretical guarantees on error tightening (Theorem 1).
AI.method: Represent user preferences with a KP-tree (sparse segment tree with sum aggregation); fit a low-rank projection once; recompute embeddings online as ratings arrive; prove monotone tightening of the prediction error envelope; evaluate sampling strategies across density regimes; compare to FunkSVD/eALS.
AI.result: Experimental results on KuaiRec show RMSE 0.810 with only 1.8% data read vs ALS 0.822 at 100% data read and 8x faster per-batch updates. New user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after first rating with no retraining. Norm-proportional sampling yields 40–130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density); uniform sampling suffices for dense matrices.
AI.conclusion: Mutable sketches enable real-time personalization with no retraining, delivering accuracy and efficiency gains; sampling strategy should be chosen based on data density.

title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. Building on the CD/PD separability, we propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. PRISM achieves 86.2--87.7\% accuracy on SafeAgentBench with 11.7--13.7\% FPR, while same-scale LLM judges over-block safe tasks at 24.7--39.0\% FPR. We further introduce PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a contrastive benchmark of 1{,}000 physical-risk pairs without direct harm keywords, to test whether methods detect physically grounded danger rather than explicit unsafe wording. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6\% accuracy and 0.7\% FPR, whereas a Qwen2.5-3B judge rejects 67.8\% of safe tasks. PRISM also replicates on SafeText and EARBench, supporting hidden-state probing as a representation-level method for physical safety beyond text moderation.

AI.tldr: CD and PD are separable in LLM representations; PRISM is an effective hidden-state probe for physical danger with high accuracy and low FPR; introduces PSB-1K benchmark; shows representation-level safety detection generalizes beyond text moderation.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether physically grounded danger is the same as ordinary text danger and whether separable signals exist; propose a representation-level safety probe for physical danger and validate across models and benchmarks.
AI.method: Hidden-state direction analysis; random-split null tests; train a one-layer L2-regularized logistic regression over full hidden states (PRISM); evaluate on multiple LLMs; create PSB-1K contrastive benchmark; compare to text-based judges; replicate on SafeText and EARBench.
AI.result: CD and PD form separable signals. PRISM achieves 86.2–87.7% accuracy with 11.7–13.7% FPR on SafeAgentBench; standard LLM judges block 24.7–39.0% of safe tasks (higher FPR). On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6% accuracy and 0.7% FPR; a Qwen judge rejects 67.8% of safe tasks. Replicates on SafeText and EARBench.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-state probing is a viable representation-level approach for physical safety beyond text moderation; PRISM demonstrates strong performance and PSB-1K provides a robust benchmark for physically grounded danger detection.

title: DAPGNet: Dynamic Adaptive Physics-Guided Graph Diffusion Network for Hyperspectral Image Classification
comment: 9 figures and 9 tables. Pengkun Wang and Weijia Cao contributed equally to this work
summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires reliable pixel-relation modeling under spectral variability, mixed pixels, and heterogeneous boundaries. Existing graph-based HSI classifiers usually construct graph topology from spatial proximity, superpixel connectivity, or learned feature affinity. However, the spectral physical prior carried by contiguous bands has limited influence on topology estimation and message propagation. This paper presents DAPGNet, a dynamic adaptive physics-guided graph diffusion network that injects a structure-constrained physical prior into relation-level graph learning. DAPGNet first encodes contiguous spectral responses into node-wise multiscale physical-prior representations. A two-stage graph constructor then combines spectral-spatial affinity, physical-prior consistency, and spatial distance to form a physical-prior-aware sparse topology. During graph diffusion, learned edge weights are transformed into additive attention biases, while a physical gate performs node-wise and feature-wise interpolation between graph-aggregated features and projected physical-prior features. Cross-scale fusion integrates node states from different diffusion depths, and the network is optimized with main classification, auxiliary supervision, and second-order spectral smoothness regularization. Experiments on Indian Pines, WHU-Hi-LongKou, Houston2013, and Houston2018 show that DAPGNet achieves the best OA, AA, and Kappa among representative CNN-, Transformer-, Mamba-, and graph-based baselines. It improves AA over the strongest competing method by 3.64 to 7.31 percentage points across the four datasets. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further support the complementary effects of physical-prior extraction, prior-aware topology construction, physics-gated propagation, and spectral smoothness regularization.

AI.tldr: Proposes DAPGNet, a dynamic adaptive physics-guided graph diffusion network for hyperspectral image classification that leverages contiguous spectral priors to guide topology and propagation, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: HSI classification suffers from spectral variability, mixed pixels, and heterogeneous boundaries; existing graph methods underutilize the spectral physics across contiguous bands; there is a need to encode physical priors into graph topology and diffusion to improve relation learning.
AI.method: Encode contiguous spectral responses into node-wise multiscale physical-prior representations. A two-stage graph constructor combines spectral-spatial affinity, physical-prior consistency, and spatial distance to form a physical-prior-aware sparse topology. During graph diffusion, learned edge weights are transformed into additive attention biases, while a physical gate performs node-wise and feature-wise interpolation between graph-aggregated features and projected physical-prior features. Cross-scale fusion integrates node states from different diffusion depths. The network is optimized with main classification, auxiliary supervision, and second-order spectral smoothness regularization.
AI.result: Experiments on Indian Pines, WHU-Hi-LongKou, Houston2013, and Houston2018 show DAPGNet achieves the best OA, AA, and Kappa among representative CNN-, Transformer-, Mamba-, and graph-based baselines. It improves AA over the strongest competing method by 3.64 to 7.31 percentage points across the four datasets. Ablation and sensitivity analyses support the complementary effects of physical-prior extraction, prior-aware topology construction, physics-gated propagation, and spectral smoothness regularization.
AI.conclusion: The physics-guided graph diffusion with physical priors (DAPGNet) effectively leverages spectral priors to improve HSI classification, delivering state-of-the-art performance and robust ablation-supported insights.

title: Decoding Market Emotion from Blockchain Activity: A Data-Driven Sentiment Classifier
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC 2026)
summary: The growing use of Bitcoin as a decentralized digital asset and investment tool has sparked strong interest in understanding its market behavior. This study presents a new approach to analyze Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain and financial data with social media posts. Unlike models that aim to predict prices, this work focuses on explaining market sentiment using blockchain transactions, historical price data of Bitcoin, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications. The method merges sentiment trends with on-chain and financial metrics, normalized into a dataset for detailed market analysis. Multiple machine learning models were tested using cross-validation, with Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) emerging as the most reliable model for classifying sentiment, achieving an average F1-score of about 0.84. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a game theory-based method for model interpretability, was used to quantify the contribution of on-chain features to the model's predictions, improving transparency. The results indicate that this data combination yields meaningful predictive signals and insights, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and future improvements with deep learning.

AI.tldr: A data-driven framework to explain Bitcoin market sentiment by fusing on-chain, price, and Twitter sentiment data; XGBoost yields a robust F1 ~0.84; SHAP explains feature contributions; suggests usefulness for crypto analysis and potential deep learning upgrades.
AI.motivation: Explain market sentiment using diverse data sources rather than directly predicting price; increase transparency and interpretability in crypto analytics.
AI.method: Construct a normalized dataset combining on-chain metrics, historical Bitcoin prices, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications; compare multiple ML models with cross-validation; identify XGBoost as best; use SHAP to quantify on-chain feature contributions.
AI.result: XGBoost achieved average F1 ~0.84 for sentiment classification; SHAP analysis provides feature-level interpretations; data fusion yields meaningful signals and insights.
AI.conclusion: The integrated on-chain, price, and social data pipeline supports data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and lays groundwork for enhancements with deep learning.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
summary: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

AI.tldr: AutoSynthesis is an end-to-end multi-agent system that automates quantitative evidence synthesis (meta-analysis), from search to report, showing results comparable to manual analyses and enabling scalability.
AI.motivation: Quantitative evidence synthesis is essential but mostly manual and hard to scale; automation is needed to improve efficiency, consistency, and reproducibility across disciplines.
AI.method: An end-to-end multi-agent system that formulates search strategies, retrieves literature, screens eligibility, extracts statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, performs random-effects meta-analysis, analyzes heterogeneity across moderators, assesses risk of bias, and outputs a PRISMA-aligned transparent report.
AI.result: Applied to 28 studies with >20 quantitative claims extracted; pooled effect estimates were similar to Hedges' g from expert meta-analyses, indicating strong concordance with manual syntheses.
AI.conclusion: AutoSynthesis demonstrates scalability and reliability of automated quantitative evidence synthesis, supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

title: Ray-based phase error correction for miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP under single-directional hyperbolic projection
summary: Fringe Projection Profilometry (FPP) systems using miniaturized DOE pro-jectors often suffer from severe phase artifacts due to nonlinear projection characteristics and limited pattern controllability. We propose a ray-based phase error correction framework that models phase artifacts along projection rays from the projector pinhole, incorporating projector geometry without re-lying on image-domain processing or neighboring pixels. A projector pinhole estimation method based on a single-directional hyperbolic fringe pattern is introduced, through which projector geometry can be recovered without stereo calibration. In addition, a data-efficient strategy constructs the re-finement model from a single calibration pose. Experiments on miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP systems demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection conditions, confirming the robustness and physical consistency of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Ray-based phase error correction for fringe projection profilometry with miniaturized DOE projectors, modeling artifacts along projection rays, estimating projector geometry from a single hyperbolic fringe, and building a data-efficient refinement from a single pose; results show improved reconstruction under nonlinear projection.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear projection characteristics and limited pattern controllability in compact DOE projectors cause significant phase artifacts in FPP, necessitating a physically grounded correction that does not rely on image-domain processing.
AI.method: A ray-based model of phase errors along projector rays from the pinhole incorporating projector geometry; projector pinhole estimation using a single-directional hyperbolic fringe to recover geometry without stereo calibration; a data-efficient refinement model constructed from a single calibration pose.
AI.result: Experiments on miniaturized DOE projector-based FPP demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy under nonlinear projection, indicating robustness and physical consistency of the approach.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a physics-informed, geometry-based correction for phase artifacts in compact FPP systems, reducing calibration burdens by enabling pose-derived geometry and single-pose refinement.

title: teLLMe Why (Ain't Nothing but a Jam): Exploratory Causal Analysis of Urban Driving Data
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on UrbanAI. 6 pages
summary: Traffic agencies now have access to large volumes of video-derived data for studying safety and congestion. Most of these data are observational and collected without interventions, which makes causal questions such as "How would rain change traffic density?" difficult to answer. We present teLLMe, a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets. The system starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations and combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, enabling users to specify treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. teLLMe returns a "Causal Card" that summarizes effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, followed by a short natural-language explanation. Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show that the system can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit. The system is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than a source of definitive causal claims.

AI.tldr: teLLMe enables exploratory causal analysis of urban driving data by building a structured event table, applying PC-based causal structure learning with bootstrap stability, and estimating effects via DoWhy; an LLM maps natural-language questions to causal queries, yielding Causal Cards for hypothesis generation rather than definitive claims.
AI.motivation: Observational dashcam data are abundant, but answering causal questions (e.g., rain vs traffic density) is difficult due to hidden confounding; a user-guided system is needed to surface plausible causal relationships with explicit uncertainty and assumptions.
AI.method: From annotations, build event table; perform causal structure learning with PC algorithm; bootstrap-based stability checks; estimate effects with linear regression and DoWhy; map NL questions to structured causal queries via a schema-aware LLM; produce Causal Cards including adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, plus brief NL explanation.
AI.result: Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show plausible relationships among weather, peak hours, and traffic density; surface uncertainty and modeling choices; system supports hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than definitive claims.
AI.conclusion: teLLMe is a hypothesis-generation tool that aids expert causal reasoning; emphasizes transparency about uncertainty and modeling choices.

title: MAGiSt3R: Multi-Agent Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction from Monocular RGB Videos
summary: This paper presents MAGiSt3R, a multi-agent 3D reconstruction framework performing reconstruction and camera tracking for monocular RGB videos at almost 10 FPS. MAGiSt3R relies on a feed-forward model from the 3R family to process RGB videos and regress local point maps, and on a merging model, MAGMA, that combines local maps at both intra-agent and inter-agent levels to obtain the final global point map. Furthermore, MAGiSt3R performs pose graph optimization to mitigate cumulative camera drift occurring along the feed-forward pipeline. We evaluate MAGiSt3R on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior reconstruction and camera tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent 3D reconstruction for monocular RGB videos at ~10 FPS, using local map regression (3R-like) plus MAGMA map merging and pose graph optimization to reduce drift; evaluated on synthetic and real data with superior accuracy vs. state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of accurate, real-time 3D reconstruction from monocular multi-agent video streams, where drift and scale ambiguity hinder reliability and real-time performance is desired.
AI.method: A feed-forward local map regressor from the 3R family produces local point maps; MAGMA merges local maps at intra-agent and inter-agent levels to build a global map; pose-graph optimization mitigates cumulative drift in the feed-forward pipeline.
AI.result: Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show superior reconstruction and camera-tracking accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, with near-real-time performance (~10 FPS).
AI.conclusion: MAGiSt3R delivers accurate, real-time multi-agent 3D reconstruction from monocular video with drift mitigation, demonstrated across diverse datasets.

title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to improve utilization and throughput. To schedule and control the execution of search agents, SearchOS introduces a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model and tool interactions to record grounded evidence and react to stalls or budget exhaustion, and provides a reusable hierarchical skill system comprising strategy and access skills to augment the agents' search process and avoid repeating failed search patterns across runs. On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS leads all metrics among the evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines, paving the way toward robust information-seeking collaboration.

AI.tldr: SearchOS introduces a system-level, stateful, multi-agent framework for robust tool-integrated information seeking, outperforming baselines by externalizing search progress and using pipeline-parallel scheduling with grounded evidence.
AI.motivation: Interaction histories in web-search agents distort progress tracking, causing loops and wasted budgets. Explicit, persistent state and collaborative coordination are needed to improve information-seeking quality and completeness.
AI.method: Formulates open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations. Develops SOCM (Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, Failure Memory) to externalize evolving state. Implements pipeline-parallel scheduling, Search Tool Middleware Harness, and a hierarchical skill system (strategy and access skills) to manage sub-agent execution and avoid repeating failed patterns. Evaluates on WideSearch and GISA against baselines.
AI.result: SearchOS achieves leading performance across evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines on WideSearch and GISA, demonstrating improved utilization, throughput, and robustness in information-seeking tasks.
AI.conclusion: A practical, scalable framework that externalizes search progress, ties evidence to sources, and provides reusable coordination techniques to reduce search inefficiency and enhance collaborative information seeking.

title: Symbal: Detecting Systematic Misalignments in Model-Generated Captions
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often introduce errors when generating image captions, resulting in misaligned image-text pairs. Our work focuses on a class of captioning errors that we refer to as systematic misalignments, where a recurring error in MLLM-generated captions is closely associated with the presence of a specific visual feature in the paired image. Given a vision-language dataset with MLLM-generated captions, our aim in this work is to detect such errors, a task we refer to as systematic misalignment detection. As our first key contribution, we present Symbal, which utilizes a structured, dual-stage setup with off-the-shelf foundation models to identify systematic misalignments and summarize results in natural language. As our second key contribution, we introduce SymbalBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate automated methods on our proposed task. SymbalBench consists of 1.7 million image-text pairs from two domains (natural and medical images), organized into 420 vision-language datasets with annotated systematic misalignments. Symbal exhibits strong performance on this benchmark, correctly identifying systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets, a nearly 4x improvement over the closest baseline. We supplement our evaluations on SymbalBench with real-world evaluations, showing that (1) Symbal can accurately surface systematic misalignments in captions generated by four MLLMs and (2) Symbal is a powerful tool for auditing off-the-shelf image-caption datasets. Ultimately, our novel task, method, and benchmark can aid users with auditing MLLM-generated captions and identifying critical errors, without requiring access to the underlying MLLM. Code is available at https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/Symbal.

AI.tldr: Symbal detects systematic misalignments in MLLM captions using a dual-stage pipeline with off-the-shelf foundation models; introduces SymbalBench benchmark (1.7M image-text pairs across natural and medical domains, 420 datasets) and reports 63.8% dataset-level accuracy (≈4x better than baselines); code available.
AI.motivation: Misalignments in image captions by multimodal LLMs can be systematic and tied to specific visual features. Automated detection is needed to audit captions without full access to the LLMs.
AI.method: A structured, dual-stage pipeline (Symbal) leveraging off-the-shelf foundation models to detect systematic misalignments and summarize results in natural language; creation of a large-scale benchmark (SymbalBench) with annotated systematic misalignments.
AI.result: Symbal achieves 63.8% accuracy in identifying systematic misalignments across 420 datasets on SymbalBench, about 4x improvement over the closest baseline; real-world evaluations show Symbal detects misalignments in captions from four MLLMs and is effective for auditing datasets.
